Latest Update: Redistricting battle could spill into 2028

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (944 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Wes Moore, here at the Capitol in January, wants to see his state's congressional map redrawn.
  • The redistricting fights that underscored this year’s battle for the House could continue into the 2028 election cycle, although lessons from last Tuesday will likely shape those efforts.
  • In a recent development, house Republicans had hoped that newly introduced congressional maps in seven states would help them limit losses in the face of an unfavorable political environment.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Maryland Gov. Wes Moore, here at the Capitol in January, wants to see his state's congressional map redrawn. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

The redistricting fights that underscored this year’s battle for the House could continue into the 2028 election cycle, although lessons from last Tuesday will likely shape those efforts.

In a recent development, house Republicans had hoped that newly introduced congressional maps in seven states would help them limit losses in the face of an unfavorable political environment. But nearly a week after the election, the GOP appeared on track to flip just three redrawn seats while losing a host of seats in Texas, Florida, North Carolina, Ohio and Alabama that were reconfigured in their favor.

“The question is whether the results have let some air out of the [redistricting] balloon or not,” remarked Erik Nisbet, a professor at Northwestern University’s School of Communication.

It has been revealed that republicans may question the utility of redrawing more state maps in the 2028 cycle, while Democrats will need to weigh how to spend their political capital. But the fresh lines approved over the past year could still prove more favorable for Republicans in future elections.

“This was a wave election, and there’s no guarantee that the Democratic generic ballot would be D+13 — which is the reason why redistricting didn’t work for Republicans — in the next cycle,” Nisbet added.

Upcoming maps appear possible, if not likely, in at least a few states. Maryland voters last week approved an amendment that would clear the way for new boundaries ahead of the 2028 elections. Democratic Gov. Wes Moore, who easily won a second term last week, mentioned he hopes to see a new map, citing the threat of President Donald Trump continuing to push for friendlier lines in GOP-led states. Maryland Democrats could draw a map that would favor them in all eight of the state’s House seats, including the Eastern Shore district of Rep. Andy Harris, the state’s lone Republican in Congress.

Advocates for a fresh map in Wisconsin got a boost last week when Democrats flipped both the state House and state Senate, setting up a Democratic trifecta. Gov.-elect David Crowley remarked he would sign a bill redrawing the state’s congressional map if legislators sent one to his desk.

Republicans in recent years have had a lopsided edge in the congressional delegation for Wisconsin, a perennial battleground state. But Democrats flipped two House seats last week, with Rebecca Cooke and Mitchell Berman unseating GOP Reps. Derrick Van Orden and Bryan Steil, respectively, bringing the state delegation to an even 4-4.

Democrats could also look to redraw the lines in New York and Virginia. Earlier this year, voters in the commonwealth approved a new map that would have given Democrats up to four pickup opportunities, but the Virginia Supreme Court later struck it down on procedural grounds. Even without the new map, Democrats flipped two House seats in Virginia last week and came within 2 points of flipping a third.

Democrats in Upcoming York, meanwhile, took initial steps toward mid-decade redistricting earlier this year, but 2028 is the earliest they could hold elections under a new map.

On the Republican side, several states have been mentioned as candidates for new maps in 2028.

Officials in GOP-led Mississippi have held hearings this year on redistricting, which could target Democratic Rep. Bennie Thompson. Republicans are also aiming to redraw the state’s legislative lines ahead of next year’s off-year elections.

In a recent development, it’s not clear whether states that were unsuccessful in redrawing their district lines for 2026 will try again when their legislatures convene next year. Republicans in both South Carolina and Indiana fell short in their push to pass newly introduced maps and could decide to revisit the issue. But Democrats flipped a House seat in each state last week, and some Republican incumbents won reelection by narrower margins than usual. Still, Republicans maintained their legislative majorities in both states, though Democrats broke their supermajorities in the South Carolina and Indiana state houses.

An analysis by DecisionDeskHQ offers a potential warning sign for Republicans in the Palmetto and Hoosier states: Under the GOP-drawn maps that were not adopted for 2026, Democrats could have flipped even more seats last week.

Redistricting appears off the table in a handful of states where latest maps for 2028 had once been considered possible.

Georgia’s outgoing Republican governor, Brian Kemp, said last week that he would not call a special session to address redistricting before the end of the year, after Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms was elected to succeed him.

There were no House flips in the Peach State in the midterm elections, though several Republicans won by closer-than-anticipated margins.

In New Jersey, Democratic Gov. Mikie Sherrill told the New Jersey Globe that she also did not “see a path forward for redistricting right now.”.

Industry observers note that democrats flipped two House seats in the Garden State last week. Navy veteran Rebecca Bennett defeated Republican Rep. Thomas H. Kean Jr., while Cape May Mayor Zack Mullock scored a surprise win over GOP Rep. Jeff Van Drew.

With their latest majorities in Washington, Democrats could propose legislation to ban partisan gerrymandering.

That’s something John Bisognano, the president of the National Democratic Redistricting Committee, anticipates happening, but he mentioned Democrat-led states should be prepared to respond to fresh maps drawn in Republican-controlled ones.

“If they are going to continue to take those actions, Democrats in states across the country need to be prepared to respond, and we, of course, now have significantly more opportunities than we did before Tuesday to respond to those states,” he noted.

Most transgender youth satisfied after choosing hormone therapy

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that this is a human-written story voiced by AI.
  • An overwhelming percentage of transgender and gender diverse young people in the United States express satisfaction with gender-affirming hormone therapy.
  • It has been revealed that almost 400 transgender and gender diverse young people reflected on their decision to take hormone therapy in the largest such survey to date.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that this is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

An overwhelming percentage of transgender and gender diverse young people in the United States express satisfaction with gender-affirming hormone therapy.

It has been revealed that almost 400 transgender and gender diverse young people reflected on their decision to take hormone therapy in the largest such survey to date. Nearly 97 percent affirmed it was the right decision, researchers report November 9 in JAMA Pediatrics. Only about 3 percent, or 10 individuals, stated they regretted the step, and of those, seven felt the experience was harmful.

With concerns around youth well-being fueling limits on gender-affirming hormone therapy, the researchers write, “the results provide further support for the existing standards of care [and] do not support efforts to categorically restrict or ban access.”.

Sources indicate that gender-affirming hormone therapy — with the masculinizing hormone testosterone or the feminizing hormone estrogen — allows a person’s body to better match their gender identity. Around 3 percent of 13- to 17-year-olds in the United States identify as transgender.

Among the study’s 376 young people, who were former patients of a clinic for transgender and gender diverse youth, nearly 92 percent began hormones at 17 or younger. Thirty percent took estrogen and 70 percent took testosterone, with the amount of time since starting the hormones averaging five years.

It has been revealed that as per clinical guidelines for transgender health care, young people interested in medical treatment, joined by parents or guardians, began with an assessment visit with a mental health professional. For the study, participants took a yearly survey, filled out anytime from one month prior to six months following the anniversary of this initial visit. The research team analyzed surveys submitted from 2023 to 2025.

Sources indicate that the new research adds to growing evidence on the benefits of gender-affirming hormone therapy for transgender young people. Gender-affirming hormones improve the alignment these young people experience between their appearance and their gender, increase their satisfaction with life and reduce depression and anxiety.

Recent findings suggest that but state bans have curtailed young people’s access to gender-affirming care, which can include hormone therapy and puberty blockers. As of November 2026 in the United States, 28 states have laws or policies that limit this care, according to the health policy organization KFF. More than half of transgender young people age 13 to 17 reside in states that restrict gender-affirming care. The American Academy of Pediatrics and the Endocrine Society support gender-affirming health care for young people and provide evidence-backed guidelines for treatment.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Bernard Cuillier, chef, restaurateur and longtime culinary leader, passed away on November 1, 2026.

Born in France, Cuillier built a career in international hospitality, with more than four decades of experience in culinary operations, restaurant management and the cruise industry.

After joining The Apollo Group in 1992 as executive chef, he pursued several independent business ventures between 1997 and 2012, including Bistro des Amis, a French restaurant in Houston, Texas.

He later returned to Apollo as culinary director, supporting multiple cruise line clients in culinary concept development, menu innovation, operational standards and crew training.

His assignments included serving as culinary director for the American Queen in 2012 and other new initiatives over the course of the years.

“Bernard was an exceptional culinarian who brought tremendous knowledge, creativity and passion to everything he did,” said Philippe Faucher, senior vice president of The Apollo Group.

“Beyond his culinary achievements, he took great pride in developing others and helping young chefs reach their potential. Having known and worked alongside Bernard for many years, I will remember him not only as an outstanding professional but also as a mentor and dear friend. He will be greatly missed.”.

A recognized World Master Chef, Cuillier was also president of the Académie Nationale de Cuisine’s American chapter (ANC-USA), where he promoted culinary education, professional development and participation in international culinary competitions.

Cuillier is survived by his wife, Marie, his children and his extended family.

NASA's Voyager 1 mission forever changed our view of Jupiter

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (833 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Livescience

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • 18), humanity's most distant spacecraft will hit a upcoming milestone.
  • Industry observers note that while we celebrate this achievement on Earth, Voyager 1 will observe its "light-day" in darkness; mission scientists turned off the probe's camera in 1990, immediately after it snapped its iconic "Pale Blue Dot" and "Solar System Family Portrait" images from beyond the orbit of Neptune.
  • Sources indicate that one of the most significant pieces of Voyager 1's legacy is its trip to Jupiter.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This Wednesday (Nov. 18), humanity's most distant spacecraft will hit a upcoming milestone. NASA's Voyager 1 probe, which has been exploring our solar system at increasingly remote depths since 1977, will reach 16.09 billion miles (25.89 billion kilometers) from Earth — a distance so vast, it takes light 24 hours to traverse the space between Voyager and our planet.

Industry observers note that while we celebrate this achievement on Earth, Voyager 1 will observe its "light-day" in darkness; mission scientists turned off the probe's camera in 1990, immediately after it snapped its iconic "Pale Blue Dot" and "Solar System Family Portrait" images from beyond the orbit of Neptune. But before that, Voyager 1 had already taken tens of thousands of images of our cosmic neighborhood, and some of them totally transformed our understanding of the outer planets.

Sources indicate that one of the most significant pieces of Voyager 1's legacy is its trip to Jupiter. From January to April 1979, the probe observed the solar system's largest planet and several of its giant moons up close, reaching a minimum distance of 174,000 miles (280,000 km) in March 1979, according to NASA. As it approached, Voyager snapped a photo of the gas giant every 96 seconds to create this incredible time-lapse movie of Jupiter's turbulent atmosphere.

A time-lapse animation of Voyager 1 approaching Jupiter over the course of a month in 1979.

Voyager observed discrete bands of Jupiter's atmosphere spinning at various speeds and in different directions, like a cosmic Rubik's Cube being twisted by an invisible hand. Clouds speed by as if on conveyor belts as giant, planet-size storms swirl.

Voyager's time-lapse film captures about 60 full days on Jupiter — the equivalent of about a month on Earth, since each Jupiter day is roughly 10 Earth hours —- providing the most comprehensive and high-resolution look at the planet yet. The observations significantly built on the data captured by NASA's Pioneer 10 and 11 Jupiter probes, which released half a decade prior, showing the planet's atmosphere to be much more dynamic than astronomers realized.

In a recent development, just before making its closest approach to the planet, Voyager spotted something remarkable: Jupiter had a thin, faint ring system. Made primarily of dust, the rings appeared only when Voyager saw Jupiter backlit by the sun. No telescope had ever seen this before, but ground-based observatories soon confirmed the rings' existence, and Voyager 2 took even clearer pictures of the rings when it reached Jupiter in July 1979.

Voyager 1 discovered a thin ring of dust around Jupiter when it was backlit by the sun.

In a recent development, we now know that all four outer planets — Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune — have rings. Today, scientists suspect Jupiter's dusty rings are replenished partially by volcanic eruptions on the planet's volatile moon Io.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Industry observers note that this discovery, too, can be linked to Voyager. While making a close approach to Io, the spacecraft witnessed the first-ever volcanic eruption on a world beyond Earth. This observation showed that moons, not just planets, can be geologically active. In this image, a giant volcano called Loki Patera (the largest volcano on Io, measuring an estimated 125 miles, or 200 km, wide) spews its guts into space.

Voyager 1 witnessed a volcanic eruption (blue) on Io — the first volcaic eruption seen beyond Earth.

It has been revealed that taken together, these observations of Jupiter and its moons demonstrated the largest planet and its moons to be a far more dynamic, complicated and chaotic system than anyone had realized. Moreover, the close-up views of these distant worlds made them more than just dots in the sky. It made them fully realized worlds — places to explore, map and eventually visit. Just this week, China's space agency revealed its intention to send a lander to Jupiter's moon Callisto in the first-ever landing mission to the Jovian system.

Voyager 1's work continues in interstellar space, which it officially reached in 2012. With its camera off, it studies the radiation environment of space using magnetic field and plasma detectors — the last two of its 10 science instruments still receiving power. Scientists suspect the legendary probe will fully run out of power in the 2030s.

  • A draft resolution that Massie read aloud on the House floor on Monday accused Hegseth of eight violations of law or the Constitution, including that he violated the 1973 War Powers Resolution in his prosecution of the Iran war and acted illegally in military campaigns in Venezuela, Yemen, the Caribbean Sea and the eastern Pacific Ocean.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., conducts a news conference outside the Capitol on Monday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

Industry observers note that rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., took to the House floor Monday to unveil a resolution that would impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, and a vote on the glitch could occur by Wednesday.

A draft resolution that Massie read aloud on the House floor on Monday accused Hegseth of eight violations of law or the Constitution, including that he violated the 1973 War Powers Resolution in his prosecution of the Iran war and acted illegally in military campaigns in Venezuela, Yemen, the Caribbean Sea and the eastern Pacific Ocean.

Massie's resolution also charges Hegseth with disregarding protection of civilians in wartime and suppressing the free speech of a U.S. senator.

Massie unveiled his intention to file the resolution as a matter of the privileges of the House.

In a recent development, speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., will now have to rule as to whether the resolution constitutes a proper question of the privileges of the House. There is precedent from prior instances when impeachment was found to be valid as it relates to the House’s constitutionally granted powers.

He must schedule a vote to occur within two legislative days. Assuming that the speaker rules that Massie's resolution is privileged, the House could vote on the resolution itself, or on a motion to table it or refer it to committee.

Industry observers note that if the House were to impeach Hegseth under this process, it would mark a historical anomaly. According to the Congressional Research Service, recent attempts to impeach an official as a matter of the privileges of the House have not resulted in approval of the resolution. In cases in which an official has been impeached, the House has nearly always chosen to conduct an investigation first.

In an interview on Oct. 26, Massie put the chances of his resolution being adopted at 50-50.

In comments to reporters outside the Capitol after his floor remarks, Massie said he suspected some Republicans may back his resolution but he indicated he has neither asked for nor received any such assurances from any of them.

Industry observers note that he predicted there could be some GOP support in the Senate if Hegseth is impeached and it goes to trial. He noted that if the trial does not start until 2027, any Republicans who might vote to convict Hegseth would presumably be joined by most if not all of a more sizeable Senate Democratic caucus.

Massie's odds of success for his resolution may now be greater than his previous 50-50 prediction given the results of the Nov. 3 midterm elections, which gave Democrats control over both chambers in the next Congress — a vote motivated largely by opposition to the Iran war and its inflationary impact.

The questions now are, first, how many House Republicans will defy President Donald Trump and vote to impeach Hegseth; and, secondly, how many incumbents who lost their reelection bids on Nov. 3, a cohort that is disproportionately Republican, might be absent for the impeachment vote?

Massie mentioned some Republicans who lost their reelection bids may feel freer to vote to impeach Hegseth. And he also said Republicans who were reelected and will have to face voters in 2028 may also think about how their vote on an impeachment resolution would reverberate politically.

Recent findings suggest that "It's going to be everybody's conscience, and then they'll have to live with that vote," Massie stated. "And they're going to have to live with that vote two years from now if they're not part of the retirement caucus. And if they were part of the retirement caucus, what do they have to lose?".

Asked why he did not bring articles of impeachment against President Donald Trump, Massie mentioned: "I think the president needs to see one of — this is a metaphor — one of his horses shot out from under him, and then maybe he'll he will see things differently.".

If the House does vote on Massie’s resolution, Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., who is expected to become the House speaker in the next Congress, stated on ABC’s “This Week” on Sunday that he would be a “hard yes” on it.

Hegseth has “got to go,” Jeffries stated. “The so-called secretary of Defense has abused his power, undermined our national security and engineered this reckless and costly war of choice in Iran, which has skyrocketed prices on the American people and made the country less safe.”.

Most if not all House Democrats are expected to agree.

In a recent development, last week, Rep. Adam Smith, D-Wash., the ranking member of the Armed Services Committee and its likely chairman in the next Congress, indicated in an interview with The New Republic that he would support Massie’s impeachment resolution, and he predicted it would be adopted.

Sources indicate that referring to Massie’s measure, Smith said, “By every estimation, it will pass and he will be impeached. And off that goes to the Senate. Then the Senate is legally required to spend all of their time dealing with that until it’s done with.”.

Industry observers note that "Every second Pete Hegseth remains at the top of the Pentagon, our servicemembers are at risk," Rep. Jason Crow, D-Colo., a senior member of the Armed Services Committee, said in a post on X on Sunday.

Sources indicate that also on Monday, Everett B. Kelley, the national president of the American Federation of Government Employees, a union that represents some 820,000 federal and D.C. government employees, sent a letter to House members urging a “yes” vote on Massie's Hegseth impeachment resolution.

The letter cited the risks Kelley mentioned the Iran war has posed to the lives of the Defense Department's uniformed and civilian personnel, and the missive noted Hegseth's stripping of workplace rights and protections for the department's civilians.

"By adopting Rep. Massie’s resolution, the House can begin the long overdue bipartisan effort to reclaim its constitutional powers and authority, restore checks and balances, and take responsibility for the lives of military personnel and civilian employees that Mr. Hegseth’s capricious leadership has jeopardized," Kelley wrote.

Sources indicate that massie announced in mid-September his intention to file an impeachment resolution against Hegseth. But Johnson adjourned the House before the vote would have occurred.

Massie’s upcoming resolution is substantially the same as his earlier one, with the same eight articles of impeachment.

The first three of these alleges that Hegseth’s conduct of the Iran war violated the War Powers Resolution.

Massie's measure indicates Hegseth prosecuted the Iran war without congressional authorization and in the absence of an attack on the United States or an imminent threat.

Further, the measure alleges that Hegseth continued the war despite the House and Senate adopting in June a concurrent war powers resolution calling for the withdrawal of U.S. forces from the fight.

And, the resolution says, Hegseth continued the Iran war after the expiration of the War Powers Resolution’s 60-day termination period and any potential 30-day withdrawal period.

The House has only voted twice to impeach a member of the Cabinet. In 1876, Secretary of War William Belknap was impeached over allegations of corruption, and his abrupt resignation likely contributed to his acquittal in the Senate.

In 2024, the House voted 214-213 to impeach Alejandro Mayorkas, then-secretary of Homeland Security, for “willful and systemic refusal to comply with the law” and “breach of public trust.” The Senate dispensed with the charges without a trial.

#42548. Breaking: Can robots save Earth orbit?

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2454 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Astronomy ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Can robots save Earth orbit?

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2454 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Astronomy

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • There are likely fewer satellites in Earth orbit right now than there will be at any point for the rest of your life.
  • It has been revealed that it’s a sobering thought.
  • One possible solution lies in the emerging satellite-servicing industry — also known as in-space servicing, assembly, and manufacturing (ISAM).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There are likely fewer satellites in Earth orbit right now than there will be at any point for the rest of your life.

It has been revealed that it’s a sobering thought. The threats from our ever-more-crowded skies are well documented: light pollution from megaconstellations, aluminum oxide accumulating in the upper atmosphere as satellites burn up on reentry, and the possibility of a chain reaction of collisions and debris that could render entire orbital regions unusable for generations — to name a few. So what can we do?

One possible solution lies in the emerging satellite-servicing industry — also known as in-space servicing, assembly, and manufacturing (ISAM). Satellites can be refueled, repaired, and repositioned — extending their operational lives and reducing the need to launch replacements. The technology has been demonstrated and the industry is expanding.

But unlocking the potential of this technology will also require a sea change in how space is regulated, experts say. “Servicing needs to go hand in hand with regulation to be effective,” claims Jonas Bahlmann, a doctoral researcher at the University of Luxembourg who studies space sustainability. Some regulations may need to be eased or eliminated, and others created in order to incentivize the industry to tackle the problem. If done right, fresh regulations could create a win-win — slowing the crowding in Earth orbit while boosting the bottom line of the launch providers, but it’s a problem without easy answers.

According to recent reports, the first spacecraft to undergo repair in space was NASA’s Skylab space station, released on May 14, 1973. During launch, the station lost its micrometeoroid shield. Designed to protect the spacecraft from impacts, the shield also shaded Skylab from the Sun. Without the shield, the craft wasn’t habitable for human occupants as internal temperatures could become unbearably high.

On May 25, 1973, NASA sent up the station’s first crew with newly designed hardware to replace the shield. Across a series of spacewalks, the crew installed the nylon and Mylar parasol, successfully completing the first on-orbit repair.

Brian Weeden, who directs commercial space research at the Aerospace Corporation’s Center for Space Policy and Strategy, claims over the decades since, ISAM has gone through three distinct waves.

The first wave rode the space shuttle. Astronauts on a shuttle mission serviced the Solar Maximum Mission in 1984 and, across five shuttle missions between 1993 and 2009, repaired and upgraded the Hubble Space Telescope. Initially, Weeden tells Astronomy, the shuttle was seen “as a vehicle you could reuse; you could do servicing of satellites and [these] kinds of things.” Ultimately “that never really panned out,” he concludes. Each shuttle launch cost $1 billion, two orbiters were lost in the Challenger and Columbia disasters, and the entire program was eventually retired in 2011.

Recent findings suggest that the second wave, which began in the mid-2000s, swapped astronauts for robots. DARPA’s Orbital Express mission showed spacecraft could service each other autonomously. In 2007, the mission’s servicing satellite ASTRO transferred hydrazine fuel and installed a battery for its counterpart satellite NEXTSat while the two were in low-Earth orbit (LEO). Several other experiments followed, like NASA’s Robotic Refueling Missions on the International Space Station (ISS), which demonstrated refueling of satellites not designed for servicing and advanced cryogenic fuel storage across its three phases beginning in 2011. Still, these second-wave missions were more technology demonstrations than a business model.

“But then about 10 years ago, you started to see this … third wave of real interest,” Weeden says. These newly introduced missions draw on three basic servicing tasks — refueling a satellite, repositioning its orbit, and repairing or upgrading its hardware.

In a recent development, virginia-based aerospace and defense contractor Northrop Grumman became the first commercial firm to service a satellite when its Mission Extension Vehicle-1 (MEV-1) rolled out in 2019 to extend the life of an aging communications satellite in geosynchronous Earth orbit (GEO). Rather than transferring propellant, MEV-1 docked directly to the satellite and became its new thruster. MEV-2 followed, docking in 2021 with a similar communications satellite.

Sources indicate that in March 2021, Astroscale — a satellite-servicing organization headquartered in Tokyo — launched ELSA-d, a mission aimed in the other direction: moving a spacecraft lower to speed its reentry for debris removal. ELSA-d demonstrated that a robotic spacecraft could capture an object in orbit, the core capability any debris-removal service depends on. The mission was aborted early due to thruster issues before it could attempt to capture an uncontrolled, tumbling object.

Sources indicate that that same year, Orbit Fab, a satellite-refueling tech giant based in Lafayette, Colorado, introduced Tanker-001 Tenzing: a technology demonstration that they call the first commercial fuel depot in orbit. Tenzing is a small, 77-pound (35 kilograms), microwave-sized satellite that houses a full tank of storable high-test peroxide fuel and Orbit Fab’s proprietary refueling interface, which is known as the Rapidly Attachable Fluid Transfer Interface (RAFTI). Tenzing has not been used to refuel any satellites, but is one step on Orbit Fab’s journey to make in-orbit refueling routine. The company is targeting 2026 for its first refueling missions and envisions an architecture where shuttles deliver fuel from depots like Tenzing to customers in orbit.

According to recent reports, in September 2025, NASA contracted Katalyst Space Technologies, a small robotic-servicing company based in Flagstaff, Arizona, to send its LINK spacecraft to rendezvous with the aging Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory and reposition the X-ray telescope into a higher, safer orbit. The mission launched in July 2026. Unfortunately, the craft experienced control issues after launch, and on Aug. 19, NASA announced the mission would not attempt to capture Swift.

Perhaps the most capable example of a third wave ISAM spacecraft is Northrop Grumman’s Mission Robotic Vehicle (MRV). Launched on July 21 of this year, the spacecraft is billed as a next-generation on-orbit servicing vehicle. It features robotic arms, developed with DARPA funding, that can inspect a malfunctioning satellite, swap components, and install upgrades. It also carries three Mission Extension Pods (MEP) that it can attach to satellites as cheaper alternatives to a full MEV. Once the first three MEPs are deployed, replacements will launch and rendezvous with MRV. A built-in standardized refueling port will ensure MRV can sustain its mission for at least a decade. The spacecraft will arrive in geosynchronous orbit in 2027 to perform its first demonstrations.

Unlike the two waves of on-orbit servicing before it, Weeden says this one hasn’t lost steam. Where earlier eras produced isolated demonstrations, this wave has laid the foundation for an industry that may soon see companies competing and selling ISAM services. A 2026 study led by Igor Levchenko of the University of Milano-Bicocca in Italy and published in the journal npj Space Exploration agrees. They project ISAM turning into a sustained economic sector by 2030.

Recent findings suggest that the study, however, highlights a gap in the industry. So far, projects have been aimed at servicing large, expensive satellites in geosynchronous orbit whose value justifies the cost. But the region with the most pressing concerns about debris, overcrowding, and atmospheric pollution is low Earth orbit — the domain of small, cheap satellites like SpaceX’s Starlink.

SpaceX has handled its debris problem without much need for ISAM. Only two of the roughly 12,000 debuted Starlink satellites have broken apart in orbit, each producing mere tens of tracked debris objects. That debris, states Weeden, will “come down within 20 years.” SpaceX designs Starlink satellites for a five-year lifespan and places them in orbits that decay naturally within five years. This is done in part to comply with a Federal Communications Commission (FCC) rule that mandates operators to deorbit satellites within five years of the end of their mission — a rule intended to keep Earth orbit free of debris. But this same replacement cycle also means burning up satellites every few years, putting more aluminum oxide into the atmosphere.

Recent findings suggest that some forms of satellite servicing in LEO are well within current technological capabilities. But right now, there’s little incentive. Launching a new Starlink satellite is cheaper than servicing an old one, and no regulations are pushing launch providers to do otherwise.

According to recent reports, what’s needed is a change in the rules — but that’s easier noted than done. The U.S. accounts for over half of all annual rocket launches, giving U.S. regulators substantial influence over LEO. Yet U.S. regulations have lagged behind a rapidly growing industry, say analysts. U.S. commercial space activity runs through three federal agencies: the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) licenses launches, the FCC licenses the radio spectrum satellites use, and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) licenses satellites that gather data about Earth from space.

That framework dates to the 1980s, built around the industry as it existed then. Newly emerging sectors have shaken things up. “Satellite servicing [doesn’t] easily fit into those existing three buckets,” Weeden claims. There is no agency explicitly charged with authorizing servicing missions. Lawmakers have been working to enhancement the framework for decades, but progress has been slow. Weeden calls it a wicked problem, a term from public-policy theory for issues with no fixed win condition.

“It’s complex. It’s never-ending,” he says. If left as-is, Weeden warns, the regulatory ambiguity could scare off investors. Made too restrictive, it could delay missions or push companies to relocate.

While U.S. regulations are stalled in the 20th century, other spacefaring nations have taken steps forward. The U.K., Japan, New Zealand, and France have built or are currently building licensing frameworks for servicing missions. If the U.S. were to follow suit and create regulatory clarity for commercial space activity, those new rules could be leveraged toward sustainability efforts — something that’s already happening in Europe. The European Space Agency (ESA) is pushing for an explicit sustainability policy goal — the Zero Debris Approach, which aims to limit new debris in Earth and lunar orbit by 2030.

As a step toward that, ESA has approved Europe’s first debris-removal mission, ClearSpace-1, which is scheduled for a 2029 launch to capture and deorbit a defunct Earth-observation satellite.

Recent findings suggest that but missions like ClearSpace-1 on their own aren’t enough. While deorbiting space junk eases the crowding in LEO, it does so at the atmosphere’s expense. To address the full suite of problems, sustainability experts argue fresh regulations will have to incentivize an entirely new way of doing business in space.

It has been revealed that in space policy and industry circles, people speak of a circular space economy — a concept that reframes spacecraft’s linear life-cycle. “In circular-economy terms,” Bahlmann says, “we … speak of narrowing, slowing, and closing resource loops.” Design satellites to require fewer resources, keep them in service longer, and recover the materials from retired hardware.

The circular space economy is not possible without regulatory reform, Bahlmann notes. In his view, outdated regulations, like the FCC’s five-year deorbit rule, reinforce the linear model.

Bahlmann thinks new regulations should incentivize companies for building satellites with standardized interfaces and modular components that make future servicing possible in the first place rather than restricting them or perpetuating the build, use, dispose status-quo.

According to Bahlmann, this also requires clearer international rules covering who can authorize a mission, who’s liable if something goes wrong, who owns a piece of hardware once it’s dead, and who’s allowed to touch it. Without answers to those questions, Bahlmann notes, “it will be difficult to develop a circular space economy if technically serviceable hardware cannot legally be touched.”.

A 2025 study published in Journal of Spacecraft and Rockets found, using game theory, that removing dangerous debris already saves operators more in avoided collision risk and tracking costs than the cleanup itself costs.

Recent findings suggest that the problem is that remediators bear the entire cost while operators keep the savings. The study proposes a regulatory fix — a third-party body collects fees from the operators who benefit and pays out to the companies doing the cleanup — win-win.

According to recent reports, another possibility is implementing a so-called international “orbital-use fee.” In a 2020 study published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, economists modeled what happens if operators paid an annual fee for every satellite they keep in orbit. Each satellite poses a threat to other satellites through the potential cost of a collision — the more satellites launched, the higher that collective cost climbs. The orbital-use fee calculates the dollar value of that risk and charges it back to the operator each year, similar to a carbon tax. This lowers collision risk for everyone. And, the researchers found it could more than quadruple the industry’s long-run value, from around $600 billion to $3 trillion. Another win-win.

These kinds of incentives could also open the door to entirely upcoming ISAM markets. One such example comes from Levchenko’s team. They propose something they call small mission extension vehicles, or SMEVs: cheap, universal, mass-produced servicers built to service many satellites through simple, standardized tasks like swapping interchangeable parts.

Sources indicate that the technology to build SMEVs exists. The problem is cost. SMEVs only make sense if they’re cheaper than replacing satellites. Bringing down costs and making SMEVs a reality could be incentivized through orbital-use fees or other regulatory changes championed by proponents of the circular space economy.

“My impression is that the industry will continue to grow and that we will launch more, not less, year by year,” Bahlmann notes. In fact, new regulations put in place to incentivize servicing over disposal may encourage operators to launch more satellites. Bahlmann offers increases in fuel efficiency as an analogy: “Driving becomes cheaper per kilometer, which can encourage people to drive more and partially offset the expected savings.”.

Industry observers note that but he believes growth and sustainability can coexist. “The circular space economy is not about degrowth, but about enabling growth in a way that creates economic and social value without compromising the environment,” says Bahlmann. The question, he adds, is what that growth looks like. “Without the right design choices and incentives, more efficient services could simply enable more activity and ultimately add to congestion rather than help us avoid a potentially catastrophic outcome.”.

Industry observers note that wicked as the problem may be, something’s got to give. Bahlmann puts it plainly: “For a long time, the linear approach worked well. We did not have to think much about debris. But it is becoming increasingly clear that we cannot continue like this forever.”.

In a recent development, brooks Mendenhall is a staff writer at Astronomy, based in Chattanooga, Tennessee, fueled by an unending curiosity about the universe. A former classroom teacher, he has a knack for breaking down complex concepts for a wide audience.

We know how to stop computer worms. But what if AI helps them persist?

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1656 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencenews

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This is a human-written story voiced by AI.
  • Industry observers note that AI is already powering fresh, more adaptable forms of cyberattack, but hackers typically wield the technology from afar.
  • Recent findings suggest that recent experiments have demonstrated two different ways this could happen.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

Industry observers note that AI is already powering fresh, more adaptable forms of cyberattack, but hackers typically wield the technology from afar. What if they set the AI models themselves loose to self-replicate and spread in a malicious manner?

Recent findings suggest that recent experiments have demonstrated two different ways this could happen. Two independent teams showed how a cyberattacker could turn an AI model into a “worm,” a type of malware that, unlike a computer virus, spreads on its own. And AI unlocked a upcoming worm power: adapting attacks to different devices.

In a recent development, the results hint at a latest way AI could be used to ramp up cybersecurity threats — not just to computer systems but to smart devices such as security cameras or refrigerators. The good news is that the world still has time to build up defenses as several obstacles remain before this type of malware would work in the real world, says AI researcher Jonas Guan.

AI could indeed make a worm “much harder to stop,” he states, but “there are a lot of kinks to iron out before something like this really works at scale.”.

According to recent reports, here is how a worm cyberattack works. A malware worm squirms through the internet, copying itself onto whatever systems it can hijack. Hackers can then mine hijacked systems directly for their data or link them together into a botnet and use its computing power, often to send spam email or overwhelm websites with traffic, knocking them offline.

Historically, computer worms have been small, simple programs preprogrammed to take advantage of specific security weaknesses. So they could only get into devices that had that weakness. When defenders patched a worm’s target, it could no longer spread. With an AI model directing its actions, however, a worm can adapt and learn on the fly, choosing its line of attack depending on the device, claims Guan, of the University of Toronto.

That adaptability enables the worm to burrow into many different types of devices, both experiments showed. When hackers unleash AI from afar, they orchestrate what the model does. An AI worm that copies itself widely could hypothetically escape anyone’s control.

Still, there’s a caveat to the experiments’ results, notes Michael Alexander Riegler, a cybersecurity researcher at Simula Metropolitan Center for Digital Engineering in Oslo, Norway. Both teams’ test environments made it easier for the AI worm to spread than it would be in the real world, says Riegler, who was not involved in either study.

According to recent reports, and there’s another practical obstacle to the unleashing of AI worms. They use more computing power and take up more space than a conventional worm. The Mirai worm, which took down a slew of websites including Reddit and Spotify in 2016, was a few kilobytes in size, while the medium-sized AI models in the experiments were tens of gigabytes. That’s still way smaller than the massive, top-of-the-line models behind the “rogue AI” incidents that made headlines earlier in 2026. (And those weren’t worms, because they didn’t copy themselves and spread.).

Sources indicate that most devices — including typical laptop computers — don’t have enough space or the right kind of chips to run worm-capable AI models, Guan states. But upcoming versions of devices, such as security cameras, are coming out with advanced hardware for running AI, researchers at the AI firm Anthropic write. And at the same time, even smaller AI models are becoming more capable of sophisticated cyberattacks. These developments could expand the pool of devices an AI worm could exploit.

Sources indicate that “The ingredients are converging” to make AI worms more realistic, Riegler says. How swiftly they will converge is up for debate. Anthropic puts the timeline at months into the future, but both Riegler and Guan say it will probably take longer.

The Mirai worm spread itself through smart devices including home routers, security cameras and even baby monitors. It broke into these devices by trying a small set of common default usernames and passwords. “Just using this very simple technique, this Mirai botnet was able to infect hundreds of thousands of devices,” indicates cybersecurity expert Zane Ma of Oregon State University in Corvallis, who presented an analysis of the attack at a 2017 security symposium. High-profile downed sites such as Reddit were actually collateral damage: A small group of young hackers had created the worm to mess with gaming servers.

Rebooting an infected device cleared Mirai. Changing its default login credentials prevented reinfection through the same route. But an AI-powered worm might make cleaning up this type of cybersecurity breach much more difficult. Why? Because the AI worm acts more like an octopus, Guan notes.

According to recent reports, guan and colleagues tested this octopus-worm in a virtual network. Anchored by several powerful computers that each had a chip called a graphics processing unit, or GPU, the faux networks also contained simulations of smart devices, including office printers and security cameras.

The octopus’s AI model head started on a single machine with a GPU. From there it sent out tentacles to take control of smaller devices. Upon encountering a upcoming device, the head would use AI to proposal how its tentacle could hack in. Often, a hack wouldn’t work, but the octopus wouldn’t give up. It would use info about how it failed to come up with a new hack to try. That ability is “a new, hypercharged way of attacking systems,” Riegler indicates. Whenever it found a computer with a large enough GPU, it would copy its head onto that new machine.

An attacker would probably launch an octopus-style AI worm from the cloud. Click through this slideshow to see how it might spread autonomously. First, it takes over and copies itself onto a device with the right kind of hardware (chip icon) to house an AI model (first image). From there, it sends out tentacles (red arrows) to hack into any connected devices, like 3-D printers and security cameras (second image). Devices that don’t have enough space for the AI model become jumping-off points for the octopus-worm to discover upcoming places to copy itself (third image).

Sources indicate that J. Hirshfeld; adapted from J. Guan et al/arXiv.org, 2026.

The head could also search a simulated internet for information about newly discovered vulnerabilities. (The team didn’t connect it to the real internet for obvious reasons — protection against an AI octopus invasion — and spent considerable effort making sure their creation couldn’t escape the lab, Guan says.).

The octopus-worm even came up with a way to survive a reboot, something Guan says they hadn’t asked it to do. The team posted a preprint of their findings at arXiv.org on June 2, and the paper is now going through peer review.

It has been revealed that meanwhile, at Anthropic, researchers indicated another way an AI worm might work by building on Guan and his colleagues’ research. If an octopus-worm wasn’t weird enough, Anthropic dubbed its creation a “digital slime mold”, a name that captures the model’s slow, oozing behavior. Anthropic declined to comment for this story, but Guan says the company’s work demonstrates that “unlike human reasoning, AI reasoning can be distributed.” That means an AI worm wouldn’t necessarily need to hijack a powerful computer to copy and run itself — it could spread its “thinking” out among smaller devices.

Sources indicate that and that’s exactly what the slime mold version of an AI worm does. It breaks itself up and runs pieces of the model on multiple smaller devices. In their report posted online October 12, the Anthropic researchers used 15 Android smart TVs that they had networked together.

Anthropic’s chopped-up model processes data thousands of times more slowly than what’s possible with GPUs similar to the ones Guan and colleagues relied on. That’s because the model’s data has to travel over internet connections that could take it all around the world during processing, rather than remaining in one place, within chips optimized for AI processing. That pace was too slow to demonstrate an ability to spread like a computer worm, Guan notes. So the Anthropic team ran a separate experiment with an AI worm running on GPUs that highlighted it could spread and adapt its attacks to different kinds of devices.

According to recent reports, whether AI worms are coming in months or whether we have longer to prepare, defenders should get ready now, Guan says. And AI worms do have weaknesses.

It has been revealed that for one thing, the large size of an AI worm could be its downfall. Even if smaller AI models become more capable, these are still significant programs that guzzle computing power. You might not notice if your fridge or microwave suddenly started sending lots of traffic onto the network, but your internet service provider would. They’d realize “there’s something weird going on on these devices,” Ma claims. From there, they could quarantine affected devices, disconnecting them from the internet to prevent further spread.

Recent findings suggest that ma also points out that most smart devices in a person’s home aren’t directly connected to the public internet. Most home networks use a router as a central hub, and that provides a layer of protection against a worm attack.

Strong passwords, regular updates and other normal security measures would also protect against the attacks demonstrated in both experiments, Riegler says.

Guan and some colleagues are now testing specific defenses to stop AI worms, including devising an AI-driven defender. Trying to anticipate emerging threats and protect systems ahead of time is “what I’m passionate about,” Guan says. “We are working on the problem day and night.”.

Voyager 1 reaches 1 light-day from Earth

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (620 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Astronomy

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • 18, Voyager 1 will become the first spacecraft to reach a distance of 1 light-day from Earth.
  • It has been revealed that NASA released the twin Voyager spacecraft in 1977 to tour the giant planets: Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune.
  • Each spacecraft runs on a radioisotope thermoelectric generator, the same kind of power source that drives NASA’s Curiosity and Perseverance rovers on Mars.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

At 5:16 a.m. EST on Wednesday, Nov. 18, Voyager 1 will become the first spacecraft to reach a distance of 1 light-day from Earth. A command radioed from home will need 24 hours to arrive, and a reply another 24 to come back. NASA is asking the public to celebrate by sending the spacecraft a signal on the evening of Tuesday, Nov. 17.

It has been revealed that NASA released the twin Voyager spacecraft in 1977 to tour the giant planets: Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune. Voyager 1 flew past Jupiter and Saturn, while Voyager 2 went on to Uranus and Neptune and is still the only spacecraft to visit either one. Both then kept going. They’re now the only probes ever to study interstellar space directly, the region beyond the Sun’s magnetic field.

Each spacecraft runs on a radioisotope thermoelectric generator, the same kind of power source that drives NASA’s Curiosity and Perseverance rovers on Mars. Plutonium-238, the fuel source, gives off heat as it naturally decays, and the generators turn that heat into electricity. But because the output fades by about 4 watts every year, engineers have spent years shutting off components and instruments to stretch the spacecraft’s lives. This year, a risky maneuver nicknamed the “Major Bang” turned off several devices in one coordinated move to buy the spacecraft and their remaining instruments several more years of operation. Today, Voyager 1 only runs two of its original 10 instruments, and Voyager 2 runs three.

Voyager 1 is closing in on 1 light-day from Earth (about 16.1 billion miles [25.9 billion kilometers]) — farther than any spacecraft has ever gone. Its twin is about 2 billion miles (3.2 billion km) closer to Earth, near enough that a signal takes about 20 hours to reach Voyager 2.

Voyager 1 lifted off Sept. 5, 1977, two weeks after Voyager 2 but on a shorter trajectory as it was traveling to Jupiter. After visiting Saturn in 1980, it drifted away from the solar system’s planets for good. A decade later, it captured the famous photograph of Earth known as the Pale Blue Dot. In August 2012, it became the first spacecraft to enter interstellar space, and Voyager 2 followed in 2018. Voyager 2 won’t reach the light-day mark until November 2035. You can see both missions’ exact locations on NASA’s mission status page.

Recent findings suggest that A light-day is a distance measuring how far light travels in 24 hours. At about 186,000 miles per second (299,792 km per second), that adds up to roughly 16.1 billion miles (25.9 billion km). For scale, the Moon is just 1.3 light-seconds away, the Sun about 8.3 light-minutes, and Neptune a bit over 4 light-hours. Proxima Centauri, the nearest star beyond the Sun, lies more than 1,500 light-days away.

Industry observers note that at a speed of nearly 38,000 mph (61,000 km/h), Voyager 1 is anything but slow. Still, it needed more than 49 years to cover the distance light crosses in a single day.

Astronomy usually asks readers to dim their lights. But tomorrow night is an exception: To celebrate Voyager 1’s accomplishment, NASA invites everyone to flash Voyager’s call sign, V-G-R, skyward in Morse code on Tuesday evening. Use NASA’s automated flasher on your smartphone or tablet. Or grab a plain flashlight and do it manually: V: dot-dot-dot-dash; G: dash-dash-dot; R: dot-dash-dot. Dots are quick blinks of the light, and dashes are long flashes of about a second. Pause between letters.

Brooks Mendenhall is a staff writer at Astronomy, based in Chattanooga, Tennessee, fueled by an unending curiosity about the universe. A former classroom teacher, he has a knack for breaking down complex concepts for a wide audience.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Looking for a sky event this week? Check out our full Sky This Week column.

November 17: Spotlight on the Pleiades.

The peak of the Leonid meteor shower, caused by the dusty debris of Comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle, is best seen early this morning after the Moon has set and the shower’s radiant rises high in the hours before dawn.

Sources indicate that two hours before sunrise, Leo is high in the southeast, with bright Jupiter and Mars joining the curved shape of the Sickle asterism. The Leonids’ radiant is located just inside the cuved blade’s inner edge, near 3rd-magnitude Zeta (ζ) Leonis to the upper left (north) of Mars and Jupiter. The two planets appear roughly side by side in the sky around this time, with ruddy Mars at left and more golden-yellow Jupiter at right. Regulus sits just to their lower left.

In a recent development, to catch the most meteors, you’ll actually want to look a little ways away from Leo, about 40° to 60° to the left or right of the constellation. This is where meteors with the longest trains will also occur. Although this shower isn’t particularly strong, you can expect to see roughly a half-dozen or more Leonid meteors per hour. The Leonid shower produces some of the fastest-moving meteors we experience all year, streaking through the sky at some 44 miles (70 kilometers) per second.

Recent findings suggest that sunrise: 6:49 A.M.Sunset: 4:41 P.M.Moonrise: 1:19 P.M.Moonset: 12:03 A.M.Moon Phase: Waxing gibbous (67%)*Times for sunrise, sunset, moonrise, and moonset are given in local time from 40° N 90° W. The Moon’s illumination is given at 10 P.M. local time from the same location.

Recent findings suggest that the solar system is a dynamic place. Let’s return to the predawn sky on November 19th to check out the inner planets’ progress relative to the stars of Virgo. An hour before sunrise, both Mercury and Venus are again well above the eastern horizon, with the stars around them still visible before twilight brightens too much.

In a recent development, compared with earlier in the week, Venus now sits to the upper left of Spica, rather than directly above it. Venus will pass 1.8° due north of Spica later today at 6 P.M. EST. Now moving steadily east, it will track along the ecliptic, slowly headed for Libra. Mercury has already reached the Balance, sitting within its domain and to the far lower left of Kappa (κ) Virginis, as opposed to the pair’s close proximity a few days ago.

Recent findings suggest that pull out your telescope to see how the planets’ appearances have changed, too. Mercury is now 55% lit and 7” across, while Venus is 18% lit and has shrunk more noticeably, now 47” across.

How the ‘blue tsunami’ crested in North Carolina

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1627 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • North Carolina Rep.-elect LaKesha Womack talks to reporters Sunday at the AC Hotel in Washington as she arrives for newly introduced member orientation.
  • LaKesha Womack faced towering odds as an underfunded Democrat making her first run for public office in a North Carolina district that Donald Trump carried by 15 points two years ago.
  • It has been revealed that but as early voting surged in mid-October, she sensed she might pull off an upset over Republican Rep.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

North Carolina Rep.-elect LaKesha Womack talks to reporters Sunday at the AC Hotel in Washington as she arrives for newly introduced member orientation. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

LaKesha Womack faced towering odds as an underfunded Democrat making her first run for public office in a North Carolina district that Donald Trump carried by 15 points two years ago.

It has been revealed that but as early voting surged in mid-October, she sensed she might pull off an upset over Republican Rep. Tim Moore, the influential former speaker of the North Carolina House and a chief architect of the gerrymander that aimed to keep the 14th District safely red.

“There were a lot of pins and needles,” remarked Womack, a 49-year-old ordained minister who works at a Charlotte-based nonprofit. After seeing long lines at polling places extend into Election Day, she grew more confident: “People were ready to exercise their voice.”.

Womack – who raised less than $60,000 to Moore’s $2.1 million – eked out a 2-point win in the district, which reaches from the Charlotte suburbs to mountain counties in the west.

It has been revealed that saddled with an unpopular president and broad dissatisfaction with the status quo, Republican incumbents across the nation experienced a midterm drubbing last week. As of Monday evening, House Democrats had netted 42 seats, with more races left to be called. The GOP in North Carolina, a state that Trump carried three times, was among the hardest hit.

Democrats have so far flipped five House seats in the Tar Heel State. Besides Womack, the “blue tsunami” also swept in Paul Barringer, a lawyer who founded an outdoor clothing line, and High Point Mayor Cyril Jefferson. And Army veteran Richard Ojeda, who once served in the West Virginia Senate, defeated Rep. Richard Hudson, the chairman of the National Republican Congressional Committee.

Recent findings suggest that democrats also won two races that had been seen as competitive for much of the cycle. Farmer Jamie Ager flipped an open seat in the state’s mountain west, while Rep. Don Davis held on to his Eastern North Carolina district, which Republicans had redrawn in their favor.

Meanwhile, in the state’s hilly northwest corner, 11-term Republican Virginia Foxx, the chairwoman of the powerful Rules Committee, is fighting for her political future: As of Monday afternoon, former journalist Chuck Hubbard led her by 99 votes in the 5th District, though The Associated Press had yet to call the race.

That was also true in the neighboring 10th District, where GOP incumbent Pat Harrigan had a 1-point edge over Democratic physician associate Ashley Bell. Also uncalled were a pair of contests in Eastern North Carolina, where Republican Rep. Greg Murphy clung to a 233-vote edge over Democratic former state Rep. Raymond Smith and GOP Rep. David Rouzer led Democratic social worker Kimberly Hardy by less than a point.

“Nobody could have predicted this,’’ mentioned David Wilson Brown, who leads the Democratic Party in Gaston County near Charlotte and has lost two bids for the House, including to Foxx in 2020. “It’s a watershed moment.”.

The Democratic rout in the midterm elections was powered by victories in states with newly introduced GOP-favored maps, including Texas, Ohio and Florida.

But Democrats’ success in North Carolina was especially striking given the steep structural disadvantages the party faced. Since Republicans flipped the state legislature in 2010, and with it control of the redistricting process, no House GOP incumbent had lost a general election in the Tar Heel State until last week.

This year’s  congressional map – the state's sixth in seven election cycles – was engineered by the Republican-led legislature to help the party capture 11 of the state's 14 House seats.

But the Democratic surge was so big that it easily overpowered the GOP’s built-in edge. Democratic candidates were also lifted by former Gov. Roy Cooper, whose 20-point Senate win provided the underticket with powerful coattails.

According to recent reports, “In order for them to gerrymander our state in the way that they did, they were spread very thin,” Brown stated, referring to state Republicans. “So they were kind of ripe to be defeated that way.”.

The repeated rounds of redistricting may have also erased some of the advantages of incumbency, according to Peter L. Francia, a political science professor at East Carolina University. “If you carve up a district every two years, you've taken away some of that [advantage]. And I think that that came back and hurt Republicans in this cycle.”.

Doug Heye, a GOP strategist and a former spokesman for the Republican National Committee, said redistricting “ticked off a whole lot of voters, and really activated the Democratic base.”.

On the Republican side, voters were “less motivated because they were unexcited about Trump,’’ Heye added.

Republican incumbents accustomed to winning by comfortable margins weren’t prepared for a political environment driven by anger over the war in Iran and angst about the rising cost of living.

Industry observers note that “Clearly, a lot of those Republicans didn’t take their elections seriously,” Heye said. “They won last time with 18 points. They weren't on anyone's radar screen, so they didn't think they had to do anything.”.

Womack credits her win to a grassroots campaign centered on economic concerns. While her race wasn’t on the national radar – Moore, after all, won by 16 points in 2024 – and her campaign didn’t have money for ads, she was out in the district doing events every day.

Recent findings suggest that “There are a lot of working families right now who are in the missing middle,” she remarked in an interview. “They make too much money to get help, but they don't make enough money to get ahead. … Someone who can be working a full-time job, but still doesn’t have enough money to buy groceries or to afford their medications or to have access to health insurance.”.

It has been revealed that womack mentioned her own struggles have shaped her approach to politics. This week, she’s slated to appear in court on a felony charge for allegedly failing to return a rental car in 2019. The incident wound up in one of Moore’s attack ads.

“There are so many people who [understand] what happens when you're down on your luck and you don't have enough money to make good financial decisions,’’ she mentioned. “Most people don't want those bad decisions to be a definition of their character for the rest of their life.”.

Early in the midterm cycle, Democratic opposition research group American Bridge prepared detailed dossiers on Republican House incumbents in North Carolina.

It has been revealed that “Someone like Virginia Foxx, she’s been on the Hill forever,” said Pat Dennis, the group’s president. “She was somebody … who under the radar could be vulnerable. So we started really early.”.

American Bridge’s political arm spent $340,000 on ads targeting Foxx. One spot featured a man who identified himself as a Trump voter expressing anger at the government’s response to Hurricane Helene, which devastated the mountain communities of Western North Carolina two years ago.

Other Democrats scoffed at the group’s decision to spend money targeting entrenched Republicans far from the main House battleground.

Sources indicate that “There was a lot of reluctance from people to really believe that that data was correct, but it was,’’ Dennis said. “Then over the summer, we saw her numbers collapsing, so we put paid media behind it and it really paid off.”.

Hubbard ran against Foxx two years ago and lost by almost 20 points.

Recent findings suggest that “I kind of had a notion I was going to do this again,’’ he said in an interview Saturday while en route to Washington for freshman orientation. “I don’t like to lose at checkers, much less a congressional race.”.

After a court-drawn map resulted in a split North Carolina delegation after the 2022 elections, state Republicans won back control of the map-making process and went on to win 10 of the state’s 14 House seats under a upcoming map two years later.

At Trump’s urging, Republicans made further tweaks to the North Carolina map last year, but the original gerrymander finally came back to bite the GOP in 2026, according to Hubbard.

Industry observers note that “North Carolina is one of the most severely gerrymandered states,’’ he mentioned. “And what happened was they had to steal from Peter to pay Paul. It's been referred to by political scientists as a dummymander.”.

As the vote count in the 5th District continues, Foxx, whose campaign declined to comment for this story, has requested the presence of nonpartisan election observers.

They “will serve as vital, watchful eyes to ensure that this sacred process is not impeded and that all legal votes are counted in a consistent, thorough manner,’’ she posted on social media.

But even before the final races are called, Republicans are already looking to the next election.

Recent findings suggest that heye, who expects North Carolina to remain a purple state in 2028 and beyond, cautioned the Democrats who won last week not to get too comfortable in Washington. He invoked Fred Heineman, the former Raleigh police chief who rode the 1994 “Republican Revolution” to Congress – and lasted a single term.

“Some of them will lose, and some of the people who lost may run two years from now and get their seat back,’’ he said.

One GOP operative, who requested anonymity to speak candidly, offered up a similar assessment.

Trump “didn't keep his promises” and that “just got voters very angry and suppressed the GOP base from coming out because, in a midterm election it's a base turnout contest,’’ the strategist said.

“But these Democrats are renting these districts for two years.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, this is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

Many fields of science have struggled under the second Trump administration, with funding cuts and delays plaguing research in fields such as public health and climate science. But some topics have found firmer footing, including artificial intelligence and quantum science.

These technologies, along with supercomputing, “are going to be the three legs of the stool that is going to transform how science and engineering is done,” says Darío Gil, undersecretary for science at the U.S. Department of Energy.

Industry observers note that in November 2025, President Donald Trump issued an executive order to launch the Genesis Mission, a $5 billion whole-of-government effort to advance science via artificial intelligence. The initiative began with the DOE but has since expanded to more than 15 federal agencies.

In June, the president issued an executive order that aims to accelerate the development of tools such as quantum computers, quantum sensors and quantum networks. And in July, the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy issued a 123-page report describing its vision for a “golden age” of federal science, in which agencies align investments in research and development with administration priorities.

Federal agencies spent some $4.2 billion on AI R&D in 2025, according to an arm of the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy that quantifies such investments.

It has been revealed that many scientists are enthusiastic about the opportunities for AI and quantum research. But some caution that a measured approach is needed. “My strongest opinion … is that I want to see all fields of science supported,” indicates Brad Marston, a physicist at Brown University and president of the American Physical Society. “Priorities have to be chosen, but getting a good balance is notable, because you never know where some advance will come from.”.

Through Genesis, the DOE plans to use its troves of data as well as experimental and computing facilities to produce a common set of AI tools and a shared ecosystem for science. “That’s conceptually a very powerful idea,” says astronomer Rachel Mandelbaum of Carnegie Mellon University in Pittsburgh. “And if it pans out as intended, it could drive great advances in science and technology.”.

Sources indicate that this year, DOE funded nearly 300 projects through Genesis — including one led by Mandelbaum. Her team’s effort aims to unify immense datasets from astronomical facilities around the world, such as the Vera C. Rubin Observatory, the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument and the Zwicky Transient Facility. That would enable AI models to be trained on the data, which could help uncover hidden astronomical insights.

H. Stockebrand/RubinObs/NOIRLab/AURA/SLAC/DOE/NSF.

Other projects include efforts to accelerate nuclear reactor development, create simulations of the U.S. electric grid and study nuclear fusion. And federal agencies including the National Science Foundation and the National Institutes of Health have launched their own Genesis efforts, centered around the mission’s National Science and Technology Challenges, which include topics in health, biology, energy, space, national security and more.

Recent findings suggest that many scientists were already wielding AI in their work. But Genesis “really did create an inflection point,” notes John Sarrao, director of SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory in Menlo Park, Calif. SLAC is now involved with 20 Genesis projects and leads two.

In a recent development, compared with AI, quantum technologies are less mature. With quantum computing, “we’re still at mile one or two or three of a marathon,” claims Celia Merzbacher, executive director of the Quantum Economic Development Consortium, a coalition of public and private institutions that works to bolster quantum tech in the United States. Nevertheless, researchers hope the two technologies can amplify one another. AI could help design and develop quantum computers, for example, while quantum computing reveals promise for efficiently tackling certain machine learning problems.

Recent findings suggest that accordingly, several Genesis projects involve quantum error correction, quantum sensors and quantum materials. And the DOE’s Quantum Genesis initiative aims to develop scientifically useful, error-corrected quantum computers by 2028.

According to recent reports, AI and quantum were not always hot topics. “Both of those areas … were kind of backwaters until recent advances,” Marston notes. Before the development of deep neural networks, for example, AI was mostly a curiosity. “It points to the importance of having a balanced approach to science funding,” he says. What starts as an obscure scientific specialty may suddenly explode into wide relevance.

Sources indicate that in the context of limited resources, prioritizing one area of research necessitates deprioritizing another. While some funding for the DOE’s portion of Genesis came from the One Major Beautiful Bill passed in 2025, much of the rest came from the DOE’s budget.

In a recent development, as excited as Mandelbaum is about Genesis, she is concerned about funding for non-AI related work. A cosmology grant her group received from the DOE didn’t align with Genesis mission priorities and was reduced this year, she states. “If the reality is that some of this [funding] is coming out of the baseline research budget in my field, then I think that it would be beneficial for the DOE to engage the scientific community about those trade-offs,” Mandelbaum says.

In response to these concerns, Gil says that the money going to Genesis from the DOE’s Office of Science — about $400 million so far — is small compared to the office’s total FY2026 budget of $8.4 billion.

Sarrao states that it’s important to build on the momentum of Genesis while still supporting the DOE’s core research. His impression is that things are trending in the right direction. “Are there really exciting opportunities? Yes, 100 percent,” Sarrao says. “Are there risks if you get the balance wrong? Equally well, 100 percent.”.

Nov. 18, 1989: The Cosmic Background Explorer rolls out

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (384 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Astronomy

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that A glow undetectable to the human eye permeates the universe.
  • Sources indicate that extracting clues from the CMB has taken multiple generations of telescopes on the ground, lofted into the atmosphere, and launched into space.
  • According to recent reports, the Cosmic Background Explorer (COBE) launched on Nov.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that A glow undetectable to the human eye permeates the universe. This light is the remnant signature of the cosmic beginning — a dense, hot fireball that burst forth and created all mass, energy, and time. The primordial cosmic microwave background (CMB) radiation has since traveled some 13.8 billion years through the expanding cosmos to our telescopes on Earth and above it.

Sources indicate that extracting clues from the CMB has taken multiple generations of telescopes on the ground, lofted into the atmosphere, and launched into space. Specifically, three satellites — COBE, WMAP, and Planck — revealed that our current cosmos, which is complex and filled with clusters of galaxies, stars, planets, and black holes, evolved from a surprisingly simple early universe.

According to recent reports, the Cosmic Background Explorer (COBE) launched on Nov. 18, 1989. One of its instruments measured the intensity of the microwave glow at wavelengths ranging from 0.1 to 10 millimeters across the entire sky. The COBE science team’s first announcement, in 1990, was the result of that measurement. The radiation’s intensity plotted by wavelength makes it obvious that the CMB has a very specific intensity curve, where the strongest signal is at 2 mm. That wavelength corresponds to a temperature of 2.725 K. (The wavelength of light, and thus how much energy that light carries, is directly related to its temperature; redder light has less energy and a lower temperature than bluer light.).

Recent findings suggest that COBE’s other instrument broke apart the seemingly uniform 2.725 K glow into more detail, looking for spots where the temperature is warmer or colder than average. It turned out there is a difference of only a tiny fraction of a degree, about 0.00001 K, between hotter and colder spots.

Recent findings suggest that this nearly identical cosmic glow with exactly the right temperature was concrete evidence that the entire sky — the entire observable universe — began in a Massive Bang. With such tiny temperature differences across vast regions of sky, those spots must have been in contact at early times. COBE leaders John Mather and George Smoot won the 2006 Nobel Prize in Physics for their work.

Liz Kruesi is science writer with a background in physics who specializes in astronomy and space-related news.
