#42506. American science is broken. Meet the people fixing it

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 17m • 📚 Deep Dive (3416 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencenews ↗ Open Full Page

American science is broken. Meet the people fixing it

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 17 min read (3416 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencenews

⏱️ ~17 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that the February sun was setting outside her family’s West Virginia home when Rebecca Lindsey found out she was being fired in 75 minutes.
  • Sources indicate that “Every week, it was like, ‘This is the week we’re all going to get fired,’ ” says Lindsey, who had worked as a contractor and later a civil servant at the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration for nearly 15 years.
  • In a recent development, but at 3:45 p.m.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the February sun was setting outside her family’s West Virginia home when Rebecca Lindsey found out she was being fired in 75 minutes. Lindsey, who until early 2025 managed the federal government’s climate.gov website, had just begun to think her job might be safe during the second Trump administration.

Sources indicate that “Every week, it was like, ‘This is the week we’re all going to get fired,’ ” says Lindsey, who had worked as a contractor and later a civil servant at the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration for nearly 15 years. “Every time you would hear the rumor and then it wouldn’t happen, you would think … maybe this is all just talk.”.

In a recent development, but at 3:45 p.m. on February 27, 2025, Lindsey and around 800 of her NOAA colleagues received a mass termination email saying they no longer “fit the Agency’s current needs.” In June, Lindsey’s sister and the data visualization lead for the project, Mary Lindsey, was fired alongside the remaining climate.gov contractors. The website URL was redirected, hiding the site — and its decades’ worth of climate visualizations, educational tools and extreme weather trackers — from the public.

The Lindsey sisters decided to fight back. Along with another terminated NOAA employee, they split a $65,000 grant from the nonprofit Surge Climate Talent and released a crowdfunding campaign to rebuild and update climate.gov. The site, now called climate.us, notched one million views in its first month.

But as proud as they are of their work, the project is a patch, not a fix. Rebecca Lindsey predicts it would take at least seven employees and $1.8 million annually to resume 80 percent of the old site’s work. “Climate.gov was more than just a website; it was a climate literacy program,” she claims. To rescue the full mission, they still have a long way to go.

Courtesy of M. Lindsey and R. Lindsey.

The Lindsey sisters are far from the only tale of makeshift resilience. Over the last year, untold numbers of U.S. scientists and their supporters have rebuilt data dashboards, formed recommendation groups for childhood vaccines and screenings, and doled out research funds for hundreds of stranded early-career scientists. They’ve reconstituted committees to advise space missions, rehomed key reports on climate and Arctic science, and even turned to social media to spread public health alerts in the wake of a massive realignment of the federal science enterprise.

“I don’t think anyone could have foreseen the amount of destruction and deliberate breaking down of norms and infrastructure” over the last two years, notes Christina Madison, a clinical pharmacist and public health communicator known on social media as The Public Health Pharmacist.

Sources indicate that since January 2025, the second Trump administration has frozen or rescinded billions of dollars in research funding on topics from climate change to vaccine hesitancy and is trying to redirect it — often without congressional approval — to administration priorities such as artificial intelligence and quantum computing. During deliberations for the FY2026 and FY2027 budgets, the White House proposed slashing future science funding by one-third.

Industry observers note that “When this was first starting, it really, truly felt like an alternate universe,” says Sean O’Leary, a pediatric infectious disease researcher at the University of Colorado Anschutz. “The science was always what drove the decision making, and now we’re at a place where it’s not.”.

Recent findings suggest that in 2025 alone, the federal government shed some 20 percentof its science workforce. And in May 2026, the Office of Management and Budget proposed a sweeping set of rules to expand the authority of federal political appointees in selecting science grants.

Approximate proportion of the scientific workforce who left federal service in 2025.

Yet some researchers see the destruction as an opportunity to rebuild their corners of U.S. science — or even reimagine it, says Michael Osterholm, an epidemiologist at the University of Minnesota in Minneapolis. “If there’s any good that can come out of what has been a horrible situation, it’s that it’s given us time and provided a pause to think through clearly: Is this the way we want to continue?”.

In a recent development, university of Ottawa ecologist Julien Martin spent a decade building a respected lab that probed how social behaviors affect the evolution of bushy-tailed, cat-sized rodents called marmots. So when the National Science Foundation began its sweeping grant cuts, Martin found himself doing something unexpected: uploading cute marmot videos to OnlyFans, an online video subscription platform better known for hosting pornography.

In a recent development, the effort, called OnlyMarms, netted $6,000 — a mere drop in the funding bucket. But the project went viral, leading outside supporters to launch a cryptocurrency token that earned the lab an additional $150,000. And direct donations, including an anonymous $300,000 gift, gave the lab enough to fund one Ph.D. student’s entire degree.

Industry observers note that “When you see that so much money could be obtained by doing essentially nothing about science, it’s quite shocking,” Martin says. He welcomes the support, but having to spend so much time on non-research tasks has also felt demeaning. “Sometimes, you have to question: Is the science funding broken? Are we just competing for pennies?”.

According to recent reports, in 2025, the National Institutes of Health and the NSF canceled or suspended more than 7,800 existing grants, totaling billions of dollars. (Some 5,200 grants were later reinstated.) Each agency issued roughly a quarter fewer grants in 2025 than their previous 10-year averages.

In a recent development, universities and research centers were hit hard. “It was really dire,” notes Emily Young, who leads medical research grantmaking at the San Diego-based Prebys Foundation. In phone calls with researchers, many told her they had halted ongoing experiments, such as developing measles vaccines for people with autoimmune disorders.

It has been revealed that but the thing that really stood out, Young says, was how the sudden drop in funding was affecting postdocs and early-career researchers. “Young people were going from feeling like they had an avenue for a really promising career … to feeling like they were in a worthless career.”.

So, in May 2025, the foundation awarded $7 million total in emergency grants to seven local institutions, including San Diego State University, the University of California, San Diego and Scripps Research. The grants targeted more than 80 research programs involving early- and mid-career scientists that were facing hundreds of millions of dollars in lost federal funding.

In a recent development, larger science philanthropies also stepped into the breach. The Gordon and Betty Moore Foundation gave $55 million total to 30 universities to support 400 postdoctoral researchers. The Alfred P. Sloan and Spencer foundations, among others, partnered to provide 83 quick-turnaround grants of around $25,000 each to researchers whose NSF education grants had been canceled.

Some wealthy universities also offered bridge funding to their researchers; Johns Hopkins University gave awards up to $250,000 to individuals with unexpected funding gaps, and the Yale School of Medicine arranged to fund up to 90 percent of terminated or frozen NIH grants.

In a recent development, after the first bout of funding chaos, science philanthropy Schmidt Sciences announced a more ambitious approach: to develop the science themselves. In January 2026, they revealed plans to construct three ground-based observatories and a space telescope larger than NASA’s Hubble by the end of the decade. The space telescope alone will cost hundreds of millions of dollars and provide open-access data to scientists worldwide, with a special focus on exoplanets and transient events like supernovas.

In November 2026, the philanthropy opened its first round of funding for early-career scientists using the observatory system; individual awards will total up to $2.5 million each.

According to recent reports, “Originally, the hope was we would play a more classic philanthropic role,” indicates Arpita Roy, an astronomer who directs the Astrophysics & Space Center at Schmidt Sciences. But given the federal funding landscape, she says, “it became pretty clear to us, if we really think these things need to exist in the world … then we need to build them out.”.

In a recent development, while private funding can be a lifeline, Young claims, it’s still a temporary measure at best. “We are not going to fill the vacuum of federal funding,” she says. “There is simply not enough philanthropic resource out there to do that.”.

Sources indicate that in 1995, the American Academy of Pediatrics and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention made a consequential decision: Rather than publish independent recommendations for childhood vaccines, as they had since the 1960s, they would issue one set jointly. Over the next 30 years, a group called the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices advised the CDC, with academy input, to expand its recommendations to include chickenpox, hepatitis A and pneumococcal infections. Cases of the three dropped by more than 90 percent, saving thousands of lives.

But in June 2025, Secretary of Health and Human Services Robert F. Kennedy Jr., an outspoken vaccine critic, fired all 17 members of ACIP and replaced many with vaccine skeptics. Kennedy also dismissed the academy representatives that informed the group.

“Essentially, we had no voice anymore,” recalls O’Leary, the pediatric infectious disease researcher at the University of Colorado Anschutz. He also serves as the AAP’s immunization schedule editor. “So we made a decision to not participate until we could say, ‘OK, this is a body that can be trusted.’ ”.

Industry observers note that in July 2025, the academy and other public health groups sued over the ACIP firings. The committee was unable to meet due to the lawsuit, and over the next six months, the CDC removed recommendations from its childhood vaccination schedule including hepatitis A and B, COVID-19 and meningococcal disease. The American Academy of Pediatrics issued its own schedule including those vaccines in January 2026.

Svetlana Repnitskaya/Getty Images Plus.

Industry observers note that the loss of trustworthy federal recommendations leaves “an impossible gap to fill,” O’Leary claims. But when it came to stepping in, “from my perspective, there was not an alternative.” The academy has since collaborated with the Vaccine Integrity Project, a upcoming group led by Osterholm, to conduct the scientific reviews that inform vaccine recommendations.

It has been revealed that vaccines weren’t the only childhood health matter to get a shakeup. In April 2025, HHS terminated the Advisory Committee on Heritable Disorders in Newborns and Children, which formulates newborn screening recommendations for genetic disorders, many of which can be deadly or disabling. At the moment, some 98 percent of U.S.-born infants are screened at birth.

When the genetics community raised concerns, Cynthia Powell, a retired pediatric geneticist at the University of North Carolina School of Medicine in Chapel Hill, gathered around 15 representatives of professional medical societies to create the Newborn Screening Collaborative. With support from the American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics, the group began meeting in early 2026.

According to recent reports, while the collaborative cannot give direct recommendations to HHS, it hopes to conduct evidence reviews for states and the small, parent-led advocacy groups that form around rare diseases, Powell indicates. It plans to focus on conditions that already have treatments under development, like a rare metabolic disorder known as Sanfilippo syndrome type A.

Approximate number of NIH and NSF grants canceled or suspended in 2025. Some 5,200 have since been reinstated.

“This Newborn Screening Collaborative is another effort not to leave a complete void,” claims Jewel Mullen, an epidemiologist at the University of Texas at Austin who was lead editor on a May 2025 newborn screening report for the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering and Medicine.

Sources indicate that other researchers are filling gaps in awareness about public health threats. A philanthropy-backed group called the Evidence Collective posted about the diarrhea-causing cyclosporiasis outbreak before the CDC’s Health Alert Network did. The collective, made up of more than 30 medical communicators, has more than 10 million followers across social media and notched 11 billion impressions in 2025.

“I don’t think that we will ever be able to fully replace the infrastructure that was there through the federal government,” says Madison, a founding member of the collective. But “there is a concerted effort now to look at: How do we take the momentum that we have with these organizations, and then make it sustainable?”.

Although stopgap measures are succeeding so far, scientists see them as Band-Aids at best. “We’re going to do it for as long as we’re needed,” Osterholm claims. But “I look forward to the day when we’re not going to be needed anymore.”.

In April 2025, nearly 400 scientists working on the National Climate Assessment, a recurring, congressionally mandated report, received an email that it was being reevaluated and they were being released from their work. One of them — Rutgers University climate scientist Bob Kopp — wasn’t surprised. “I don’t think you have to speculate very far” to know why, Kopp states. He cites a directive in the White House’s 2027 budget request to “stop wasting biological and environmental research resources on climate change.”.

However, “there was an immediate and deep sentiment by the science community to continue the work,” indicates environmental engineer Costa Samaras of Carnegie Mellon University in Pittsburgh, who had also been involved with the climate report. He and colleagues asked the American Geophysical Union and the American Meteorological Society to help organize the U.S. Climate Collection, a new set of papers from scientists about climate research, risks and solutions that will keep the public informed until federal assessments resume.

While the work is promising, “a volunteer effort of 170 scientists cannot substitute for a $30 million effort of 600 people,” Kopp notes.

The American Geophysical Union similarly stepped in with crucial financing for the Arctic Report Card, an annual report from NOAA that has provided information about the changing Arctic since 2006. Its editors were blindsided when they found out during a routine meeting in August 2026 that NOAA was withdrawing its support.

AGU’s in-kind offer to support the project just one month later was “tremendous,” indicates Twila Moon, a glaciologist at the National Snow and Ice Data Center in Boulder, Colo., who edits the report card. “But [it] is not a kind of model that is sustainable into the future.”.

AGU President Brandon Jones agrees. Nevertheless, at the time, the organization “had this sense of what was moral, what was right, what was ethical,” Jones says. And given AGU’s resources, “it seemed like it was our turn to show up and step up and act like the union that we’ve always been.”.

According to recent reports, the Planetary Society, a nonprofit space advocacy organization based in Pasadena, Calif., took the lead on several committees that NASA dropped. In January, the agency cited executive orders as it withdrew financial and logistical support from eight groups of space scientists and experts that advised NASA’s planning teams on exploring asteroids, comets and planets.

“It was pretty well-managed and organized [before], and then really fell apart because of the intrusion of the executive orders,” indicates Jack Kiraly, chief of advocacy at the Planetary Society. The organization now hosts the advisory groups’ websites, documents and meetings. “We’ve basically been having to reinvent this whole system.”.

Chris Gunn, Courtesy of Schmidt Sciences.

Climate.us isn’t the only site saving federal data. In November 2024, many environmental organizations “started preparing for the worst,” states Brittany Janis, executive director of the Open Environmental Data Project. Her group and nine others banded together to create the Public Environmental Data Partners, a network of 400 volunteers that archive environmental data and tools they suspected “would probably be on the chopping block.”.

Industry observers note that in February 2025, the Environmental Protection Agency deleted a tool called EJScreen, which maps places where people face high levels of risk from environmental burdens such as hazardous waste and ozone. Within 48 hours, the partnership had stood up EJScreen on a upcoming website, using open-source files to reverse engineer and refine the data pipelines. It has since received 1,000 views a month, Janis notes.

Nearly $2 million in philanthropic funding has helped the project pay staff, host data and hire engineers. It has restored the Federal Emergency Management Agency’s Future Risk Index, which projects county-level economic losses from climate change; the White House Council on Environmental Quality’s Climate and Economic Justice Screening Tool, which identifies communities overburdened by pollution; and the Department of Homeland Security’s Homeland Infrastructure Foundation-Level Data tool, which maps infrastructure at risk of natural disasters.

“We should not misunderstand the administration’s closing off of this data [to mean] that they don’t think data is vital,” Janis claims. “They recognize how important it is — and how valuable it is to causes that they disagree with.”.

Sources indicate that at the University of Chicago, the Data Mirror Project preserves datasets larger than one terabyte, including those from the U.S. Census Bureau and the National Park Service. The project has a guiding principle: LOCKSS, which stands for lots of copies keeps stuff safe, claims colead Lisa Chinn, who is head of research data services at the university library. An agency doesn’t have to delete its data to create problems, she adds. Firing website staff can lead to wonky links, corrupted files and pages that degrade into Wingdings gibberish.

The thought of losing all that data can be stressful, Janis indicates, but “there’s a lot of parachutes that have gone out.”.

Recent findings suggest that even as researchers, volunteers and scientific organizations pick up the pieces of the federal science enterprise, some are already imagining newly introduced ways of shaping it. “The world was not perfect in 2024,” notes Rutgers’ Kopp. “Reconstruction is an opportunity to improve upon the way things are done.”.

To Mullen, the epidemiologist at the University of Texas at Austin, transparency is key. Latest bodies like the Vaccine Integrity Project and the Newborn Screening Collaborative should make their meetings and deliberations as open as possible, she claims, especially when “people think that those with the loudest voices or the biggest wallets are going to be the ones that have the greatest influence behind the scenes.”.

Powell, of the Newborn Screening Collaborative, is hoping for greater efficiency in the disease recommendation process. Previously, it could take as long as three years to bring a condition from an initial vote to a final recommendation; with the collaborative, she hopes it could take one to three months.

Janis, of the Open Environmental Data Project, hopes to develop more creative and flexible data tools for researchers based on their needs. And Madison from the Evidence Collective and Martin of OnlyMarms believe that the science infrastructure needs to diversify its funding sources to prevent future shocks.

“If we really think these things need to exist in the world … then we need to build them out.”.

In a recent development, however, Janis notes that there are inherent risks in having the private sector support public goods such as open information. And Kopp warns that “attempts to replace something that was well-functioning … are not going to necessarily end up with something that is better or even as good as what was there before.”.

It has been revealed that at the end of the day, one of the key elements in establishing a newly introduced science system is “faith that you will still exist in a year or 10 years or maybe even 20 years,” says Katharine Jacobs, an environmental scientist who directed a previous National Climate Assessment under President Obama. Without stable institutional funding, “we are all essentially wasting our time, bashing our heads against the wall, trying to create a system that we can’t support,” Jacobs says.

For the Lindsey sisters, being involved in public service — even outside the government aegis — has been empowering, especially during what they see as an otherwise dark period for science.

They have raised more than $600,000 from individual donations since August 2025. And in February, they received a one-time grant from the Doris Duke Foundation and others that will cover their salaries and benefits until February 2027.

“If we can get the money, I can see us doing this indefinitely,” Rebecca Lindsey notes. She still hopes to retire one day, and she fights off worries that the government might come knocking about their unsanctioned work. But “we had a public that trusted us,” she says about jumping into the fray. “It was a risk worth taking.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Carnival Cruise Line has opened bookings for the Carnival Sunrise, Sunshine and Valor’s 2028-29 season sailing from Upcoming Orleans, Galveston, Miami and Mobile.

The schedule includes more than 160 itineraries ranging from four-day getaways to 14-day Carnival Journeys cruises and offers opportunities to visit 21 destinations across The Bahamas, Caribbean, Mexico and Central America.

Highlights include the Sunrise expanding Miami operations, the Sunshine going year-round in Galveston and the Valor featuring extended Carnival Journeys cruises from Mobile.

More than 50 sailings across the three ships will visit Carnival’s exclusive destination Celebration Key, which the company expects will welcome 3.5 million guests in 2027.

The Carnival Sunrise will open the deployment with a spring season from Miami beginning in April 2028, offering four- to eight-day sailings visiting The Bahamas and Caribbean and calling at Celebration Key, Nassau, Grand Turk, Ocho Rios, Grand Cayman, Cozumel, Aruba, Bonaire, Curacao and RelaxAway, Half Moon Cay.

Starting June 2028, the ship will reposition to New Orleans, from where it will offer six-, seven-, eight- and nine-day cruises to The Bahamas and Western Caribbean year round, visiting destinations such as Celebration Key, Nassau, Key West, Cozumel, Belize, Grand Cayman, Montego Bay and Isla Tropicale.

The cruise line underlined a series of seven-day Bahamas cruises featuring Celebration Key, Nassau and Key West as a highlight.

The Sunrise will also operate a 14-day Carnival Journeys cruise to the Caribbean and Panama, visiting Aruba, Curaçao, Cartagena, Colón and Limón.

The Carnival Sunshine will operate year-round from Galveston for the first time, with 29 four-day cruises to Cozumel or Progreso, as well as 24 10-day voyages to the Western Caribbean, Eastern Caribbean and Caribbean and Panama.

Select Eastern Caribbean itineraries feature calls to Celebration Key, Grand Turk, Amber Cove and RelaxAway, Half Moon Cay.

The Carnival Valor will continue offering six-, seven- and eight-day itineraries from Mobile to The Bahamas and Western Caribbean, including sailings to Celebration Key, Nassau, Bimini, RelaxAway, Half Moon Cay, Cozumel, Belize, Grand Cayman, Montego Bay and Ocho Rios.

There will also be two 14-day Carnival Journeys voyages: a Caribbean and Panama itinerary visiting Aruba, Curaçao, Cartagena, Colón and Limón, and a Southern Caribbean itinerary calling at San Juan, Aruba, Curaçao, Amber Cove, Grand Cayman and Ocho Rios.

Rep. Ken Calvert wins all-Republican race in California

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (508 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, california Rep.
  • Young Kim in a redrawn Southern California district that pitted the two Republicans against one another.
  • Calvert was leading his rival by 7 points Monday night when The Associated Press called the race for California’s 40th District with more than 70 percent of the vote in.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, california Rep. Ken Calvert walks down the House steps after votes on Sept. 3. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call).

Rep. Ken Calvert defeated Rep. Young Kim in a redrawn Southern California district that pitted the two Republicans against one another.

Calvert was leading his rival by 7 points Monday night when The Associated Press called the race for California’s 40th District with more than 70 percent of the vote in.

Calvert, who chairs the powerful House Defense Appropriations Subcommittee, is the longest-serving Republican in the California delegation, first winning election to Congress in 1992.

The race was reshaped by the Golden State’s upcoming voter-approved House map, drawn by state Democrats in response to mid-decade redistricting by Texas Republicans. The new map dismantled Calvert’s 41st District in Riverside County, transforming it into a safely blue Democratic seat in the Los Angeles area. That prompted him to run for the redrawn 40th District, which included a sizable percentage of his current constituents.

The rare intraparty general election was possible because Calvert and Kim finished in the top two slots in the state’s June primary. Under the California system, all candidates run on the same primary ballot, with the top two vote-getters, regardless of party, advancing to November.

Calvert had already declared victory last week, saying on social media that there was “no greater honor than serving my neighbors and our communities in Congress.”.

Kim’s defeat is the second of her congressional career — she lost her initial bid during the 2018 blue wave before winning election to the House two years later.

Sources indicate that in her concession message, Kim singled out California Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom, who led the redistricting effort last year that targeted five Republican-held districts. Democrats flipped all five seats last week.

“It’s unfortunate that Gavin Newsom’s political redistricting scheme forced two Republican members from Congress into this race,’’ she remarked in a statement.

The race between was marked by rancor, with Calvert alleging that Kim was not a true conservative and supported higher taxes. Kim accused Calvert of growing rich off stock trades over his decades in Washington.

Calvert will serve in a delegation with a dramatically smaller GOP presence next year, with Democrats likely to hold 48 of California’s 52 House seats. Just two other California Republicans – Reps. Vince Fong and Tom McClintock – have been reelected so far, while a third, Rep. Jay Obernolte, narrowly leads his Democratic challenger in an as-yet-uncalled race.

The Calvert-Kim battle was not the only all-party November clash in California, with several districts featuring matchups between two Democrats.

One incumbent has already been unseated, with Rep. Jimmy Gomez losing to fellow Democrat Angela Gonzales-Torres in the Los Angeles-area 34th District, according to The Associated Press.

Two other blue-on-blue contests in Northern California remained uncalled as of Tuesday afternoon: Rep. Mike Thompson was trailing venture capitalist Eric Jones in the 4th District, while Rep. Doris Matsui led Sacramento City Councilmember Mai Vang in the 7th District.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

PortMiami closed fiscal year 2026 with nearly two million passengers more than in the previous year, setting a latest record.

The port has shared that a record 10,533,854 cruise passengers, a 23 percent increase from the 8,564,225 during the previous fiscal year, visited during fiscal year 2026, which ran from October 1, 2025, to September 30, 2026.

As previously reported, the 10-million passenger milestone was achieved on September 14.

“Crossing the 10 million passenger threshold showcases the strength of our partnerships and the commitment of our team,” mentioned the recently appointed port director and CEO Jonathan Daniels.

“As we enhance our facilities and streamline operations, PortMiami is well positioned to support the next era of growth in travel and trade.”.

The port added that the momentum is continuing in the first month of fiscal year 2027.

In October 2026, there were 832,142 cruise passengers across 106 cruise calls, the highest October total in the port’s history.

This represents a 19.04 and 13.98 percent increase compared to 699,043 passenger movements and 93 cruise calls in 2025, respectively.

“These milestones reflect PortMiami’s continued momentum and the extraordinary work taking place across our seaport. Our investments in modern and resilient infrastructure are delivering results that strengthen our community and expand opportunities for residents and businesses alike,” said Miami Dade County Mayor Daniella Levine Cava.

Jim Jordan picked as new minority leader for House GOP

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1214 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Jim Jordan, R-Ohio, center, arrives for a House Republican leadership candidate forum for the 120th Congress in the Capitol Visitor Center on Tuesday, with Rep.
  • House Republicans on Tuesday opted for a new face atop their ranks, electing Rep.
  • The Ohio Republican defeated outgoing Majority Leader Steve Scalise, R-La., in a closed-door, secret-ballot election.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Rep. Jim Jordan, R-Ohio, center, arrives for a House Republican leadership candidate forum for the 120th Congress in the Capitol Visitor Center on Tuesday, with Rep. Celeste Maloy, R-Utah, walking alongside him. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

House Republicans on Tuesday opted for a new face atop their ranks, electing Rep. Jim Jordan as the incoming minority leader for the 120th Congress after Republicans suffered massive losses in last week’s midterm elections.

The Ohio Republican defeated outgoing Majority Leader Steve Scalise, R-La., in a closed-door, secret-ballot election. The final tally was 106-73.

Sources indicate that “Over the next two years, House Republicans will fight for American families. Democrats offer more government. We will offer more freedom,” Jordan said after the hourslong process.

Industry observers note that the two had been working the phones before making their pitches during a candidates forum in the Capitol Visitor Center’s auditorium on Tuesday morning. Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., confirmed last week he would not seek a leadership post in the fresh Congress, which will be seated on Jan. 3.

“Obviously Jim and I know each other, but I’ve got a proven record of how to bring people together,” Scalise said ahead of the vote, trying to play up his experience, including more than a decade on the leadership team that included a stint as whip.

As House Republicans trickled out of the candidates’ forum for breaks or to take phone calls, one member, granted anonymity to discuss a private session, remarked Scalise and Jordan “both have strong points, but they both have flaws.” Each made an unsuccessful bid for speaker in 2023 after the ouster of Kevin McCarthy, before the gavel ultimately went to Johnson.

Declining to reveal which would get his vote, the member said: “I won’t talk about a secret vote, but I know who I think is best to lead us.”.

The incoming minority conference also selected other leaders on Tuesday.

It has been revealed that majority Whip Tom Emmer of Minnesota held off a challenge from Texas Rep. August Pfluger to become minority whip in January, despite some grumbling about how tight votes were handled on the floor this year.

“We’ve got to retool our whip operation,” Texas Rep. Nathaniel Moran stated Tuesday morning, pointing to “the number of times we were held up by either discharge petitions or failed rule votes.”.

“Those were things that should not have happened in the majority,” noted Moran as he publicly backed Pfluger for whip.

But Emmer projected confidence after his whip win, comparing the moment to when Republicans were down and out after their losses in 2018 only to rebound a few years later.

According to recent reports, “To our colleagues on the left, enjoy this honeymoon phase, because come Jan. 3, 2027, you will regret ever putting your name on a ballot,” he said at a news conference, adding that Republicans under his watch would expose the “empty promises” that Democrats made to voters and push back on what he called their “radical” agenda.

In the day’s only three-way race, conference Chair Lisa McClain of Michigan defeated Reps. Erin Houchin of Indiana and Greg Steube of Florida to keep her spot.

“We had a spirited leadership election. There were crucial conversations about the future of our conference, and I listened,” McClain remarked at the news conference.

Sources indicate that in the race to lead House Republicans’ campaign arm, Rep. Brian Jack of Georgia defeated Rep. Rudy Yakym of Indiana, seen as an up-and-coming Ways and Means Committee member. That means Jack will take on a huge share of the uphill task of selecting candidates and raising funds for the 2028 cycle as he helms the National Republican Congressional Committee.

But most of the attention heading into Tuesday’s closed-door proceedings was on the minority leader race.

Johnson, the outgoing speaker, declined to endorse a candidate but had encouraging words for Jordan after his win. “He’s going to do an excellent job. He’s a good, trusted friend and brother,” he stated.

In a recent development, rep. Tom Cole, R-Okla., remarked it was a “tough choice for the conference to make,” but he wasn’t disappointed in the pick. “He was an exceptionally capable chairman of both Oversight and Judiciary. He’s excellent in an interview,” Cole said of Jordan. “He’s got boundless energy and determination.”.

Jordan’s victory means he will form a political and legal tag team with newly installed White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller in pushing back on a number of investigations House Democrats have planned for President Donald Trump, some of his second-term administration officials and his business-minded family members.

Recent findings suggest that democrats will have more than 250 seats in the chamber, with a number of races still uncalled. Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries of Upcoming York, expected to become the next House speaker, told reporters last week he predicts Democrats will have at least 255 seats when all the ballots have been counted and verification processes have played out.

“It’s a historic majority in the 21st century,” Jeffries told reporters in Washington, D.C., the day after the midterms. “The American people have chosen the economy over extremism. The American people have chosen hope over hatred. The American people have chosen common sense over corruption, chaos and cruelty. The American people have chosen House Democrats because they want to see a dramatic change in direction.”.

Political analysts have predicted an internal battle within the GOP for the direction the party takes over the next two years — and after Trump leaves office in January 2029.

Industry observers note that the Institute for Legislative Analysis, a nonprofit organization that advocates to shrink the size and influence of the government, released a vote study assessment on Monday. Its calculations led ILA to endorse Emmer and three fresh faces: Jordan, Steube and Jack.

Recent findings suggest that “It’s clear many Republican voters feel their representatives in Washington aren’t representing them,” Ryan McGowan, the institute’s CEO, stated in a statement. “It will be interesting to see whether House Republicans respond by choosing leaders … whose voting records are much more closely aligned with the party’s conservative base.”.

Recent findings suggest that several GOP sources late last week, granted anonymity to be candid, mentioned they were expecting a close outcome between Scalise and Jordan, adding Emmer was working the phones hard to remain whip. One said having either Scalise or Jordan atop the conference, with the expectation of Emmer staying on as whip, “won’t be much of a change at the top.”.

The fresh leadership team will take over Jan. 3, when Democrats are expected to, in part, use their large majority to target all things Trump 2.0. The same GOP source stated the majority party will “inevitably be pursuing impeachment by August recess despite their disciplined statements to the media pre-election.”.

Trump replied in the affirmative when a “60 Minutes” correspondent asked him in an interview that aired Sunday night if he could work with Democrats, should they also be aggressively investigating his team.

“Well, I did it for four years,” the president said of his first term. “They impeached me twice. And there are those that say that worked out to my advantage.”.

Nina Heller, Michael Macagnone and Samantha Freeman contributed to this report.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Viking has taken delivery of the Viking Halogi, its newest Longship that will sail on the Rhine River.

The ship was one of the seven named during a recent simultaneous ceremony in Amsterdam that virtually connected locations across Europe and Egypt.

“For nearly three decades, Viking has offered travelers a meaningful way to explore the history and culture of Europe through river travel,” said Leah Talactac, president and CEO of Viking.

“We are pleased to welcome the Viking Halogi to our award-winning fleet and to offer even more curious travelers the opportunity to experience Europe in Viking comfort.”.

Hosting 190 guests in 95 staterooms, the Viking Halogi will operate itineraries including the “Rhine Getaway” and “Christmas on the Rhine,” as well as the new “Oberammergau, Innsbruck & the Rhine” itinerary offered in 2030.

Like its sister ships, it features Scandinavian design and the asymmetric corridor layout that allows for true two-room suites.

As revealed during a recent earnings call, Viking’s orderbook is growing.

The company expects to take delivery of 25 additional river ships by 2030, 11 additional ocean ships by 2032 and two additional expedition ships by 2031.

This means that its fleet will comprise 123 river ships in 2030 and 28 ocean and expedition ships in 2032.

There’s a reason Nashville is known as the bachelorette capital of the world, and it has everything to do with the city’s Southern charm, group-friendly accommodations, and choose-your-own-adventure approach towards night life. No two bachelorette parties are the same, and Nashville gets that more than most cities, where a mix of high-energy Honky Tonks, crave-worthy restaurants, and quaint shopping streets round out its nightly lineup of live music across the city. There are even customizable tours for bachelorettes that celebrate the city’s biggest claims to fame (ahem, Taylor Swift, whiskey, and hot chicken).

Nashville just does bachelorettes right, especially when it comes to places to stay. There’s an Airbnb in Nashville for every group size and vibe, from a spacious loft just off Broadway to a storybook cottage in the trendy 12 South neighborhood. Plus, many of Nashville’s Airbnbs were designed specifically with bachelorette parties in mind, offering spacious rooftops, beauty bars, and plenty of party decor. Industry News: Rep. Darren Soto survives Republican-drawn map in Florida

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (416 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Rollcall

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Darren Soto, here at a hearing in July, has won a sixth term representing the 9th District.
  • Darren Soto, the most vulnerable House Democrat running for reelection, narrowly won a sixth term Tuesday in a district that state Republicans redrew in their favor.
  • Recent findings suggest that soto was leading Republican Navy veteran Dan Green by less than a point when The Associated Press called the race for Central Florida’s 9th District a week after Election Day.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Florida Rep. Darren Soto, here at a hearing in July, has won a sixth term representing the 9th District. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

Florida Rep. Darren Soto, the most vulnerable House Democrat running for reelection, narrowly won a sixth term Tuesday in a district that state Republicans redrew in their favor.

Recent findings suggest that soto was leading Republican Navy veteran Dan Green by less than a point when The Associated Press called the race for Central Florida’s 9th District a week after Election Day. His margin of victory was above the 0.5 percent threshold that would trigger a recount under state law.

Sources indicate that house Democrats have so far flipped more than 40 seats and appear on track to hold their biggest majority in the chamber in decades. Soto’s win means that no House Democratic incumbent lost to a Republican in the general election this year. And Florida Democrats defended all four seats the GOP had hoped to pick up under the state’s upcoming Republican-drawn map.

In a recent development, democratic Reps. Kathy Castor and Jared Moskowitz both won reelection from districts that shifted red, while Democrat Pia Dandiya, a former high school principal, defeated Republican Marine Corps veteran Casey Askar for a redrawn open seat in South Florida.

Soto, who declared victory last week, had been seen as the most vulnerable of the targeted Florida Democrats. The upcoming map reduced the Hispanic population of his district as the seat shifted from one that Kamala Harris would have carried in 2024 to one that Donald Trump would have taken by 18 points.

“Despite the Florida Republican legislature’s efforts to redraw me out of this district, my record of delivering for Florida indicated voters that I am a reliable fighter for them in Congress,” Soto said in a Nov. 4 statement.

In a Tuesday memo detailing how House Democrats secured their historic majority, the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee took aim at Republicans’ mid-decade redistricting efforts, saying their “attempts to steal seats … supremely backfired.”.

Recent findings suggest that while Florida Republicans were unsuccessful in flipping the four Democrat-held seats, the party held all of its House seats in the Sunshine State. Republican Rep. María Elvira Salazar narrowly won reelection in the Miami-area 27th District over Democratic challenger Eliott Rodriguez, the AP reported Tuesday. In the 7th District outside Orlando, Republican former TV news anchor Ryan Elijah defeated Democratic Navy veteran Bale Dalton, a former NASA chief of staff who conceded Tuesday.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

StarDream Cruises has partnered with the Singapore Tourism Board (STB) for a three-year seasonal deployment of the Star Voyager in Singapore through 2029.

The deployment of the nearly 2,000-guest ship from StarCruises’ fleet will provide travelers with more cruise itineraries to explore Southeast Asia by sea, according to a press release.

It is also expected to create opportunities to attract regional and international fly-cruise visitors to sail from Singapore.

“Singapore has been an key market for our cruise operations for more than 30 years, and the seasonal deployment of Star Voyager builds on our long-standing presence here,” noted Michael Goh, president of StarDream Cruises.

“Through our partnership with STB, we look forward to offering travelers more opportunities to discover Asia by sea, while contributing to Singapore’s continued growth as a leading cruise hub in the region.”.

Jean Ng, assistant chief executive, Experience Development Group, Singapore Tourism Board noted that the three-year seasonal deployment of the Star Voyager, alongside the Genting Dream’s year-round sailings, reflects the cruise line’s continued confidence in Singapore as a leading cruise hub.

With itineraries departing from Singapore, the Star Voyager will take guests to destinations across Southeast Asia, including Jakarta, Krabi, Phuket, Melaka, Langkawi, Penang, Port Klang (Kuala Lumpur), Pulau Pangkor and more.

Onboard, guests can enjoy international entertainment, regional-themed programs and signature events, including the Red Carpet Gala.

According to the press release, Singapore’s strong international air connectivity and diverse tourism products and experiences make it an attractive homeport and cruising destination for international fly-cruise visitors.

Additionally, the Star Voyager’s mid-sized profile enables access to a wider range of ports across Southeast Asia, bringing more cruise visitors to regional destinations.

The Star Voyager recently wrapped up its fall season from Hong Kong, which ran from September 30 to November 13, 2026, offering two-, three- and five-night cruises.

The Best Airbnbs in Amsterdam, From Canal Houses to a Boat on the Amstel River

📅 25 Mar 2025 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1969 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cntraveler

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, amsterdam today looks remarkably similar to how it did on my first visit as a high schooler over a decade ago, with its maze of canals, steady flow of bikes, and gabled façades—many of which have stood there since the 17th century.
  • Recent findings suggest that what has changed since then is the crowds.
  • According to recent reports, whether you're looking for a classic canal house in the Jordaan, a design-forward houseboat along the Amstel, or a multi-level family home near Vondelpark, the rentals on this list can help you settle into the city in your own way.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, amsterdam today looks remarkably similar to how it did on my first visit as a high schooler over a decade ago, with its maze of canals, steady flow of bikes, and gabled façades—many of which have stood there since the 17th century. To a history-loving teenager visiting Europe for the first time, the Dutch capital was a wonderland of Van Goghs. It felt so different from my hometown, yet still approachable, and sparked my lifelong love of travel.

Recent findings suggest that what has changed since then is the crowds. Amsterdam is now one of Europe's most visited cities, so you'll need to book tickets to the major sites well in advance, especially during summer. The same goes for accommodations. On more than a dozen return trips (many by train from Belgium, where I used to live), I have stayed everywhere from youth hostels to boutique hotels to Airbnbs. And over the years, I've learned that renting an Airbnb offers a completely different way to experience the city.

According to recent reports, whether you're looking for a classic canal house in the Jordaan, a design-forward houseboat along the Amstel, or a multi-level family home near Vondelpark, the rentals on this list can help you settle into the city in your own way. Read on for a few of my favorite Airbnbs in Amsterdam, whether you're here for the art, the nightlife, or to explore by bike.

We've vetted these listings based on Superhost and Guest Favorite status, ratings, amenities, location, previous guest reviews, and decor.

Number of guests: 3Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: Canalside location, separate kitchen, quiet street.

Sources indicate that couples or small families who want to stay in the heart of old Amsterdam will adore this renovated one-bedroom inside a historic canal house on one of the city's widest canals. The roughly 650-square-foot space sleeps up to three, and the separate kitchen has a large dining table. Step outside and you're around the corner from lively Nieuwmarkt, where cafés line the market square. Or, check out the dim sum spots in nearby Chinatown. Despite the proximity to so much activity, previous guests say the street itself stays peaceful at night. Just be prepared to haul your luggage up a steep staircase, as is expected for most Amsterdam buildings.

Neighborhood: Centrum (Nieuwmarkt)Things to do nearby: Rembrandt House Museum, De Oude Kerk.

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 3 bedrooms, 2.5 bathsWhy we love it: Private garden, dedicated playroom, fireplace.

According to recent reports, as in most substantial European cities, space is at a premium in Amsterdam, which makes this industrial-style town house a real find for families. It even has a dedicated playroom packed with toys and books. It sits in Oud-West, a grid-like neighborhood just outside the central canal ring, steps from the daily Ten Kate Market. When the weather cooperates, fire up the Weber grill in the private garden out back. Inside, a gas fireplace warms the light-filled living room and kitchen. But you may not find yourself cooking much, since the home's location puts you right near the Foodhallen. Three bedrooms sleep up to four, with a king bed, a double bed, and a toddler bed.

Neighborhood: Oud-WestThings to do nearby: Foodhallen, Ten Kate Market, Vondelpark.

Number of guests: 8Bed and bath: 4 bedrooms, 3 bathsWhy we love it: Heated pool, private garden, Nintendo Wii.

Groups who want to dip in and out of city life should take a look at this detached four-bedroom house in a tranquil, residential corner of Amsterdam Noord. The nearby metro reaches Central Station in about five minutes (or you can bike there in 15), and the countryside is close by too. The highlight, however, is the large private garden, where you'll find a heated pool (open roughly April through October) and a sauna. There's also a grill and space to dine outdoors. During the colder months, your crew will probably prefer curling up on the cozy couch for a movie or a round of games on the Nintendo Wii. Practical perks include a washer and dryer, a dedicated workspace, and four bedrooms.

Neighborhood: Amsterdam NoordThings to do nearby: Eye Filmmuseum, A'DAM Lookout, NDSM Wharf.

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1.5 bathsWhy we love it: King-size bed, canal views, amenities for kids.

According to recent reports, if your image of the perfect trip to Amsterdam includes staying in an authentic canal house, then consider this character-filled apartment in the leafy Jordaan neighborhood. Guests enter through the roomy breakfast area on the ground floor, and upstairs, you'll find a living area filled with plush furniture, jewel-toned accents, and views of the canal, Anne Frank House, and Westerkerk (Western Church). There's one true bedroom with a king bed and a pull-out couch in the living room. The hosts, who warmly welcome families with little ones, provide lots of kid-friendly necessities, like a high chair.

Neighborhood: JordaanThings to do nearby: The 9 Streets, Anne Frank House, Dam Square.

Number of guests: 7Bed and bath: 3 bedrooms, 1.5 bathsWhy we love it: Piano, record player with vinyl collection, fireplace.

Recent findings suggest that if you're looking to house a group, this rental might be the perfect fit. The three bedrooms (a king, a double, and a single) and one-and-a-half bathrooms are scattered across multiple floors. Gather in the dining area (there's also a full kitchen) or around the fireplace in the cozy living room stocked with board games, a vinyl collection, and even a piano. Stained-glass windows and art-covered walls are fitting for the prime location near the Rijksmuseum and Van Gogh Museum. However, be prepared to carry your luggage up some steep and narrow steps.

Neighborhood: VondelparkThings to do nearby: Stedelijk Museum, Van Gogh Museum, Rijksmuseum.

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 1.5 bathsWhy we love it: Air-conditioning, sparkling water on tap, large garden patio.

This spacious luxury apartment in a historic building offers some perks that can be hard to come by in Amsterdam: air-conditioning (in the living room and one bedroom), no stairs to climb, sparkling water on tap, and a living room that opens onto a garden patio with a lovely view of the Rijksmuseum. Families with small kids can also request a travel crib, high chair, and other gear. Plus, there isn't much for little hands to grab onto thanks to the minimalist decor. The two bedrooms each feature plush king beds.

Neighborhood: MuseumpleinThings to do nearby: Stedelijk Museum, Van Gogh Museum, Rijksmuseum.

Number of guests: 2Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: Fitness equipment, chef's kitchen, dedicated workspace with printer.

Want to feel really at home for an extended stay? Save this open-proposal loft housed inside a converted 19th-century police station, which stands out with a dedicated workspace (desk, monitor, printer) and fitness equipment (kettlebells, dumbbells, rowing machine). There's also a chef's kitchen and an Art Deco–style bathroom. French doors open up onto a back terrace, and huge bay windows offer a view of a 17th-century church and the Noordermarkt, where an open-air market sets up shop twice a week.

Neighborhood: JordaanThings to do nearby: Noordermarkt, Anne Frank House, The 9 Streets.

Number of guests: 2Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: Sage espresso machine, speakers and sound system, easy tram access.

This bright one-bedroom in Oud-West sits just outside the central canal ring and combines high ceilings and ornate moldings with a modern, open kitchen and sunlit living space. Double doors lead to a quiet queen bedroom with a larger balcony in the back. A smaller front balcony overlooks the street, where a tram stops just outside and connects guests with the rest of the city. Guests will also find a supermarket right across the street and restaurants and cafés around the corner.

Neighborhood: Oud-WestThings to do nearby: Vondelpark, Foodhallen, De Filmhallen.

Number of guests: 2Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1.5 bathsWhy we love it: Waterfront views, indoor fireplace, washer and dryer.

Recent findings suggest that think you have to choose between space and character in an Airbnb? Think again. This sleek, 2,600-square-foot houseboat on the Amstel River—yes, the river that gave Amsterdam its name—offers one bedroom, one-and-a-half baths, a full kitchen, and three terraces. In summer, watch boats drift by or take out the provided paddleboards—then cool off inside in the air-conditioning. After winter rolls in, curl up by the suspended fireplace as you gaze out of the floor-to-ceiling windows.

Neighborhood: De PijpThings to do nearby: Heineken Experience, Albert Cuyp Market, Sarphatipark.

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: Room-darkening shades, television with Chromecast and Netflix, access to outdoor patio.

It has been revealed that it may be on a quiet street, but this compact studio puts you close to the action, with Central Station just a couple of minutes' walk away. Light floods in through the three large windows with canal views, and the orange and copper-colored accents create a warm and inviting vibe. There's also access to a private rooftop terrace if you need a bit of fresh air. Be prepared to carry your luggage up a tricky flight of steep and narrow stairs in this fairly typical Amsterdam building that dates back to 1790.

Neighborhood: CentrumThings to do nearby: Dam Square, De Oude Kerk.

Number of guests: 2Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: Canalside location, television with Netflix, washer and dryer.

Stay right on the famous Keizersgracht (Emperor's Canal) in this first-floor apartment equipped with a washer and dryer and a full kitchen with a stove, fridge, and sink. Large, front-facing windows flood the crisp white apartment with natural light and offer a front-row seat to the city life buzzing by outside. It's also just around the corner from the Anne Frank House. The bedroom features a king-size bed, ideal for relaxing after a long day of exploring.

Neighborhood: Grachtengordel (Canal ring)Things to do nearby: Anne Frank House, The 9 Streets, Dam Square.

Number of guests: 2Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: Canal view, garden access, host's personal art collection.

According to recent reports, laid-back solo travelers or couples will appreciate this homey rental located on a quiet street near a few museums within walking distance of the lively Leidseplein Square. It’s wonderful for those looking to take a step back from the hustle and bustle—not the best pick for all-night partiers. The living space blends modern and vintage flourishes, featuring French paintings that are part of the owner's personal art collection and front windows overlooking a canal. A floor-to-ceiling window in the back opens to a lovely shared garden with outdoor seating where you can have coffee or tea on warm mornings.

Neighborhood: JordaanThings to do nearby: Leidseplein, Rijksmuseum, Van Gogh Museum.

What are the best neighborhoods to stay in Amsterdam?

In a recent development, book a stay in the Grachtengordel (canal ring) for the quintessential Amsterdam experience. The Jordaan has a similarly atmospheric feel with slightly quieter surroundings, while the Museum District puts the city's famous art museums right at your doorstep.

When is the best season to visit Amsterdam?

Sources indicate that spring is one of the best times to visit. It's when the city wakes up from the long winter and the Netherlands's colorful tulips burst into bloom (plan a day trip to the famous Keukenhof Gardens, about 40 minutes away). Come for King's Day on April 27, when the entire city turns bright orange with street parties and canal boat parades, or visit on the brink of summertime, in late May or June, and you'll enjoy much longer days, with daylight sometimes lasting past 9 p.m.

Latest Update: Thune will lead Republicans through the minority

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1064 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., leaves a meeting in the Capitol on Tuesday, before his election as incoming minority leader later in the day.
  • Senate Majority Leader John Thune was reelected as the Republican leader on Tuesday and will steer the conference through their time in the minority.
  • The South Dakotan ran uncontested despite a push from some of his colleagues to delay the leadership elections following Republicans’ stunning defeats last week in the midterms, which saw them lose at least seven seats and the majority.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., leaves a meeting in the Capitol on Tuesday, before his election as incoming minority leader later in the day. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

Senate Majority Leader John Thune was reelected as the Republican leader on Tuesday and will steer the conference through their time in the minority.

The South Dakotan ran uncontested despite a push from some of his colleagues to delay the leadership elections following Republicans’ stunning defeats last week in the midterms, which saw them lose at least seven seats and the majority.

“Obviously, the election result was not what we hoped for,” Thune told reporters, referring to the midterms. “But I think it’s important that we take the lessons from that and internalize the message the American people were sending to us.”.

While he and the rest of the leadership slate sailed through the conference contests by voice vote, it wasn’t without drama.

Sources indicate that before the leadership elections began in the Old Supreme Court Chamber early Tuesday morning, the conference held a meeting at the request of a group of GOP five senators, led by Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis.

In a recent development, the conversation, which several senators described as “frank,” ended up pushing back the leadership elections by a few hours. But they were not postponed to another day as some had hoped.

“This has never been anything against John Thune,” stated Johnson, as he made good on his commitment to leave the room early if the conference proceeded with its election. “What I didn’t agree with was holding the election right away, giving nobody an opportunity to really challenge any leadership position.”.

Recent findings suggest that “Part of the concern here is who wants the job? God bless him for serving,” Johnson added.

The conference conversation Tuesday morning turned into an “open-mic” with both conservatives and those who lost their elections speaking, according to senators.

In a recent development, sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., told reporters, “To rush into this and to just ratify all the same leadership — I mean, what message does that send?”.

But no contender to Thune emerged despite the angst, and a motion to proceed to the election, introduced by Thune’s fellow South Dakotan Sen. Mike Rounds, was accepted.

In a recent development, sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., said voters who rejected Republicans last week were reacting to high gas prices, the war in Iran and the cost of living, not to how Senate leaders were running the conference.

“I don’t think anybody in Texas who voted for the Democrat governor was voting against John Thune. If you diagnose that as a problem, you’re misdiagnosing the problem,” Paul stated.

Whip John Barrasso, R-Wyo., was reelected to his position, as was the chairman of the Senate Republican Conference, Tom Cotton of Arkansas. Sen. James Lankford of Oklahoma was again selected as vice chair of the conference, while Sen. Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia was reelected as Republican Policy Committee chair.

“Our first step is to make sure the American people know that we heard what they said, and the American people’s priorities are our priorities. That’s the way we regain their trust,” Barrasso said afterward.

Recent findings suggest that sen. Bernie Moreno of Ohio got the nod to chair the National Republican Senatorial Committee, meaning he will helm the campaign arm as the party looks ahead to the uncertain waters of 2028.

Moreno said, “I was in the retail automobile business, so when you don’t listen to your customers, your customers punish you. I think we have to own it, and I think we have to learn from it.”.

Sen. John Kennedy, R-La., stated on Monday evening, “What we as a conference right now need is honesty. We need focus. We need to try to reach a consensus on what we need to change.”.

Kennedy was among those pushing to delay the leadership elections and told reporters on Tuesday he voted present instead of yes on whether to proceed to them.

It has been revealed that sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., who ran for GOP leader twice — once in 2022 against Sen. Mitch McConnell, R-Ky., and in 2024 against Thune — declined to run again to challenge Thune. But in a Dear Colleague letter on Monday, he detailed what he’d like to see in the lame-duck session before Democrats take power, including confirming every nominee President Donald Trump has sent to the Senate, funding the government without an omnibus, banning stock trading, passing the permitting bill that is advancing this week in the Senate, passing the National Defense Authorization Act, balancing the budget and pushing through a sweeping voter ID bill known as the SAVE America Act.

Senate Republicans on Tuesday also voted on a resolution on their path forward that was spurred by a motion from Scott, aides noted.

“It is the sense of the GOP Conference that we will maximize the 54 days we have with congressional majorities, to confirm every judicial nominee and every executive nominee that the conference approves of, to pass our core Republican priorities, and to do everything humanly possible to pass a reconciliation bill before Jan. 3,” the resolution reads in part.

That long list of goals highlights the expectations Thune has faced as leader, where he led one-third of Republicans’ trifecta in Washington. In the next Congress, Democrats will hold the majority in both chambers of Congress after their larger-than-expected wins, while Trump finishes out his term as president.

Thune remarked he told his conference: “As I look back on the last couple of years, my question is, what would you have me do differently?”.

“Given the constraints we had to deal with, all the stuff that was coming at us on a daily basis, a narrow margin in the House, the White House, the Democrats over here who were obstructing two long government shutdowns — I think we came out of it as well as could have been expected, and got a lot of stuff done,” Thune told reporters.

In a recent development, “If you believe the exit polls, it was the war, it was the economy, it was inflation, it was fuel prices,” Thune added. “So no, I wasn’t apologizing for anything that we did. And I think on the political side, I don’t know what else I could have done.”.

Explora Journeys has opened sales for its Winter 2028-29 Journeys Collection, with six ships sailing to 230 destinations across 74 countries and territories and five continents from September 2028 to May 2029.

The collection introduces 70 maiden ports of call, including Dakar in Senegal, Valparaíso in Chile, Sharm El Sheik in Egypt, Doha in Qatar, Manila in the Philippines and Dalian in China.

The organization remarked in a press release that with 63 late departures and 26 overnight stays in ports as varied as Tokyo, Ushuaia and Muscat, guests have more time to explore and connect with each destination, from its early morning rhythm to its atmosphere after dark.

The itineraries can be combined to create longer Journeys and can also be experienced in shorter segments. Guests who reserve by December 1, 2026 can benefit from the 5 percent Explora Early Booking Benefit combined with The Exclusive Invitation, offering cumulative savings of up to 40 percent across all suite categories.

Recent findings suggest that guests aboard the Explora I and IV will discover Petra and Luxor, AlUla, Dubai and Abu Dhabi. Visiting Saudi Arabia, Egypt and Jordan, as well as Oman, Qatar and Bahrain, guests can anticipate Latest Year’s Eve in Dubai.

As summer unfolds across the Southern Hemisphere, the Explora II visits Rio de Janeiro, Montevideo and Buenos Aires. Beyond these, South America presents Patagonia, the Falkland Islands and Tierra del Fuego.

The Explora III will explore Japan’s spring blossoms, South Korea, China and Southeast Asia. Guests can enjoy scenic sailings through Ha Long Bay, Coron and Komodo, alongside overnight stays in Seoul, Hong Kong and Singapore.

Recent findings suggest that the Explora V charts a course across the Caribbean, featuring the shores of Saint Barthélemy and the Grenadines to Los Roques, Virgin Gorda and Bocas del Toro. On offer is a Upcoming Year’s Eve celebration off San Juan.

The Explora VI offers a program across the Mediterranean, Atlantic Islands and West Africa, with an inaugural journey along the West African coast encompassing Mauritania, The Gambia, Senegal and Cabo Verde.

  • Industry observers note that as climate change and shifting weather patterns have brought drought to the region, wildfires have increasingly ravaged a rainforest whose plants never evolved defenses against such a fiery foe.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In this age of climate change, wildfires are increasingly becoming a common occurrence. Forests in the American West evolved alongside wildfire, albeit far less intense than today’s blazes. But for some forests, fire is a wholly fresh phenomenon. Nowhere is this more true than in the Amazon Rainforest, where a recent study analyzing sediment cores (long tubes of ancient mud drilled from lake beds across the Amazon) reveals that the forest experienced virtually no wildfires throughout the past glacial period. In fact, fires only started happening with any regularity following the arrival of one particular animal in the region: Homo sapiens.

Industry observers note that as climate change and shifting weather patterns have brought drought to the region, wildfires have increasingly ravaged a rainforest whose plants never evolved defenses against such a fiery foe. The first real wake-up call arrived in the summer and fall of 1987, when satellites recorded an estimated 170,000 fires sweeping through the Amazon. Photos of blackened, smoldering earth in one of the lushest places on the planet shocked the world.

“Environmentalists have long warned of the destruction that is increasing with each new dry season, and witnesses every year report more cemeteries of trees,” The New York Times reported back in 1987. “The scientists’ findings show that in 1987 the burnings ruined more forest cover than previously thought and proved to be major polluters of the earth’s atmosphere.”.

Fast-forward four decades, and the Amazon is on the edge of a potentially devastating tipping point, exacerbated by this year’s “Super El Niño.” El Niño is hardly a upcoming visitor to South America. Peruvian fishermen named the phenomenon long ago for the warm currents that arrived around Christmas (El Niño refers to the Christ child), but its fingerprints go back much further. Sediment cores from Ecuador’s Laguna Pallcacocha suggest that El Niño’s modern rhythm, returning every two to seven years, took hold roughly 5,000 years ago. Archaeologists have linked catastrophic El Niño floods and droughts to the decline of Peru’s Moche civilization around the sixth century CE.

According to recent reports, el Niño’s effects are felt across the continent. When the equatorial Pacific warms, the Walker circulation—a loop of air over the tropical Pacific—shifts eastward. Air that normally rises over the Amazon to form storm clouds instead sinks, and the rain stops. The result is a seesaw between droughts and floods. During the 1982–83 event, one of the strongest El Niños on record, floods swamped northern Peru and Ecuador while drought withered southern Peru and the Bolivian Altiplano. The Amazon, especially its northern and eastern reaches, tends to be on the dry side of the seesaw: droughts occurred in 1997–98, in 2015–16, and again in 2023–24, when the Rio Negro at Manaus fell to its lowest level since records began in 1902.

Industry observers note that that raises a question: If El Niño has been drying out the Amazon for thousands of years, why did the forest so rarely burn? The answer is that in the Amazon, lightning mostly arrives with the rain, so historically speaking, dry spells didn’t have the match to start the fire. But humans used fire to clear land, and deforestation has left fragmented forest edges that are hotter, drier, and more flammable. Brazil’s meteorological agency has already revealed that this year’s El Niño will delay the arrival of the region’s rainy season, and the parched landscape will be extremely vulnerable to wildfires. It also doesn’t help that the forest is still recovering from the last El Niño, which caused unprecedented damage.

Industry observers note that “It’s similar to if you are already sick and then you get an infection,” Oxford University's Erika Berenguer told The Guardian earlier this year. “That infection is going to have much greater impacts on your body because your immune system is already compromised fighting the sickness.”.

Recent findings suggest that as The Upcoming York Times warned in the 1980s, a burning forest pumps carbon dioxide into the atmosphere. But scientists now fear something worse: If enough of the Amazon burns, the forest could reach a tipping point, disrupting its own moisture cycle and turning large swaths of the region into savanna. Since the Amazon Rainforest is Earth’s largest carbon sink on land, that transformation would have disastrous consequences for the world’s fight to curtail global warming, among other economic impacts.

Brazil increased its firefighting budget following the 2023–2024 fire season and saw significant improvements the following year, but the region will need to remain on high alert as the “lungs of the world” walks headlong toward potential disaster.

Sources indicate that aluminum luggage offers superior durability and protection compared to fabric or plastic alternatives. Scientists Say De-Extinction Is Impossible—Because Extinction Isn’t What You Think It Is

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, what does it mean for a species to go extinct?
  • Industry observers note that in April 2025, the de-extinction manufacturer Colossal Biosciences did just that, announcing (with George R.R.
  • Recent findings suggest that “Would a chimpanzee with 20 gene edits be human?” Pontus Skoglund, a geneticist at the Francis Crick Institute in London, wrote on Bluesky following the announcement.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, what does it mean for a species to go extinct? At first glance, the idea is pretty simple: Here today, gone tomorrow. But this uncomplicated view of existence on the planet is what leads some companies to think that, if you use 21st century tools to tweak the genomes of existing animals—even those separated by millions of years of evolution—then you can effectively bring the dead back to life.

Industry observers note that in April 2025, the de-extinction manufacturer Colossal Biosciences did just that, announcing (with George R.R. Martin) the return of the dire wolf in the form of three genetically modified pups named Romulus, Remus, and Khaleesi. Almost immediately, the claims of the dire wolf’s return were challenged by scientists who noted that the resulting animals were merely genetically modified gray wolves with just 20 gene edits.

Recent findings suggest that “Would a chimpanzee with 20 gene edits be human?” Pontus Skoglund, a geneticist at the Francis Crick Institute in London, wrote on Bluesky following the announcement. “If you lined up a dire wolf genome with a gray wolf genome, there would be millions of differences. These individuals seem optimistically 1/100,000th dire wolf.”.

According to recent reports, now, a upcoming article published in the journal Biology Letters argues that the very idea of de-extinction misunderstands what extinction means in the first place. The problem, according to Wheaton College marine biologist Andrew Davinack and biochemist Charlotte K. Daniels, is “lineage–genome conflation,” or the belief that reconstructing a genome is the same as bringing back an extinct lineage.

In a recent development, “We argue that de-extinction cannot recover extinct species because extinction represents the termination of an evolutionary lineage, not just the disappearance of genetic information,” the authors write. “Species are historically continuous population-level lineages shaped by gene flow, mutation, drift, selection, demographic history and ecological interaction. A reconstructed genome, even if highly accurate, represents at most a partial snapshot of an individual organism.”.

According to recent reports, in the case of the dire wolf, even if Colossal reconstructed the species’ genome perfectly, one big missing piece would be the dire wolf’s ecological niche, which disappeared over the 10,000 years since it last roamed North America. As the authors note, the “prey assemblages, competitors, parasites, climate and selective conditions” differ greatly from the time of the Late Pleistocene, and a species can’t be so easily removed from its ecological context. Even the film Jurassic Park—a very common comparison to Colossal Biosciences—argued this point, saying the “dinosaurs” (spliced with frog DNA, by the way) had no real ecological role to play in the modern world.

“The dire-wolf case therefore illustrates lineage–genome conflation in its clearest form: selected traits inferred from an extinct lineage were reconstructed within the cellular, developmental and genealogical context of an extant one,” the authors write.

It has been revealed that but the dire wolf isn’t the only de-extinction project being eyed by Colossal Biosciences. The company has frequently communicated its interest in bringing back the woolly mammoth and even partnered with Peter Jackson (yes, that Peter Jackson) to announce its efforts to de-extinct the giant moa, a flightless bird endemic to Latest Zealand.

While these are all flashy announcements, complete with celebrity ambassadors for the project, Colossal is also working on projects that Davinack and Daniels say are more worthwhile, such as the effort to introduce genetic diversity in populations of the endangered American red wolf or the black-footed ferret.

Sources indicate that “Genomic-assisted breeding or gene editing may allow some of that variation to be reintroduced into living populations,” the authors write. “Such applications do not reverse extinctions of course, but they may slow genomic erosion, reduce inbreeding depression and restore adaptative potential before lineage termination occurs.”.

In other words, let’s take care of the animals already in crisis before we start resurrecting ones from the distant past.
