Threats to broadcasters hang over FCC nominee hearing

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1053 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that FCC nominee Danielle Thumann Severs waits to testify during her confirmation hearing with the Senate Commerce Committee on Tuesday.
  • President Donald Trump's Republican nominee to the Federal Communications Commission faced opposition Tuesday from Senate Democrats who fear the commission could be controlled exclusively by Republicans under Chairman Brendan Carr, who they vowed to investigate in the next Congress.
  • Appearing before the Senate Commerce Committee, nominee Danielle Thumann Severs limited her commitments to independence from Carr, including on regulating broadcasters based on their content decisions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that FCC nominee Danielle Thumann Severs waits to testify during her confirmation hearing with the Senate Commerce Committee on Tuesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

President Donald Trump's Republican nominee to the Federal Communications Commission faced opposition Tuesday from Senate Democrats who fear the commission could be controlled exclusively by Republicans under Chairman Brendan Carr, who they vowed to investigate in the next Congress.

Appearing before the Senate Commerce Committee, nominee Danielle Thumann Severs limited her commitments to independence from Carr, including on regulating broadcasters based on their content decisions.

Much of the hearing focused on Carr and his threats to use the FCC to punish broadcasters he disagrees with.

Recent findings suggest that sen. Ben Ray Luján, D-N.M., mentioned that he expects Carr will not last long in his position once Democrats take control of Congress in the fresh year.

Recent findings suggest that “Mr. Carr, if you're listening now, know you're going to be in this body once a month, if not more, and in the House of Representatives as well, answering questions … so we can get to the bottom of the nonsense and the cover-ups that have been taking place,” Luján remarked.

The nomination of Thumann Severs, who presently serves as senior counsel to Carr, has led to consternation among Democrats due to continued vacancies at the FCC. The five-member commission is intended to have three members of the president’s party, including the chair, and two in the minority.

Currently Carr serves alongside fellow Republican Olivia Trusty and Democrat Anna M. Gomez, whose term expired earlier this year. Gomez may continue to serve through next year under the law if a replacement is not nominated and confirmed.

Democrats are concerned that if Thumann Severs were to be confirmed, the commission’s three Republican members could constitute a quorum on their own, allowing Trump to fire Gomez.

Sen. John Hickenlooper, D-Colo., said Senate precedent is to move pairs of one Democratic and one Republican nominee for the FCC and that he “strongly” believed the Thumann Severs nomination should have been paired with a renomination of Gomez in order to continue having “both parties at the table.”.

“A bipartisan FCC is essential to avoid things like large-scale media consolidation [and] I think also, more fundamentally, to protect a free and diverse press [that] serves everyone,” Hickenlooper said.

In addition to urging Trump to renominate Gomez, Democrats underlined the need for a second Democratic member of the commission.

Hickenlooper highlighted Thumann Severs’ close work with Carr, who Democrats and some Republicans have been critical of for comments about using the FCC’s public interest standard against television stations airing programming Carr disagrees with.

Thumann Severs’ work at the FCC right now focuses on the Wireline, Public Safety and Homeland Security, and Consumer and Governmental Affairs bureaus, rather than the Media Bureau.

Industry observers note that committee Chair Ted Cruz, R-Texas, has also been critical of Carr’s comments. On Tuesday, he listed the FCC’s request for ABC-owned stations to submit early license renewals alongside earlier incidents in which he mentioned Democrats encouraged the weaponization of the FCC against conservative voices.

“The First Amendment places notable limits on the government’s ability to regulate speech,” Cruz said. “The FCC possesses significant regulatory authority over communications, so there is always a risk that it could weaponize its authority against Americans with whom it disagrees.”.

Thumann Severs committed to Cruz that she would base licensing decisions on “the law and the record” and not use the FCC’s authority to “pressure or punish” broadcasters for protected speech.

It has been revealed that however, when Sen. Edward J. Markey, D-Mass., questioned Thumann Severs on whether the FCC could punish broadcasters the president disagreed with, Thumann Severs repeated one of Carr’s arguments in discussing the FCC’s role.

According to recent reports, “Broadcasters are subject to public interest obligations as part of the public trustee model in exchange for the licenses that they hold,” she noted. “As part of those public interest obligations, they are subject to many different rules and requirements, and the FCC is charged with enforcing and investigating the public interest standard against broadcasters.”.

Under repeated questions from Markey about Carr’s previous remarks, Thumann Severs said she would base her decisions “in the facts and the law and the record.”.

According to recent reports, luján also asked Thumann Severs to name issues where she had disagreed with Carr or Trump. While she noted her decisions would be her own, she declined to name any examples of disagreement.

In addition to questions about Carr, Democrats asked the nominee about the FCC’s E-Rate program, which provides low-cost connectivity for schools and libraries, and the Universal Service Fund, which funds the E-Rate program and other programs.

In a recent development, thumann Severs remarked that she believes the E-Rate program has been successful and that the FCC has a statutory obligation to provide some kind of discounted service to schools and libraries. But she was less forthcoming on whether the FCC could shut down the program as it presently exists without congressional approval or whether the program should be restricted only to rural areas.

Late last month, Democratic members of the House Energy and Commerce Committee, led by Communications and Technology Subcommittee ranking member Doris Matsui, D-Calif., sent a letter to Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., and Cruz urging Gomez’s renomination with any move to confirm a Republican nominee.

“Commissioner Gomez has shown the experience and judgment to continue that work,” the members wrote. “We therefore ask that the Senate pair any new Republican nominee with her renomination to a full term, consistent with the bipartisan design Congress built into this agency.”.

On Monday, the Leadership Conference on Civil and Human Rights also sent a letter to committee leadership urging a delay on the hearing and any vote on Thumann Severs’ nomination until Gomez can be renominated.

“Independent agencies should not be extensions of presidential will: their leaders should exercise independent judgement based on their expertise and statutory mandates,” the group wrote.

Cruz did not indicate Tuesday when the committee might vote on Thumann Severs’ nomination, and no markup has yet been announced by the committee of hers' and those of three others for two posts at NASA and one at the Transportation Department who also testified.

Tech Report: Inside the 2026 Condé Nast Traveler Points of View Summit

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1841 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cntraveler

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, on November 12, our ninth annual Points of View Summit brought together trip designers, luxury planners, and on-the-ground experts in Latest York City for a day exploring the latest in travel.
  • Global editorial director Divia Thani kicked things off with opening remarks on big-picture trends: how American travelers are driving luxury travel; the transfer of wealth to a younger generation; and a shift from spending on products to lived experiences.
  • Our editors discuss next year's editorial coverage themes, including spotlight destinations and how we're tapping into pop culture.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, on November 12, our ninth annual Points of View Summit brought together trip designers, luxury planners, and on-the-ground experts in Latest York City for a day exploring the latest in travel. While unrelenting rain poured outside, the atmosphere inside was anything but dreary and gray.

Global editorial director Divia Thani kicked things off with opening remarks on big-picture trends: how American travelers are driving luxury travel; the transfer of wealth to a younger generation; and a shift from spending on products to lived experiences. These overarching themes gave the audience a preview of what would come later in the day on panels and in breakout sessions. From a talk about Hilton Head’s Gullah culture and a run-through of reasons to visit Morocco—yes, this bit was accompanied by a post-lunch tea ceremony—to an exchange on all-inclusives with Hyatt Inclusive Collection, and a sit-down unpacking food and memory with Antoni Porowski, the day was full of thoughtful exchanges that reminded us why we journey in the first place. After much applause, the summit concluded with a cocktail party featuring wines from San Miguel de Allende and a taste of Lowcountry South Carolina by way of shrimp, grits, and fried green tomatoes—there was lots to celebrate, with a decade of Hilton Head being on our Readers' Choice Awards and its Savannah/Hilton Head International Airport drawing visitors from all over. Below, explore all that went down at our 2026 Points of View Summit.

Our editors discuss next year's editorial coverage themes, including spotlight destinations and how we're tapping into pop culture.

The day kicked off with a roundtable over what’s been on our minds and what'll be on our editorial calendar next year, just in time for our 40th anniversary. Our features director Rebecca Misner led the conversation with Thani, global features director Erin Florio, global executive director of video Dana Kravis, senior features editor Megan Spurrell, and associate editor Charlie Hobbs, who all agreed that a demand for substantive, long-form storytelling is back (though did it ever truly leave?). Spurrell shared an early preview of the now-live Best Places to Go in 2027, including destinations like the Albanian Alps for hiking, Memphis for museum openings, Yunnan for a slew of new restaurants, and more. Kravis spoke about cross-platform stories such as our new video series Made In, exploring craft in a particular destination, and upcoming video iterations of series like On Location, which unpacks beloved film and show locations. On the topic of pop culture, Hobbs highlighted a continued focus on cultural happenings, sporting events, and festivals that we're keeping on our radar as reasons to travel. Ultimately, going into 2027, Florio said, our coverage will explore “what it is that drives us to travel, as opposed to where it is we want to go"—not only the destination for destination's sake, but the experiences and impulses underlying travelers' choices.

Eduardo Schutte and Madison Flager discuss the future of the all-inclusive stay and Hyatt's rapidly growing portfolio.

Recent findings suggest that next up, commerce director Madison Flager spoke with Eduardo Schutte, Hyatt Inclusive Collection’s commercial SVP, on how all-inclusive stays have evolved and expanded far beyond your typical beachside bubbles to meet globetrotters of all kinds. In an age of optimization, it's only natural that travelers would value the ease and confidence of a bundled vacation, with less time spent planning so that they can enjoy their destination sans stress. Schutte observed that Hyatt Inclusive Collection has grown from two properties in 2013 to over 120 today, with expansion well underway in Europe, the Middle East, Africa, and Asia. “You're going to know exactly how much your vacation is, so it's much more predictable and easier to plan,” Schutte remarked. Afterwards, one lucky guest won a trip to a Hyatt Inclusive Resort. Perhaps the all-inclusive is a remedy for the times.

Erin Florio helms the conversation on summer travel, from increasing shoulder season trips to less crowded destinations.

Industry observers note that we recently unpacked why it seems everyone took a fallcation this year, and spotlighted the year-round appeal of off-season Greece. Though the once-sweltering days of the summer months might be all you’re yearning for as winter fast approaches, increasingly unpredictable weather and overcrowded destinations are shifting and expanding the typical high season. Florio led this panel with Jack Ezon, founder and managing partner of Embark Beyond; Catherine Heald, CEO and founder of Remote Lands; Jade McBride, president of Ted Turner Reserves; Scott Jordan, vice president of sales–East at Delta Air Lines; and Mei Zhang, chairman and founder at WildChina.

Recent findings suggest that to Ezon, it's less about the timing and more about the value of a trip; entry-level Mediterranean rooms can cost $4,000 to $6,000 per night, raising questions about whether the experience delivers value beyond price. Reframing a destination’s appeal beyond one season is key—going to Amalfi in October for wine or December for Christmas markets—as per Jordan, who stressed the value of meeting travelers where they're headed. He noted Delta is extending and adding seasonal service, including earlier flights to Porto and routes to Copenhagen, Sardinia, and Prague. Still, the group wondered whether greater access to Sardinia might relieve pressure on Amalfi and Como or simply congest another destination.

Zhang mentioned her clients aren't choosing between European hotspots at all; they're set on Asia, the choice becoming whether to visit Japan or China. In 2025, China saw sweeping growth in international visitors, which Zhang credited to upcoming visa policies, renewed country perceptions, and a global interest in regional lifestyles. “I just think that's part of wellness. It's drinking hot water, wearing slippers, playing mahjong, being social with family," she said. "A lot of these concepts are promoting China as a way of living, rather than as a destination.”.

Katie Mathews and Omolola Campbell on Hilton Head Island's Gullah culture.

Industry observers note that for a chat presented by Hilton Head Island, senior creative producer Katie Mathews sat down with Omolola Campbell, executive producer of The Spirit We Move With, a short documentary about South Carolina's Gullah community. The Gullah people are the descendants of West Africans who were brought to the Carolinas, Georgia, and Florida, in the 1700s and 1800s for slavery. A sixth-gen Gullah descendant herself, Campbell spoke with Mathews on the importance of leading the narrative and memorializing these stories today. In South Carolina’s case, it’s about hearing from Gullah people themselves. Campbell uses her gift shop on the island, Binya, as a space for educating customers through handwoven sweetgrass baskets, cookbooks, prints, and more. “People say that storytelling is a way of preservation. I like to say conservation, because to preserve something is to put it on a shelf, [but] Gullah culture is still alive and thriving,” Campbell remarked.

In between panels, Mei Zhang and others tried Moroccan tea.

According to recent reports, hannah Towey and Ms. Siham Fettouhi discuss lesser-known Moroccan cities and itineraries.

Recent findings suggest that after breakout sessions with editors and travel specialists, guests were served Moroccan tea before settling into a chat with news editor Hannah Towey and Ms. Siham Fettouhi, North America executive director of the Moroccan National Tourism Office. Beyond Marrakech and the desert, Fettouhi noted the country's appeal lies in its Atlantic and Mediterranean coastlines and can't-miss surfing spots. "We're talking about a country that offers you the possibility to ski literally in the morning and enjoy sunset in the beach in the afternoon," Fettouhi stated. “Morocco has never been this accessible from North America," she continued, mentioning nonstop flights now available from North America through Royal Air Maroc, Air Canada, Air Transat, Delta, and United. And domestic travel is also getting an update, as Morocco's high-speed rail network, Al Boraq, has extensions planned toward Marrakech and Agadir ahead of the 2030 World Cup.

An attendee captures Lale Arikoglu and Antoni Porowski's culinary conversation.

We closed out Points of View with a chat between Lale Arikoglu, director of special projects, and Antoni Porowski, Emmy-winning producer, Queer Eye veteran, and host of National Geographic's Best of the World series, which aired in June. While his other Nat Geo series No Taste Like Home traces family histories through food, this more recent show highlights the people behind well-known destinations' institutions and traditions—think a mustachioed clockmaker at Massive Ben's Great Clock or a family-run cheese cave in Paris. “There’s always a beautiful nerd that’s behind this larger-than-life thing that millions of us have had a chance to experience,” Porowski mentioned with a laugh, referencing folks not unlike himself, dedicated to that one experience and sharing it with others.

For Porowski, it's food that has offered a way to connect people with their roots and family histories, inspired in large part by his own journey toward embracing his Polish heritage. While planning a retirement trip for his dad several years ago, Porowski said his dad insisted they visit the Polish mountain village Zakopane. “We tried soups that I hadn't had since I was six or seven years old and got to connect through that,” he recalled. Porowski wrapped up the conversation with a handful of anecdotes from filming No Taste Like Home; a particular favorite was being in Senegal with Issa Rae, where he learned about teraanga, or the concept of generosity and sharing so integral to the West African country. Plus, the conversation would not have been complete without a rapid-fire round—see Porowski's answers below.

Sources indicate that delta does Shake Shack, which I’m not opposed to. I would say nine times out of 10—unless I’m sleeping and it's a red-eye—I’ll always have it, even if the chicken’s rubbery.

When the drinks cart goes by, what’s your go-to?

Chamomile tea, typically. This is so random, but it’s something I had as a child: sparkling water with a splash of apple juice. It feels really chic.

It has been revealed that because my parents taught me to arrive for a flight 10 minutes before it takes off when we lived in West Virginia, Jaeger Airport in Charleston, West Virginia. You can show up like 30 minutes before with checked luggage, and they will let you on.

Recent findings suggest that aisle, because I get to look at the flight attendants and see if they’re nervous during turbulence. But if they’re not, I know I’m fine.

There’s nothing more powerful than grabbing your carry-on.

Industry observers note that tomato bisque with a patty melt on sourdough focaccia from Il Buco Alimentari with sharp Vermont clothbound cheddar. That would be my appetizer, then puntarelle as my salad dish. For a main course, the shrimp from ABC Cocina—they have a lovely chili oil with lime zest and pink peppercorns—with again more bread to sop up all those oils. Since it’s my last meal, we’re doing surf and turf, scalloped potatoes, and a little broccoli rabe for fiber—no, I don’t care about fiber. For dessert, I was thinking about Campo de’ Fiori’s wild strawberries, with whipped cream and crème brûlée. I would finish it off with that Moroccan tea.

Scientists Fear a Biological Apocalypse Could Destroy Us. Now They Have a Way to Stop It.

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (968 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popularmechanics

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Some people fear a hostile alien takeover when there may be a threat lurking much closer to home (and it isn’t sentient robots).
  • Like humans, many molecules are left- or right-handed.
  • Mirror life is currently seen as a low-key but potentially apocalyptic biosecurity threat.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Some people fear a hostile alien takeover when there may be a threat lurking much closer to home (and it isn’t sentient robots). If a molecule such as DNA were to see itself in the mirror, its reflection would show the same molecule flipped around, much like the ubiquitous mirror selfie. But the mirror version can’t be stacked perfectly on top of the original, just as your left hand can’t be laid perfectly over your right. These hypothetical components of “mirror life” are not known to exist—yet. If they ever do, they could end up destroying life as we know it from the inside out.

Like humans, many molecules are left- or right-handed. Lack of actual hands aside, this means they come in two mirror-image forms. In DNA, that handedness highlights up in the direction its double helix twists. In amino acids, the building blocks of proteins, it comes from how four different groups of atoms are arranged around a central carbon atom, much like a left glove versus a right one. If one of these molecules really did have hands to hold a smartphone and take a mirror selfie, the image would show it with the opposite handedness. That mirror image is the version scientists never want to exist. It remains hypothetical for now, but bacteria and other forms of life built from mirror molecules could slip past an organism’s immune system and other defenses. Despite warnings that such organisms should never be made in a lab, a rogue scientist might want to play Frankenstein. Microscopic horrors could be unleashed as bioweapons, or a runaway experiment could escape into the world before anyone managed to eliminate it.

Mirror life is currently seen as a low-key but potentially apocalyptic biosecurity threat. Worried about what could happen if it ever emerges on Earth, a team of researchers from the University of Strathclyde and Durham University in the UK has proposed a way to detect it using polarized light. Their method relies on circularly polarized luminescence (CPL): light whose electric field rotates in a corkscrew as it travels, either clockwise or counterclockwise. Like a molecule, that rotation can be left- or right-handed. Scientists call this handedness chirality. Living things almost always use just one of the two mirror-image forms, or enantiomers, of each of their key molecules, which is thought to give them a biological and physical advantage.

Sources indicate that “This approach is based upon optical circularly polarized luminescence (CPL) signatures generated by fluorescent probes, which bind to subcellular targets (e.g. membranes, organelles, nucleic acids, etc.),” the researchers said in a study recently published in Royal Society Open Science. “Probes can either be achiral or be intrinsically chiral.”.

Sources indicate that most amino acids encoded in living organisms are left-handed, though some mirror forms do occur naturally and pose no threat. There’s only a slight chance that primordial mirror organisms survive from the early days of evolution or could arrive on meteorites. What worries the research team is artificial mirror life. They propose using fluorescent or luminescent probes that attach to biological structures and reveal whether those structures are mirror versions, based on their supramolecular chirality: the handedness that comes from how many molecules are arranged together, not just from each molecule on its own. This is only a thought experiment for now, but the approach could work and could be adapted to existing technology, such as cameras and microscopes, to search for mirror molecules and help prevent a bio-apocalypse.

It has been revealed that here’s how it would work: a fluorescent probe latches onto a target inside a cell, such as a membrane or a strand of DNA. When the probe glows, the handedness of the molecule it’s attached to shapes the light it gives off, so the light comes out spinning slightly more in one direction than the other. A probe bound to ordinary biological molecules would glow with one twist. The same probe bound to their mirror-image counterparts would glow with the opposite twist. That reversed signal would be the red flag for mirror life.

Industry observers note that mirror life doesn’t even need to exist for the CPL method to be tested. Researchers could try it on Z-DNA, a naturally occurring form of DNA whose double helix twists to the left instead of the right. Z-DNA isn’t a true mirror molecule, since it’s built from the same building blocks as ordinary DNA, just coiled differently. But its reversed twist makes it a handy stand-in for testing whether probes can tell one spiral direction from another. Using several types of probes could also help rule out false positives that might send the entire planet into a panic. Probes that have a handedness of their own may respond differently than probes without one, which helps flag misleading readings. Other probes that produce CPL have been designed specifically for RNA, which functions and behaves in especially diverse and complex ways. Some probes that incorporate amino acids also produce CPL when bound to specific molecules and could be added to the toolkit.

“Close coordination between biologists and chemists will be required to provide a library of fluorescent CPL-active biological probes that can robustly identify mirror life if it is encountered,” noted the researchers. “The CPL method could provide a first-line assay for identifying extant mirror life biohazards, while also offering a foundation for bio-surveillance efforts that would likely be necessary for practical safeguarding against artificial mirror life.”.

Are US Flight Schedules Returning to Normal? What Thanksgiving Travelers Need to Know

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1233 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cntraveler

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Travel chaos erupted at US airports over the weekend following a historic FAA ground stop that paused all flight takeoffs across the country for nearly five hours.
  • The ground stop, declared by the FAA amid air traffic control issues on Friday, November 13, stranded millions of fliers nationwide, with tens of thousands of flight delays and cancellations continuing for days.
  • Sources indicate that fortunately for travelers, both federal officials and airlines are doing everything they can to get flight schedules back on track and have airport operations running smoothly in time for the holiday rush.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Travel chaos erupted at US airports over the weekend following a historic FAA ground stop that paused all flight takeoffs across the country for nearly five hours.

The ground stop, declared by the FAA amid air traffic control issues on Friday, November 13, stranded millions of fliers nationwide, with tens of thousands of flight delays and cancellations continuing for days. Now, with the busy Thanksgiving travel period fast approaching, travelers are wondering when US air travel system will return to normal.

Sources indicate that fortunately for travelers, both federal officials and airlines are doing everything they can to get flight schedules back on track and have airport operations running smoothly in time for the holiday rush. “Recovery to normal operations will be slow and steady,” says a November 15 statement from the FAA. “We ask for your patience as airlines work to get you to your destination.”.

Industry observers note that although the incident is frustrating, experts say that travelers shouldn’t be concerned about the safety of the air traffic control system. “While the disruption was significant, travelers should take confidence in knowing that safety remained the top priority throughout the incident,” claims Geoff Freeman, president and CEO of the US Travel Association. “Our aviation professionals deserve tremendous credit for managing the crisis and getting Americans safely back on their way.".

If you have Thanksgiving travel looks and you're flying out this week, here's what to know about the current state of air travel in the US.

Recent findings suggest that the ground stop was issued due to air traffic control equipment outages and complications with telecommunications systems that the FAA uses to track and communicate with planes while they’re flying. “The ground stop was issued out of an abundance of caution,” indicates the FAA’s statement. “Safety is, and will always remain, the FAA’s highest priority. We will never compromise the safety of the flying public.”.

In a recent development, on Friday afternoon, the FAA’s network service provider, L3Harris, was updating telecommunications equipment at an FAA facility in El Dorado, Arkansas, when the challenges began, according to the FAA. The organization was deploying a new router that also began to cause system disruptions at a radar site in Amarillo, Texas. “The FAA’s legacy equipment became unstable when data began flooding the FAA FTI network, at a rate of 1,000 connection attempts every 4 to 5 seconds,” says an FAA statement. “This disrupted the system and created instability with aircraft communications and radar feeds.”.

It has been revealed that once the inconsistencies were identified, the FAA claims that L3Harris blocked those two locations, and the network stabilized. However, the exact cause of the telecommunications concerns are still under investigation.

In a recent development, regulators are still working to identify the root cause of the issue. “The work that was done on Friday, that's been done thousands of times by L3Harris in our network,” Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy noted in a Sunday interview on ABC’s “This Week.” “It's been done thousands of times by other companies, and these concerns haven't arisen, and so that's why we have to figure out what went wrong here.”.

Duffy also noted that the equipment in question is several decades old: the router was originally purchased in 2001 and was also part of a system that ran on obsolete copper wiring.

In a recent development, experts say that the archaic equipment underscores the urgent need to update the nation’s air traffic control system. “While the investigation continues, the incident exposed a troubling reality: America's aviation system remains vulnerable because we have relied on aging infrastructure for far too long,” indicates Freeman. “Friday's disruption was a wake-up call that Washington cannot afford to ignore.”.

Air travel experts say that the ground stop’s effects on Thanksgiving travel plans beginning later this week should be minimal.

According to recent reports, as of Monday afternoon, the majority of airline flight schedules were back on track. There were still about 2,800 flight delays within, into, or out of the US on Monday, and nearly 330 flight cancellations, according to FlightAware data. It also helps that fewer travelers are expected to fly this year compared to recent years. According to Mike Arnot, spokesman for Cirium, an aviation analytics company, the Wednesday before Thanksgiving is usually the busiest air travel day of the year. But in 2026, it’s not even slated to be in the top 50 busiest days for flying,.

In a recent development, american Airlines, the largest carrier at DFW, said its operations were returning to normal on Monday. “American is prepared to operate a largely normal schedule Monday, Nov. 16, following the FAA's nationwide ground stop,” the carrier said in a statement. "With crews and aircraft in position and favorable weather expected across our system, we are set up for a good start to the week and do not anticipate additional broad cancellations related to this incredibly disruptive industry-wide event.”.

Delta has also advised its passengers traveling on Monday to continue to allow extra time at the airport for any lingering effects on flight schedules. “While most flights are operating normally, some customers may still experience delays or cancellations,” the carrier noted.

Travelers should still continue to check with their airline for the latest travel updates and blueprint to be at the airport at least two hours before takeoff for a domestic flight.

In a recent development, operations are largely back on track, so many airlines have ended the flexible rebooking waivers that were issued at the beginning of the ground stop. However, two major carriers still have travel waivers in place.

According to recent reports, delta is still allowing passengers scheduled to fly through Monday, November 16, to make changes to their flights at no extra cost through November 23. Travelers’ new departure dates must be on or before November 23, according to the airline’s rebooking policy.

Industry observers note that american Airlines is waiving change fees for passengers booked to travel to or from one of 21 major US airports through Wednesday, November 18. Passengers can choose a latest travel date through November 21, but all changes must be made by November 18.

Sources indicate that even if your airline no longer has a travel waiver in place, if you’re flying with a major US carrier, you likely have the ability to change your flight without paying a fee (although a difference in fare may apply). However, these policies usually do not apply to low-cost carriers or tickets booked in basic economy class.

It’s impossible to predict if a nationwide ground stop could happen again, according to Freeman. However, modernizing the air traffic control system should reduce these types of outages over the long run.

“The FAA is making progress, replacing outdated copper communications lines with high-speed fiber, upgrading radar and radio systems, and introducing technology that allows air traffic controllers to manage flights more efficiently,” Freeman claims. “For travelers, these investments should mean fewer delays, more reliable flights, and greater confidence that the system can handle disruptions.”.

According to recent reports, airline executives echoed a similar sentiment regarding the state of US air traffic control systems. “This moment must be a call to action,” United Airlines CEO Scott Kirby said in a statement emailed to media. “It is critical for safety, our passengers, and our economy that we fix our nation’s Air Traffic Control system now.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Bernie Sanders and Elissa Slotkin hold a news conference calling for a “bold direction” for Senate Democrats on Tuesday.
  • More Democrats emerged Tuesday wanting someone besides Senate Democratic leader Charles E.
  • But Schumer maintained confidence he would be reelected to the post despite Sens.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that sens. Bernie Sanders and Elissa Slotkin hold a news conference calling for a “bold direction” for Senate Democrats on Tuesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

More Democrats emerged Tuesday wanting someone besides Senate Democratic leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., to lead their conference in the majority.

But Schumer maintained confidence he would be reelected to the post despite Sens. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., and Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., publicly calling for a different leader or a “concrete plan” that provides change.

Recent findings suggest that “I’m confident I will be elected majority leader, and our caucus is really united in focusing on bringing down costs, on ending the corruption, on ending the chaos, on ending the war,” Schumer told reporters Tuesday. “We have great unity in our caucus, and I’ll be proud to lead it.”.

Sanders stated during a news conference Tuesday the election was about “change and the need for the Democratic Party to move in a new and bold direction.”.

“I personally have known Chuck Schumer for over 30 years, and I like Chuck. Nobody works harder than Chuck Schumer. But in my view the time is now for change, and I will not be supporting Chuck to be reelected as the Democratic leader,” Sanders said, calling for an “economy that works for all, not just the people on top.”.

“Do I think Chuck has been leading in that direction?” he asked. “No.”.

Recent findings suggest that some incoming members and now incumbents have pointed to Maryland Democrat Chris Van Hollen as one possibility to challenge Schumer. Van Hollen had previously thrown cold water on the idea by saying he was instead “kicking the tires” on a presidential run in 2028 but has recently changed his tune.

A person familiar with Van Hollen’s thinking said he “has received an outpouring of calls on running for majority leader and is now in active listening mode.”.

Slotkin did not endorse anyone for leader but mentioned she had a “really productive conversation” with Van Hollen yesterday.

Industry observers note that “Whoever wants my vote is going to have to show me a concrete plan that’s definitely different. I’m a ‘no’ until and unless I see that from anyone,” she noted, urging her peers to “withhold quorum” when Senate Democrats hold their leadership elections “until you get that plan and you feel like you have a voice in that plan.”.

It has been revealed that she urged not just a roadmap for the first 100 days, but ideas for how to “communicate differently.” As for her own future, she remarked, “I am not actively seeking this job. I’m seeking change.”.

Asked about his prepares Monday evening, Van Hollen mentioned, “It’s not about me, but I am listening to the thousands of people who have been calling for change, but especially listening to our members, with a particular ear to upcoming members who have just come off the campaign trail.”.

Recent findings suggest that schumer tried to tamp down the suggestion of a rivalry. “We talk frequently, and we’re united — united in lowering costs, and united in ending this damn war,” he remarked of Van Hollen.

Others threw their support behind Schumer ahead of the Democratic leadership elections, which are expected to take place in December.

Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee Chair Kirsten Gillibrand, D-N.Y., praised Schumer for raising money and recruiting candidates like Sens.-elect Sherrod Brown of Ohio and Roy Cooper of North Carolina to help land at minimum seven seats, and potentially nine if Alaska and Mississippi ultimately swing their way.

Colom, however, has been noncommittal, telling MS NOW, “Too many of our leaders are from the same areas of the country,” pointing to the Brooklyn roots of both Schumer and current House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, who is expected to run for speaker on the House side.

In a recent development, sen. Ruben Gallego, D-Ariz., said he and Schumer have had their differences. But he implied he backs him for majority leader: “At the end of the day, these are historic numbers. It’s time for us to unify. It has been revealed that sen. Mark Kelly, D-Ariz., noted Democrats have “an opportunity to do things differently, and I think we will, regardless of who the leader is. It doesn’t really matter whose name is on the door.”.

Industry News: Something Enormous Is Buried Beneath Egypt’s Mound of the Pharaohs. We Could Only See It From Space.

  • According to recent reports, the Egyptian archaeological site of Buto (a Greek translation of the cobra goddess Wadjet), now called Tell el-Fara’in or Mound of the Pharaohs, is already known for giving up ancient secrets.
  • Sources indicate that satellites detected hidden structures beneath the existing ruins of Buto, at the Kom C mound.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

According to recent reports, the Egyptian archaeological site of Buto (a Greek translation of the cobra goddess Wadjet), now called Tell el-Fara’in or Mound of the Pharaohs, is already known for giving up ancient secrets. An astronomical observatory was previously unearthed at the site of what was once the Temple of Buto. Now, instead of discovering something meant for looking up at the stars, structures at Buto were recently found by satellite technology looking down from space.

Sources indicate that satellites detected hidden structures beneath the existing ruins of Buto, at the Kom C mound. Radar imagery from above was merged with electrical resistivity tomography (ERT) to reveal sprawling architecture dating back to Egypt’s 26th Dynasty. ERT is ideal for investigating suspected archaeological ruins without disturbing the ground until researchers have absolute certainty there’s something worth excavating. Because different subsurface materials—rock, soil, water, and brick—conduct electricity differently, pushing a low-voltage current through the ground and measuring the resistance reveals what lies beneath. Levels of resistivity show what kind of material is located at a certain level underground. That’s how an interdisciplinary team of researchers made the discovery without picking up a chisel.

“Overall, this study focuses on applying—rather than developing—methods using Sentinel-1 SAR imagery in combination with ERT measurements and archaeological excavation to delineate buried remains,” they stated in a study recently published in Acta Geophysica. “The integrated approach aims to reconstruct settlement phases and identify subsurface architectural features across the site.”.

The history of the Buto site reaches back 5,000 years to the Predynastic period, evolving all the way through the Early Islamic era. Thick layers of clay and silt obscured some of the early era’s remains, which made it uncertain whether it was worth excavating those areas. Some layers were even below groundwater level and would have complicated the excavation project. So with ESA’s Sentinel-1 satellite as their eyes, the researchers searched for patterns deep in the ground that could indicate the existence of buried structures. The Sentinel-1 mission consists of two satellites that can observe shallow layers of Earth, and their imagery confirmed it was worth investigating further. What the researchers found was an oval-shaped anomaly around 420 feet long (128 meters) by 203 feet wide (62 meters).

Sources indicate that they employed the ERT to investigate further, using a geophysical survey that involved laying down parallel survey lines across more than 58,100 square feet (5,400 square meters) along which hundreds of metal electrodes were pushed into the ground and connected to an electrode measuring system. Voltage differences from electrical currents hitting different materials slowly started to put together the image of a site that had been underground for thousands of years. Fragments of pottery, mudbricks, and other artifacts in the upper layers were left behind during the Ptolemaic period and Roman occupation. The most significant find was between three and six meters (from 10 to nearly 20 feet) deep. It was an entire mudbrick structure that survived from the Saite Period.

According to recent reports, after the invading Assyrians withdrew around 664 B.C.E., the 26th Dynasty dawned when Saite kings, beginning with Psamtik I, reclaimed the Egyptian throne. Egypt was no longer a vassal, but it was struggling to avoid another takeover. While it had lost most of its former power and glory, Egypt had kept its undying cultural heritage, which became visible in the art and architecture of the period. Egyptian builders were aware of how the flooding of the Nile could affect their structures, which is why a layer of sand was packed beneath stone remains as a foundation. The researchers are still unsure of the purpose of the structure they discovered. It may have been a temple, priestly house, or funerary complex. Religious artifacts and amulets suggest it was a secondary temple.

Industry observers note that when archaeologists actually excavated, they found an amulet of a chimera with features of a baboon, falcon, and Pataikos-dwarf, a minor deity whose amulets were usually carved out of wood and gilded. A limestone amulet of the goddess Wadjet also emerged, along with an offering basin. Amulets depicting many different deities were left in this basin, including wedjat eyes that represent the healed Eye of Horus, Anubis, Isis nursing Horus, a bronze amulet of Horus as a child, and Bes, a god of war and revelry with humanoid and feline features. A faience plaque depicted the goddess Hathor on both of its sides. She was a deity who ruled over love and beauty much like the Greek Aphrodite, and also music, dancing, pleasure, and fertility. This might explain the fragmented limestone statues found nearby, which appear to be of figures in sexual positions. Also found was a soapstone scarab of King Thutmose III.

“Future research at Buto should expand ERT surveys to other areas with larger electrode spacing, aiming to better understand the site’s deeper occupation phases and environmental context,” noted the researchers. “Our findings suggest that, in addition to the known temple, another temple may remain buried under a thick clay layer, which will be investigated through extensive measurements in forthcoming studies.”.

Voyager 1's light-day milestone: See the photos behind the discoveries

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1470 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Livescience

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that early Wednesday (Nov.
  • The milestone is largely symbolic, but it comes with practical consequences: While Voyager 1 cruises through interstellar space at roughly 16.1 billion miles (25.9 billion kilometers) from our planet, it now takes a full 24 hours for radio signals moving at the speed of light to get from Voyager 1 to Earth, and vice versa.
  • Recent findings suggest that the growing space between Voyager and Earth makes it increasingly hard to troubleshoot problems on the nearly 50-year-old probe.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that early Wednesday (Nov. 18), NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft hit a newly introduced space exploration milestone: The probe, which rolled out in 1977, became the first spacecraft to reach one light-day from Earth.

The milestone is largely symbolic, but it comes with practical consequences: While Voyager 1 cruises through interstellar space at roughly 16.1 billion miles (25.9 billion kilometers) from our planet, it now takes a full 24 hours for radio signals moving at the speed of light to get from Voyager 1 to Earth, and vice versa.

Recent findings suggest that the growing space between Voyager and Earth makes it increasingly hard to troubleshoot problems on the nearly 50-year-old probe. But with Voyager 1 still collecting data with two of its science instruments, which are expected to stay powered up into the 2030s, NASA scientists say one thing is certain: The spacecraft isn't done surprising us.

Recent findings suggest that "What Voyager has taught me is to expect the unexpected," Linda Spilker, who joined the Voyager team in 1977 and is the mission's current project scientist, told Live Science in an interview. "So many times the ideas and theories we had, Voyager was able to prove them wrong.".

Here, we look back at some of Voyager 1's most groundbreaking discoveries, told through its incredible photos.

NASA's Voyager 1 probe launches atop a Titan/Centaur-6 launch vehicle from the Kennedy Space Center in Florida.

According to recent reports, NASA's Voyager 2 probe released before Voyager 1, on Aug. 20, 1977. Voyager 1 took off a few weeks later, on Sept. 5. (The two spacecraft took slightly different routes through the solar system, allowing Voyager 1 to reach interstellar space first after a gravity boost from Jupiter and Saturn.).

Spilker, who joined NASA right out of college, attended the historic Voyager 2 launch and recalls "that feeling of watching the rocket lift up off the launchpad, feeling the roar of those rocket engines and knowing this was a mission going to visit places I'd always been curious about.".

A few weeks after launching, Voyager 1 took this photo of a crescent Earth and moon from 7.25 million miles (11.66 million km) from Earth.

On its way to the outer solar system, Voyager 1 snapped this image of a crescent Earth and its moon, captured in the same frame for the first time ever.

Voyager 1 photographed Jupiter from January to April 1979, reaching a minimum distance of 174,000 miles (280,000 km) in March 1979, according to NASA. As the spacecraft zoomed closer to the giant planet, it snapped an image every 96 seconds, creating this incredible time-lapse animation of the planet's turbulent atmosphere.

A time-lapse animation of Voyager 1 approaching Jupiter over the course of one Earth month.

It has been revealed that the close-up view revealed that Jupiter is a far more dynamic world than previously thought. But Voyager also made key discoveries about the planet's many moons.

While passing by the Jovian moon Io, Voyager 1 witnessed an explosion: the first volcanic eruption ever seen beyond Earth. This proved that there were other geologically active worlds in our solar system, opening up entirely latest avenues of inquiry and exploration.

A blue eruption on Jupiter's moon Io, the first volcanic eruption seen on another world.

"Going in, we thought that the moons would look a lot like our own moon: ancient dead worlds," Spilker noted. "And yet we found out they were very different worlds — like Io with active volcanoes. It was just an incredible change in our thinking.".

By viewing these eruptions, scientists saw parts of Io's surface being changed in real time. "As we got closer [to Io], scientists kept saying the surface is getting younger and younger, because they didn't see any massive craters, no medium sized craters, no little craters — until finally parts of its surface are just minutes old," Spilker noted.

A mosaic view of Callisto taken from Voyager 1 photos at a distance of about 250,000 miles (400,000 km).

It has been revealed that some of Voyager's close-up observations also confirmed old theories. For example, Voyager 1's flyby of the moon Callisto in March 1979 revealed vast fields of well-preserved impact craters, proving that Callisto was geologically dead.

Jupiter and its thin ring of dust backlit by the sun in a Voyager 1 image.

It has been revealed that A final surprise at Jupiter came when Voyager 1 swooped around the planet's nightside, seeing the gas giant backlit by the sun. This view revealed a thin ring system around the planet, made partly of the dust particles Io spewed into space.

According to recent reports, voyager 1 reached Saturn in November 1980 and made its closest approach to the planet on Nov. 12 of that year. Four days later, the spacecraft took this image of the planet's nightside, showing a broad shadow cast onto the surrounding rings.

"That is one of my favorite pictures: an outbound image, taken by Voyager looking at [Saturn] in a way you could never see from the Earth," Spilker noted, noting that we can only ever see Saturn's sunlit side from our planet. "The rings just look so beautiful shining there, and you can actually see the shadow of Saturn on the rings themselves. It's a really, really special picture.".

In addition to discovering a previously unknown ring, Voyager 1 spotted five newly introduced moons around Saturn and took close-up photos of several other known satellites.

Voyager 1's closeup view of Titan revealed a dense, hazy atmosphere.

In a recent development, the mission required Voyager to swing by the moon Titan in order to bend the probe's trajectory, sending it away from the solar system's planetary plane and toward a rendezvous with interstellar space. Before that, Voyager 1 revealed Titan's atmosphere to be so hazy that it completely obscured the moon's surface. This showed that Titan's clogged atmosphere was far denser than those of Earth and Mars.

By 1990, Voyager 1 was so far from the planetary plane that our solar system's planets looked like little more than specks of light. But before turning off its camera for good, Voyager 1 looked back at our cosmic neighborhood and took some of the most iconic space photos of all time.

In a series of 64 images taken from roughly 40 times Earth's distance from the sun, Voyager snapped its solar system "family portrait," a mosaic of images capturing six planets together for the first time. The portrait included views of Venus, Earth, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune.

Frames from Voyager 1's family portrait showing Venus, Earth, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune.

The image of Earth from this collection is famously known as the "Pale Blue Dot.".

Sources indicate that "We took the pictures of the planets in color, and that one is especially one of my favorites," Spilker remarked. "There's Earth captured in a sunbeam. A tiny world less than a pixel in size representing all the life that we know in our solar system — just a very special image reminding us just how special and precious our planet is.".

Earth appears as a pale blue dot in this iconic Voyager 1 image.

Voyager 1 turned off its camera immediately after taking these images, concluding its role as the greatest tourist in the history of our solar system. In 2012, Voyager 1 passed beyond the heliopause — the boundary where the sun's radiation gives way to the interstellar medium — becoming the first interstellar spacecraft in history.

Voyager 2 crossed the same boundary in 2018 and is expected to reach its own light-day in 2035. In the meantime, several science instruments remain active on both probes, allowing them to measure the strange and mysterious environment between stars.

Even way out there, the probes are still detecting whispers of the sun's power.

"We are still seeing effects from the sun that come out, hit the heliopause, and send shocks and pressure fronts out into the interstellar medium," Spilker said. "I wonder where we will finally reach the point where the sun doesn't influence what we're seeing, and we're in the pristine interstellar medium — and I hope that happens while Voyager 1 is still operating.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, A bucket list item is one thing—turning it into an itinerary is another. The difference often lies in deciding that the places we dream about are worth pursuing amid limited vacation days and financial constraints. It’s a sentiment captured by avid traveler and content creator, Lucrenzia Worthington: “If there's one thing I've learned, it's that it’s never the right time, only the time you finally decide to go.”.

With 2027 in sight, we’re taking inspiration from well-traveled women who are already thinking about the possibilities of the fresh, new year ahead and the trips they hope to pull off. Spanning photographers, artisans, interior designers, rock climbers, divers, and cookbook authors, their wanderlust is as varied as it is far-reaching. Read on for how they plan to travel next, from diving Antarctica’s crystalline waters to cooking in the fertile valleys of the Peloponnese Peninsula.

“For as long as I can remember, I’ve dreamed of diving in Antarctica. Maybe it’s growing up in Bangkok’s tropical heat, but the polar regions endlessly fascinate me: the icebergs, the seals, and penguins. I’ve visited the White Continent before, but seeing it underwater is something else entirely. In 2027, I’m joining Aurora Expeditions, a pioneer in polar diving for over 20 years. Even as an experienced diver and underwater photographer, it takes serious preparation: I’m logging drysuit dives off [the coast of] Cape Town with specialized gear to get ready for one of the most extraordinary dive sites on earth.” —Pier Nirandara, travel writer, underwater photographer, and founder of Immersiv Expeditions.

Industry observers note that “You know, I've been lucky enough to see some extraordinary corners of the world, yet one place keeps slipping down my list. It's always ’not the right time,’ always ’too complicated to book.’ But 2027 is the year: Lapland, in February. There are direct flights from Milan to Rovaniemi, Finland, and I would plan two nights there and two in Levi. I'm dreaming of a night in those super cool glass cabins where you fall asleep under the northern lights and endless starry skies, and booking experiences like visiting a reindeer farm, husky sledding, and snowshoe hikes through frosted pines—but also cozy up indoors by a crackling fire, with a warm blanket, and soak up the winter wonderland around me. If there's one thing I've learned, it's that it’s never the right time, only the time you finally decide to go.” —Lucrezia Worthington, content creator and freelance journalist.

“I've always wanted to visit Morocco, and I think 2027 is the year. My dream is to stay in a riad in Marrakech with however many friends I can persuade to join me. I want to find tagine and wander through the [medina]. I also hope to venture out to the Atlas Mountains for a weekend.” —Ríoghnach Robinson, author of Bad Words.

Recent findings suggest that “In 2027, I'm planning to return to Antalya, Turkey. I spent a week there this year and fell in love with the food, the people, and the climbing. I'll be based around Geyikbayırı and Çitdibi, where there are limestone crags in the hills with views out to the sea. I usually find a place to stay on Airbnb and lean on local recommendations for where to eat. One spot I'm definitely returning to is Coffee Roaster 404.” —Sasha DiGiulian, professional climber and founder of SEND Bars.

“Most flock to Greece for the idyllic beaches and all things Mediterranean, and while I completely understand that desire, my curiosity has landed me in the Peloponnese Peninsula, in particular the central region of Arcadia. Its fertile valleys are known for strong culinary and agricultural traditions; apples, sour cherries, slender eggplants, cheeses from mountain sheep and goats, walnuts, chestnuts, and mushroom foraging. I have been obsessing over a beautiful hotel that caught my eye: Manna, located on Mount Mainalo among hiking trails and dense forests. The mountain is also known for a very special high altitude honey cultivated from fir trees. Honestly, the honey alone is enough to get me on a plane.” —Noreen Wasti, cook, food creative, and author of Feast Your Eyes: Beautiful Recipes to Garnish, Share, and Savor.

Recent findings suggest that “In 2027, I’d love to finally visit Peru and see Machu Picchu. South America is completely new territory for me, and the landscapes, craftsmanship, and food are all calling. I’m imagining local guides, time in the Sacred Valley, and plenty of exploring. I’d also love to go home to Mauritius, but this time be a tourist. A beautiful hotel, all the food I miss, and time to enjoy the island and its lovely hospitality. Usually, my visits revolve around family and catching up. In 2027, for once, I’d like my biggest responsibility to be deciding what to have for lunch.” —Nashmita Rajiah, interior designer.

In a recent development, “I’m perpetually scouting [destinations] for In Hand’s newsletter and group trips by exploring culturally rich regions through the lens of traditional craft. I'm looking forward to an upcoming trip to the Atlas Mountains to visit the female Amazigh weavers in their homes, and learning about the by-hand process of weaving Berber rugs at the source rather than the point of sale, focusing on the culture and traditions around this generation-to-generation craft. I’m staying at Kasbah du Toubkal in Imlil, a small mountain town grounded in real Amazigh village life. It’s a trip I’ve wanted to take for years. ” —Meghan McEwen, writer and founder of group trip planner In Hand.

“What I look forward to most is traveling with friends and family. Mornings in the sea, a simple lunch in the hot sun. Afternoons are for slow wandering, and at night we'll cook significant meals from our market finds. In 2027, my family is heading to Sicily for two weeks in shoulder season, before the [summer] tourist wave. The first half we'll explore the main island, from the salt flats of Trapani to the bone white cliffs of Scala dei Turchi on the south coast. Then Favignana in the Egadi Islands, off Sicily's west coast, will hopefully be home for a week or so. The water is crystal blue, the coves are plentiful, and you can bike around the entire island easily. Tuna is still king there, though the old canning factory has long since closed. I'm dreaming of spaghetti with bottarga. At the moment I have my eyes on Villa Zu Nillu from The Thinking Traveller, perched above its own labyrinthine Roman stone quarry, into which a beautiful pool and a Mediterranean garden have been set. And I will document it all.” —Andrea Gentl, photographer and author of Cooking with Mushrooms.

According to recent reports, “After last summer’s European heatwave, we’re planning a cooler 2027 Finnish escape with my decorative arts grad school friend and her family. We always mix design with fun for the kids, so we’ll visit Helsinki’s Aalto House, the design district, and Hvitträsk museum before renting a lakeside mökki for swimming, hiking, and archipelago adventures. I want to experience the “midnight sun,” but I might regret it if the kids never sleep. Truthfully, I’m more of a lazy reptile than an outdoor adventurer, so afterward, our family of four will retreat to a less popular Italian beach for pasta, sunshine, and absolutely no obligation to do anything adventurous at all.” —Ajiri Aki, author of JOIE: A Parisian’s Guide to Celebrating The Good Life and The Joie Journal.

According to recent reports, “Long the secret destination of all the chic Italians I know, the low-key vibe of Maremma [in Tuscany and Lazio] is starting to also draw an international crowd looking for relaxed summers featuring all the best of Italy—raw nature, excellent food—minus the crowds and bling. For families, the Terre di Sacra Estate is on my wish list, either “glamping” on the beach or in one of their villas. And speaking of villas, Maremma doyenne Amanda Sposito is behind one of the most beautiful private rentals, the Villa Tre Querce, in town.” —Philomena Schurer Merckoll, founder of Riad Mena and hospitality group Egypt Beyond.

“I would love to visit Japan. Surprisingly, I have never been to Asia before, so it feels like a whole new world waiting to be explored. As a designer working with raffia and traditional weaving techniques, I am fascinated by Japan’s appreciation for craftsmanship and handmade objects. I would love to explore Kyoto’s historic temples, meet local artisans, and learn about their weaving traditions and use of natural materials. Seeing Mount Fuji in person would also be incredible: I find so much inspiration in the colors, textures, and everyday details of a place, and I would love to bring those experiences into my designs.” —Akosua Afriyie-Kumi, founder of AAKS.

According to recent reports, the Empire State Building glowed in glittering gold last night (Nov. 17) to celebrate NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft hitting one light-day from Earth. And it isn't the only building celebrating this achievement with a sparkling display.

It has been revealed that today (Nov. 18) at 5:16 a.m. EST (1016 GMT), NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft hit one light-day from Earth. About 16 billion miles (about 26 billion kilometers) away, this is the point at which it takes a full day (or 24 hours) for one light particle to get from us to the probe. So any signal we send to Voyager 1 or it sends back now takes a full day as the spacecraft continues to explore interstellar space.

To celebrate the major milestone for the farthest human-made object in history, the Empire State Building in Fresh York City lit up in gold. This golden glow references the Golden Record onboard both the Voyager 1 and 2 spacecraft.

In a recent development, and the Empire State Building wasn't the only major landmark to celebrate the occasion. The Space Needle in Seattle, Washington, and both the Willis Tower and the Skydeck Chicago in Chicago, Illinois have all been illuminated gold to mark the milestone.

It has been revealed that the Golden Record that these gold glowing buildings are referencing serves as an inanimate ambassador for Earth, carrying information about humanity, our planet, the other species who live here, the languages we speak, the music we listen to and so much more. It even includes instructions for building a record player to play the record.

The Voyager mission has, and continues to, make incredible scientific discoveries and observations throughout our solar system and now in interstellar space. But this Golden Record provides an additional aspect to the mission that connects us here on Earth to whatever unknown life may exist out there.

If some sort of life forms out in the cosmos were to ever come across Voyager and its Golden Record at any point in the distant future, they might learn a little bit about our small blue dot.

With a M.S. in Biology, Chelsea has written and worked for institutions including NASA JPL, the American Museum of Natural History, Scientific American, Discover Magazine Blog, Astronomy Magazine, and Live Science. When not writing, editing or filming something space-y, Gohd is writing music and performing as Foxanne, even launching a song to space in 2021 with Inspiration4. Passengers who were set to board the American Heritage this year will be transferred to the American Splendor, according to a statement issued by American Cruise Lines.

The American Heritage capsized and sank in the Mississippi River after being struck by a tanker while docked at the Port of New Orleans.

The organization noted that the Splendor is also a paddlewheeler and will operate the Heritage’s sailings as scheduled.

Passengers are currently being contacted with updated itinerary information, including embarkation and disembarkation locations, ACL added.

The firm also stated that it will contact guests booked on the American Heritage for cruises in 2027 and beyond with information about the status of their cruise and potential options.

ACL also noted it has resources available for impacted guests and crew members, adding that it has a crisis center set up on the ground in Fresh Orleans.

The facility remains open to assist crew or guests remaining in the area, including travel assistance and support.

A dedicated hotline was established at 203-487-9252, which impacted passengers and crew can contact with any questions or ongoing needs.

As reported by Cruise Industry News, New Orleans authorities and ACL are at the moment planning an operation to salvage the American Heritage.

The Coast Guard is said to be working closely with ACL and partners to clear any remaining pollutants from the vessel before removing it.

“Our top priority during this process is the safety of the public, responders and the marine environment,” the U.S. Coast Guard Heartland mentioned.

Part of ACL’s fleet of Mississippi paddlewheelers, the American Heritage was built at Chesapeake Shipbuilding in Maryland and entered service in 2015.

Having debuted as the Queen of the Mississippi, the 149-passenger vessel underwent a refurbishment before adopting its current name in 2021.

At the time, the manufacturer noted that the refit aimed to bring it up to the “same sophisticated standard already exhibited on American’s newest modern riverboats, while retaining traditional elements true to steamboat history.”.

Republicans tap Moreno and Jack to lead Senate and House campaign arms

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Bernie Moreno will chair the National Republican Senatorial Committee during the 2028 cycle.
  • House and Senate Republicans picked their newly introduced campaign chiefs Tuesday, tasking Ohio Sen.
  • In their new positions, both will spearhead Republicans’ push to win back majorities on Capitol Hill after Democrats seized control of both chambers of Congress by flipping more than 40 House seats and at least seven Senate seats in last week’s midterm elections.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that ohio Sen. Bernie Moreno will chair the National Republican Senatorial Committee during the 2028 cycle. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call file photo).

House and Senate Republicans picked their newly introduced campaign chiefs Tuesday, tasking Ohio Sen. Bernie Moreno and Georgia Rep. Brian Jack with leading the GOP campaign arms for the 2028 election cycle.

In their new positions, both will spearhead Republicans’ push to win back majorities on Capitol Hill after Democrats seized control of both chambers of Congress by flipping more than 40 House seats and at least seven Senate seats in last week’s midterm elections.

According to recent reports, republicans returned to Capitol Hill this week still reeling from their losses but resisted calls to delay Tuesday’s leadership elections. In the Senate, South Dakota’s John Thune was reelected Republican leader without any opposition, while Ohio Rep. Jim Jordan defeated Louisiana Rep. Steve Scalise in a closed-door, secret-ballot election to lead House Republicans next year.

It has been revealed that moreno will succeed South Carolina Sen. Tim Scott as chair of the National Republican Senatorial Committee.

“Republicans must enter this next election clear-eyed: the road ahead back to a Republican Senate majority will by no means be easy but the fight has never been so notable,” the Ohio senator mentioned in a statement.

Speaking to reporters on Capitol Hill, Moreno described his newly introduced role as “a hell of a job.” He said Republicans would be “absolute savages” on ending government corruption and continuing “to work for the American people.”.

“I suspect the best tailwind we’ll have is that the Democrats will learn all the wrong lessons,” he told reporters.

In a recent development, moreno, a close ally of President Donald Trump, is at the moment serving his first term. He first ran for Senate during the 2022 cycle but dropped out of a crowded GOP primary eventually won by JD Vance. Two years later, buoyed by an endorsement from Trump, he won a contested primary for the state’s other Senate seat and went on to oust Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown that fall.

Brown is poised to return to the Senate after defeating appointed Republican Sen. Jon Husted last week in a special election for the remaining Senate term of Vice President Vance. While Ohio has swung heavily toward Republicans over the past decade, Democrats scored big wins in the Buckeye State last week, winning several statewide offices and flipping three seats in the U.S. House.

But assuming he runs again for a full term, Brown will be on the ballot in 2028, setting up what’s likely to be a tense home-state fight.

In an apparent reference to the returning Brown, Moreno offered some Washington advice Tuesday: “Make sure you rent. Do not buy.”.

According to recent reports, the 2028 Senate map gives Republican pickup opportunities in a handful of swing states, including Arizona, Georgia, Nevada, Upcoming Hampshire and Pennsylvania. The party will also be defending battleground seats in Alaska, Iowa, North Carolina and Wisconsin. Also on the Senate ballot are races for Republican-held seats in Kansas and South Carolina, where Democrats scored surprise wins last week.

On the House side, Jack defeated Indiana Rep. Rudy Yakym III to become the next chairman of the National Republican Congressional Committee. He takes office after one of the worst elections for the GOP in recent decades and will succeed outgoing NRCC Chair Richard Hudson, who lost his own North Carolina seat last week.

House Republicans face the tough task of cutting into Democrats’ 40-plus-seat majority next cycle. But the party will have a slew of pickup opportunities, given the sheer number of seats Democrats won in historically red territory this year.

Sources indicate that like Moreno, Jack was first elected to Congress 2024, leveraging a close relationship with Trump to win an open seat outside Atlanta. He previously was White House director of political affairs during Trump’s first term and was a senior adviser to the president’s 2024 campaign. Over the past two years, he served as the NRCC’s recruitment chair.

Savannah Behrmann contributed to this report.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

MSC Cruises welcomed local authorities, media and partners onboard the MSC Divina to celebrate the beginning of the 2026-27 cruise season in Brazil.

After completing a trans-Atlantic crossing, the vessel arrived in Santos earlier this week, kicking off a series of three- and four-night cruises to destinations in the country.

During the ceremony, Adrian Ursilli, country manager for Brazil, highlighted that the 2026-27 season marks the debut of the MSC Divina in the national market.

“This ship will operate regular cruises in the country for the first time, allowing the Brazilian public to experience an incredible ship, built in honor of our diva and godmother, Sophia Loren, as well as in tribute to all the divas of cinema and the arts around the world,” he noted.

MSC will operate over 100 cruises in Brazil in 2026-27, with a five-ship fleet sailing from seven national homeports.

“Brazil is a strategic market for MSC Cruises, and we continue working together with all authorities and CLIA to further develop the Brazilian market and enable the sustainable and continuous growth of the industry in our country,” Ursilli added.

In addition to the MSC Divina, the MSC Musica also kicked off its Brazilian season earlier this week, offering a series of short cruises from Santos.

The deployment also marks the debut of the ship’s new features following a major refurbishment at the Palumbo Malta shipyard.

In line with projects carried out onboard other Musica-class vessels, the Musica introduced latest specialty dining venues, a modernized spa and a new gym.

The 2006-built ship also added MSC’s suite enclave, the Yacht Club, which offers private areas including a restaurant, a lounge and a solarium.

While the Divina will continue to offer short cruises from Santos through the end of its season in South America, the Musica will transition to weeklong itineraries starting in late December.

Through early March, the 2,550-passenger ship offers a series of seven-night cruises to Brazil’s South and Southeast coasts departing from Itajaí, Paranaguá and Rio de Janeiro.

MSC is also deploying the MSC Virtuosa, the MSC Seaview and the MSC Splendida in South America in 2026-27.
