📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, yesterday, a Hi-Fly charter airplane took off from Glasgow bound for Fresh York, with Hi-Fly crews and pilots.
  • In 2025, crazy things are par for the course, so that didn’t stop all sorts of promising headlines of a revolution in the skies.
  • In reality, anyone can charter a plane and have Hi-Fly operate it, and anyone foolish enough can pay extra for a custom paint job with their logo, or more financially insane — buy a scrapyard A380 and be on the hook for its maintenance, while paying a third party to fly it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, yesterday, a Hi-Fly charter airplane took off from Glasgow bound for Fresh York, with Hi-Fly crews and pilots. If you read the papers, it was purportedly ‘Global Airlines’ maiden flight, even though there’s no regularly scheduled service, the pilots and crew weren’t theirs, they couldn’t legally sell airline tickets on their own website and they don’t have a license to operate.

In 2025, crazy things are par for the course, so that didn’t stop all sorts of promising headlines of a revolution in the skies. This is the airline that promised stunning innovation and joy in the air, and the press gave Global Airlines an early gift, by comparing the story to Richard Branson and Virgin Atlantic. That’s just insane, as you’ll soon read.

In reality, anyone can charter a plane and have Hi-Fly operate it, and anyone foolish enough can pay extra for a custom paint job with their logo, or more financially insane — buy a scrapyard A380 and be on the hook for its maintenance, while paying a third party to fly it.

The whole ‘Global’ pitch was that people love the Airbus A380, hate all the current global airline experiences ( really?) and airline services — and a revolution in the skies, can happen again. It sounded exciting. We all like to dream. Global’s first flight would be the testament to what air travel can be and something passengers love. So, how’d they do?

When Virgin Atlantic debuted in 1984, the airline industry had been in a massively “beige” management consultant style, joy killer phase for a decade.

The fun “golden era” aircraft spaces and frills of the 60’s had largely been stripped out and bus travel comparisons were totally fair. Richard Branson’s light hearted approach to service and differentiated selling could shift dollars and votes — and measurably did.

Let me be very clear: that simplicity in differentiation is no longer the case. You cannot shift wallets and put butts in seats just by saying you have a cool airplane alone, or a bar on board (particularly when it’s just a beverage cart that states pub).

From leading (actually real) global airlines, passengers expect, at minimum, the following….

When “Global”, and by Global I really do legally, technically mean Hi-Fly the jet charter company which actually flew the scrapyard plane that “Global” bought, they did NOT have….

Travel blogger Noel Phillips shared some of the trip with his following. The following screen grabs are…. cute?

According to recent reports, the truth is, Virgin Atlantic didn’t have nearly as gargantuan of a task in the 80’s as any airline coming to market does today. In the 80’s many airlines were stuck, did lack innovation and had a pool of largely uninspired talent, with no experience outside of the airline vertical. There also wasn’t this whole technology thing, as standard expectation.

That’s all so far from the case these days and most that are specialized in the airline world are wickedly sharp. Most newly introduced people I know at airlines now also come from major tech companies, other travel verticals or impactful innovation firms.

Airlines are getting pretty good at this ole’ air travel thing.

A differentiated approach to smiles on board and a little bit of extra focus on fun, food and drinks could really shift minds and mentalities in the 1980’s, but now you gotta back it up, baby.

Everyone likes to feel special and Virgin, forever, has made people feel special at a time without tech. I’d argue Virgin has taught Delta a lot about that, and it’s a contributing factor to Delta’s rise as a premium airline. It didn’t happen overnight, and what looks easy never is.

According to recent reports, getting people to fly with you is now about safety, reliability, excellence in mobile technology, schedule and personalization. Then fine, we can care about which champagne; or caterer or lounge style or airport, and which celebs like it. Yes, these legacy airlines can appear stuffy at times, but my god, can you not marvel at the technology revolution making air travel journeys excellent?

According to recent reports, on real airlines, before I even arrive at the airport, I can use the NFC chip in my passport pressed against my phone to validate my document and bypass human interaction. I board a United, or any serious airline flight nowadays and see a notification that my bag is loaded onto a cart to be loaded on the plane, then again when it’s loaded onto the plane!

It has been revealed that I hit the wifi and I’m connected sitting at the gate. If for some reason the flight is at all delayed, or connection in jeopardy, I can instantly rebook onto any other service at no charge, without talking to a soul, with just a tap on the app.

Sources indicate that their seag back screens have blockbuster movies, boxsets and everything else you could want for a one hour, or 15 hour journey. It’s all just standard now, not innovative.

Sources indicate that the app navigates me through the airport and even tells me when my zone is boarding. AKA – stand the “f” back. The food is at least solid, the beverages are getting better because of their scale (buying power) and there are fewer poor customer service interactions because of how tech forward and seamless journeys are.

Industry observers note that all the great, massive airlines do this. This is like… baseline for a real player.

Tell me, or ask the Global Airlines CEO, James Asquith, where in the roadmap all of these essentials are? I want to make it clear that their priority for the last three years was a Soho House press conference about serving champagne in economy, maybe, “if they could get the economics right” rather than any of these basic things.

And in the end, they didn’t even deliver on the silly things they prioritized. The first Global flight wasn’t a remotely differentiated take on economy, business or first, as promised. It was 12 year old seats from another lackluster airline, without real refurb and even the long haul dignity of any seat back entertainment, which that airline which scrapped the plane offered.

If Richard Branson was at the helm, they never would’ve let that flight take off. Making a splash means at least doing one thing differently, right? An airline promising total innovation, A380 experience and differentiation cannot launch a flight which does not even meet the basic standards of budget carriers like Norse. You just can’t take off. You innovative something!

It has been revealed that let’s not forget that when Richard Branson formed Virgin Atlantic, he’d already founded a notable brand and number of businesses in the UK, was quite famous, and filed records and tech giant books in a place where they are scrutinized. He was “real”, even if some was bluster. The public could and did use his businesses.

James Asquith’s only claim to fame, other than from the Instagram account he bought followers for, to fake fame — yes, factually — is that he was the “CEO” of Holiday Swap. Omg, so major time!

The business purports to be a home swap company, though there are no financial records of any legal merit in the West, and despite my damndest multi-year attempts, no record of actual customers. Simple use of Similar Web or review sites will help your own conclusions. You can read old blog posts for more musings. The rumors of what laundered through are scary. Maybe a real journalist can find out for us?

I actually think it’s dangerous to the public to compare these two people.

I’ve had the good fortune of meeting Richard Branson many times throughout the years and he’s always been wildly impressive. Wickedly sharp, analytical, funny and personable. It’s easy to put in a good shift for PR purposes, but I’ve observed levels of deep dive knowledge that no setup encounter can protect for — and genuine interest too. He cares about his people and he worries about the details.

I also have many people in my personal life connected to the Virgin Atlantic founder and I know of nothing but admiration and respect for the man, his firm ethos and family. Business in the front, party in the back.

Recent findings suggest that my only encounter with James Asquith was when he was fuming that he wasn’t invited on an airlines press trip, slid into my Instagram DM’s wanting me to blast them – and for us to be best buds as we roast a major (actual) global airline. That airline later confidentially told me he was banned from flying, due to his antics. I politely declined and he unfollowed me. It was soooo cool.

I guess if you can’t fly other airlines, you start your own?

Industry observers note that so yeah, if you ever feel like putting your life in the hands of an airline without functioning entertainment screens, or WiFi, or regularly scheduled service, or new seats, or a mobile app, or an actual license to fly planes, definitely fly with Global. Oh, and no viable loyalty program either. Forget about earning points from daily spending and turning them into upgrades.

Those other “boring” airlines with all the bells and whistles above are clearly not ready to make travel great, with a latest golden age, again.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, president Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance salute during a Wednesday ceremony at Arlington National Cemetery in honor of Veterans Day. (Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images).

President Donald Trump on Thursday shut down his administration’s on-again-off-again talks with Iran, saying he would not seek a deal to formally end the nine-month-old conflict with Tehran.

According to recent reports, the possible end of the pursuit of a diplomatic solution came nine days after Trump and congressional Republicans suffered massive losses in the midterm elections. House Democrats will have more than 250 seats come January, and Senate Democrats will have at least 55 seats in the Senate — with Alaska’s competitive race still uncalled.

Polls leading up to Election Day and since have shown that a majority of voters, and a sizeable chunk of Trump’s Republican base, felt the Iran conflict was a mistake.

Sources indicate that vice President JD Vance penned a lengthy social media post the day after the election, blaming, in large part, the Iran war for the coast-to-coast Democratic victories. Some GOP lawmakers have also called for an end to the conflict, which drove up fuel and other commodity prices.

Recent findings suggest that "The reason we lost is the war," Vance wrote the morning after the GOP wipeout. "The president himself stated so last night.".

Industry observers note that trump has mentioned that he agrees with Vance’s assessment but that if he had to decide again whether to join Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in striking Iranian targets, he would reach the same conclusion. On Monday, he told reporters that the Iran war "militarily is effectively over.".

Vance had been Trump’s designated top negotiator in the talks with Iran’s remaining leaders, but the president said Thursday on social media that he had ordered his second-in-command to instead “focus his complete and total attention on the Massive Corruption and Crime taking place in Democrat run Cities and States throughout the U.S.”.

“We don’t need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed,” he added. “We’ve got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we’ve got their Strait!".

Recent findings suggest that the situation along the Strait of Hormuz remains contested and dangerous for commercial vessels, including ones that deliver a large amount of the world’s oil products. Iranian officials contend that they control most of the key waterway.

Sources indicate that trump, Vance and other administration officials have stated in recent weeks that they were open to continuing talks with Iran, while criticizing Tehran's negotiating tactics. Last week, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who also is Trump’s national security adviser, told reporters that Iran's latest demands were unreasonable.

Trump’s announcement Thursday could represent his latest way to try assuaging GOP voters, including members of his “Make America Great Again” base. A Reuters/Ipsos poll conducted after the midterms and released Tuesday showed that a majority of Republicans (51 percent) want Congress to pass legislation that would end the Iran conflict. Overall, 71 percent of Americans would support such a bill, the survey found.

The conflict was front-and-center during the midterms campaign.

According to recent reports, republican former Rep. Mike Rogers, who lost the Senate race in Michigan to Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, called for the Iran conflict to end "quickly.".

It has been revealed that “Michigan families are struggling with the price of everyday life. Groceries cost too much. We have to bring prices down," Rogers mentioned in one campaign ad.

On Capitol Hill, GOP lawmakers have tried giving Trump cover, while raising some concerns about high gas prices and questioning whether the president and his team have a viable exit strategy.

Industry observers note that as the midterms campaign hit the homestretch in late September, two Iowa Republicans in tight races, Reps. Zach Nunn and Mariannette Miller-Meeks, voted with Democrats on a measure to end the conflict.

It has been revealed that “With the negotiating window closed, sustained combat operations now require congressional authorization,” Nunn, an Air Force veteran, wrote on social media. “I will not support another open-ended war.”.

Nunn and Miller-Meeks both lost their seats last week, despite breaking with the president over the war.

Trump’s declaration this week of a military end to the Iran war came more than seven years after he offered some foreshadowing during a June 25, 2019, exchange with this CQ Roll Call reporter in the Oval Office.

Asked that day what his exit strategy would be if war ever broke out with Iran, he remarked: “You’re not going to need an exit strategy. I don’t do exit strategies.”.

Don’t Scan This Abroad: The QR Code Travel Scam Tourists Miss

📅 01 Aug 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1607 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theplanetd

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • QR codes are everywhere when we travel now, on restaurant tables, parking meters, hotel signs, airports, train stations, and transit machines.
  • Recent findings suggest that QR code travel scam happens when a fake QR code sends travellers to a fraudulent website.
  • Sources indicate that A scammer does not always need to hack a system or damage a payment machine.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

QR codes are everywhere when we travel now, on restaurant tables, parking meters, hotel signs, airports, train stations, and transit machines. This travel scam known as Quishing or QR code phishing is becoming the fastest growing travel scam warning out there. Most QR codes are legitimate, but scammers are using fake QR code stickers and fake payment pages to catch travellers when they are tired, rushed, or distracted.

Recent findings suggest that QR code travel scam happens when a fake QR code sends travellers to a fraudulent website. The code may be placed over a real QR code on a parking meter, restaurant table, hotel notice, airport sign, or transit machine, or it may arrive by text or email pretending to be a fine, toll, ticket, or check-in request. The safest rule is simple: Pause. Check. Then pay.Read out post: 20 Common Travel Scams and How to Avoid Them.

Sources indicate that A scammer does not always need to hack a system or damage a payment machine. Sometimes they print a fake QR code sticker and place it directly over a legitimate code.

It has been revealed that from a quick glance, the sign still looks official. The logo may look familiar. The instructions may seem normal. The page that opens may copy the colours, layout, and branding of the real manufacturer.

You think you are paying for parking, ordering food, checking into a hotel, or settling a toll. Instead, criminals may be collecting your credit card number, password, phone number, licence plate, email address, or other personal information.

The FTC has also warned about fake traffic violation texts that begin with a QR code and try to scare people into paying a fake unpaid balance.

The FTC has warned that scammers hide harmful links in QR codes to steal personal information, including by placing fake QR codes over real ones on parking meters.

Many restaurants now use QR codes for menus, ordering, or payment. Most are legitimate, but travellers should still be cautious. This is the easiest travel scam for QR code phishing as everyone uses it.

A menu QR code should usually show a menu. Be careful if it asks for information it does not need, such as your passport number, banking details, hotel room number, or a password.

Industry observers note that before scanning a QR code on a restaurant table, look at the surface. Does it look printed into the menu or table sign, or does it look like a sticker placed on top? If it looks raised, crooked, bubbled, or mismatched, ask staff for a printed menu or the restaurant’s official website.

Parking is one of the easiest places for this scam to work because travellers are often rushed and confused.

Recent findings suggest that you may not know the local parking app. You may be dealing with another language. You may be worried about getting a ticket. That pressure makes a “scan to pay” sticker feel helpful.

Before paying through a parking QR code, inspect the sticker, read the URL preview, and check whether the payment page matches the city, parking authority, or official app named on the machine.

Recent findings suggest that if anything feels off, do not use the QR code. Type the official website yourself, use the official parking app, pay at the machine, or ask local staff for help.

Airports and transit stations are full of QR codes: Wi-Fi, directions, tickets, luggage storage, forms, lounge access, and service information. Travel scams often happen when travelers are in a hurry. If you need wifi, a taxi, some food, QR codes are often the easiest way to catch you off guard.

Recent findings suggest that that does not mean every code is unsafe. It means you should slow down when a public QR code asks for payment, passwords, ID documents, or personal information.

The FBI warns that malicious QR codes can send people to fake sites, steal victim data, embed malware, or redirect payments. The FBI warns that criminals can tamper with QR codes to redirect payments, steal login and financial information, or send people to malicious websites.

The easiest way to avoid this scam is to build one habit before you scan a public QR code.

According to recent reports, do not scan just because a sign looks official. Public signs, parking meters, table cards, and posters can be tampered with.

If the message says you must pay immediately, avoid a fine, settle a toll, confirm a booking, or prevent a penalty, slow down. Urgency is one of the biggest warning signs.

Before your phone opens anything, look at the QR code itself.

We call this the scratch test. You are not damaging the sign. You are simply checking whether the QR code feels or looks different from the rest of the surface.

Canadian readers can also check the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security’s QR code safety guidance and report fraud through the Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre.

Recent findings suggest that most phones show a preview of the website before opening the page. Read it.

Look for misspellings, extra words, strange endings, random letters, shortened links, or a domain that does not match the organization, hotel, restaurant, city, or attraction.

Do not rely only on the padlock symbol. A secure connection does not automatically mean the site is legitimate. The real question is whether you are on the correct website.

The FTC has also warned about fake traffic violation texts that include a QR code and pressure people to pay a fake unpaid balance.

For payments, passwords, account logins, or identity information, the safest option is often to bypass the QR code.

It has been revealed that open your browser and type the official website yourself. Use an app you already installed from the official app store. Ask an employee for the correct payment method. Contact your hotel, airline, rental car tech giant, or bank through the phone number on your booking or card — not through the number on a suspicious page.

Sources indicate that first, do not panic. Scanning a QR code does not automatically mean your information has been stolen. The bigger risk usually begins when you enter payment information, type a password, download a file, or provide personal details.

If you scanned a suspicious code:.

Close the page immediately if the link looks wrong, the message creates urgency, or the site asks for information you did not expect to provide.

Do not download an unfamiliar app or file from a QR code.

If you entered credit card information, contact your bank or card issuer using the official number on the back of your card or through the official banking app.

It has been revealed that if you entered a password, change it through the official website or app. If you reused that password anywhere else, change it there too.

Watch for follow-up messages. A scammer who has some of your information may later pretend to be your bank, hotel, airline, rental car manufacturer, or payment provider.

Report the fake QR code to the business, parking authority, hotel, airport, or local authority so they can remove it.

A QR code may be suspicious if it looks like a sticker placed over another code, has peeling edges, opens a strange URL, uses a shortened link, creates urgency, asks for information that does not make sense, or directs you away from the official website or app.

Sources indicate that at a restaurant, a QR menu should not need your passport or banking password. At a parking meter, the payment page should match the city or parking authority. At a hotel, a check-in code should not send you to a random payment page outside the official booking system.

The BBB has also warned consumers to double-check QR codes before paying for parking.

It has been revealed that no. QR codes are part of modern travel, and many are perfectly safe.

According to recent reports, the goal is not to panic every time you see one. The goal is to stop treating every QR code as automatically trustworthy.

A few seconds of inspection can protect you from a much longer financial or account-recovery problem later.

QR codes are convenient, but convenience is exactly what scammers are using against travellers.

Before scanning a public QR code at a restaurant, parking meter, hotel, airport, train station, attraction, or transit stop, remember the rule:.

Sources indicate that inspect the code. Read the link. Go directly to the official website or app when money, passwords, or personal information are involved.

That tiny pause may be the thing that saves your trip.

It has been revealed that scanning a QR code is not automatically dangerous. The danger usually begins when you open a suspicious page, enter payment details, type a password, download a file, or provide personal information without checking whether the site is legitimate.

Inspect the physical code for stickers, raised edges, bubbles, peeling corners, or anything placed over another code. Then check the URL preview before opening the page. If the link looks strange or does not match the official company, city, hotel, or attraction, do not use it.

Before entering payment information, make sure the website belongs to the official business or authority. When in doubt, use the official app, type the website manually, pay directly at the machine, or ask staff for the correct payment method.

Contact your bank or card issuer immediately using the official number on the back of your card or your banking app. Watch for suspicious charges, replace the card if needed, and do not use any contact information from the suspicious website.

At Our Annual Points of View Summit, Experts Make Their 2027 Travel Predictions

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1559 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cntraveler

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • When planning our 2026 Points of View Summit, we wanted to be sure to set time aside to hear directly from our travel specialists—the behind-the-scenes experts who work tirelessly work to curate ambitious and deeply personal itineraries around the world.
  • Jim Berkeley, founder and CEO of Destinations and Adventures International, speaks on culinary moments.
  • Inspired by Hilton Head Island's rich tapestry of culinary traditions, senior features editor Megan Spurrell and editorial assistant Skyli Alvarez led a discussion on traveling for taste—from the rising interest in foraging over traditional cooking classes to the draw of big-name chefs contrasted with harder-to-find local gems, and the hotspots that deserve to be on our food maps.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When planning our 2026 Points of View Summit, we wanted to be sure to set time aside to hear directly from our travel specialists—the behind-the-scenes experts who work tirelessly work to curate ambitious and deeply personal itineraries around the world. Spliced between compelling panels on Lowcountry heritage, summer travel trends, and the evolving appeal of all-inclusive stays, the breakouts allowed for extended discussions with Traveler editors on a range of themes. From culinary experiences inspired by Hilton Head Island's Gullah cuisine, to the evolving dynamics of multigenerational travel and a new guard of ultra-luxe globetrotters, we got the inside scoop on where travelers are going and how they're getting there.

Jim Berkeley, founder and CEO of Destinations and Adventures International, speaks on culinary moments.

Inspired by Hilton Head Island's rich tapestry of culinary traditions, senior features editor Megan Spurrell and editorial assistant Skyli Alvarez led a discussion on traveling for taste—from the rising interest in foraging over traditional cooking classes to the draw of big-name chefs contrasted with harder-to-find local gems, and the hotspots that deserve to be on our food maps.

Recent findings suggest that our specialists all agreed that travelers yearn for “authentic” food moments, though defining authenticity—and actually finding it—often becomes tricky. To Omolola Campbell, sixth-gen Gullah descendant and executive producer of Gullah short documentary The Spirit We Move With, it's about who provides the experience. “Taking a cooking class is much different than getting it from a local chef who can tell stories about why a dish means so much to this locality,” she said, explaining how so many of South Carolina's Gullah dishes contain okra because its seeds were sown into the hair of West Africans who were brought to the South for slavery. The plant has come to represent resilience, and it's that integral context, according to her, that gives a meal its soul. “That's how you differentiate the person who really knows why they're cooking what they're cooking,” Campbell concluded.

Dana Kravis, Madison Flager, and our travel specialists explore multigenerational travel trends.

Sources indicate that when it comes to multigenerational trips, the grandchildren are choosing the destinations and the grandparents are paying—it's their way of leaving a legacy amongst those dearest to them. During a discussion led by global executive director of video Dana Kravis and commerce director Madison Flager, our travel specialists observed that, because people today tend to wait longer to have children, grandparents are older than they used to be. Travelers in their 80s and 90s are increasingly joining trips, shifting the multigenerational travel dynamic away from the traditional picture of grandparents in their 70s. To trip designers, this means there must be layers of options catering to different activity and exertion levels.

In a recent development, many in this session agreed the most successful family trips provide opportunities for separating and coming back together. Three itinerary choices in one day are ideal, so younger folks can be out and about, with the whole family reuniting for mealtimes and perhaps an afternoon activity. Boat and yacht experiences were especially recommended as spaces where the family is forced to be together—grandkids cannot simply run off and do their own thing.

What's luxury to one traveler might seem the furthest from it to another; some long for jam-packed, once-in-a-lifetime itineraries, while others want total disconnection and the privilege to do absolutely nothing for a week. Features director Rebecca Misner and commerce writer Jessica Sulima led this breakout, as specialists debated the definition of luxury itself. “Luxury is being able to pass on meaning to kids [and] exposing families to the broader world and its cultures,” Virgi Schiffino Kennedy, managing partner at Lux Voyage, said of its intangible appeal. To Ruchi Harnal, founder of Harnal Travel, true luxury “is not about the resort or the villa but the personalization of the trip.” As for who’s spending money on trips? Thomas Robinson, MR at Dehouche, has observed that Gen Z and Millennials are more inclined to spend but want to know where that money goes. Additionally, the specialists largely agreed they’re seeing a shift away from parents taking their children on trips, and towards 30- and 40-somethings treating their parents to a vacation. In Harnal's experience, milestone birthdays and anniversaries are driving clients to book a trip.

Between rising temperatures and overtourism, our specialists discuss the factors impacting European summer destinations.

Industry observers note that what is the impact of overtourism, price inflation, and rising temperatures on our Euro summers? Director of special projects Lale Arikoglu and commerce editor Meaghan Kenny opened the floor for our specialists. “If you’re thinking of traveling to the Dolomites, consider Switzerland instead. There’s history and beautiful scenery with fewer crowds,” Brian Dore, owner of CIU Travel, noted. For the hiking curious, some added that Switzerland offers plenty of one-day hiking trails or “soft adventure” travel—three-to-four days combined with a lake or city destination. Others agreed that traveling to the Alps offers a significant advantage—higher elevations means cooler temperatures—and that Slovenia is a great alternative to Italy. To dodge the crowds, travelers might also consider Belgium, Denmark, or Norway (where ocean ships and river cruises are opening earlier in March). For families, consider Umbria (hot tip: plenty of festival and craft opportunities for kids), Austria, Ireland, or Croatia.

It has been revealed that for those who want to stick with more tried-and-tested European itineraries next summer, consider going as early as possible, for instance, in May instead of August. When it comes to traveling to France specifically, folks advised flying into Paris or Nice, then venturing out to the countryside or oft-overlooked Atlantic Coast. And our specialists could not stress it enough: Always, always check the temperatures in advance of your trip.

As discussed by Mei Zhang, chairman and founder at WildChina, during the panel on summer travel, the demand for travel to Asia is only increasing. Global features director Erin Florio and editorial assistant Kat Chen continued the conversation with travel specialists on the destinations and experiences driving this growth. For Silk Road Treasure Tours president Zulya Rajabova and her clients, it's the destinations with indispensable craft identities, such as Samarkand in Uzbekistan with its millennia-old design traditions, that make the continent so varied yet distinct. Meanwhile, Marigold Wood, travel designer at Blonde Atlas, explained that she's been recommending routes going through China, such as Yunnan's tea trails, which offer trekking and hiking opportunities. For Ethan Crowley, lead trip designer at Asia Desk Ltd, educating his travelers on navigating countries like Cambodia, beyond their most-visited landmarks, is key.

If 2026 was the year of the fan, 2027 is ushering in even more reasons to travel for entertainment. Associate editor Charlie Hobbs and commerce writer Jessica Chapel helmed this breakout on the sporting events, music festivals, and art fairs that specialists are seeing people travel for (and the subsequent hurdles they must overcome to). From Pink at the Sphere, where access requires a Venetian hotel package to the Ryder Cup at Adare Manor, where full-house and package buyouts, high-demand events are increasingly forcing bundled purchases.

The specialists also highlighted how limited legal protections in the States enables extreme ticket scalping for stadium concerts and makes domestic events increasingly unaffordable. Stephanie Malakie, founder of Empress Travel Club pointed to a related challenge: With so many events and providers, travel advisors find it hard to filter the options and identify the right fit for clients. Rather than just acquiring a ticket, specialists agreed the focus should be on curating the surrounding experience or tapping into evergreen and niche experiential travel, with events like the Jets playing in London or F1 in Shanghai. Cultural milestones like Vatican City trips featuring Papal Blessings or European Christmas markets pair well with entertainment, too. To Zhang, set-jetting to filming locations also offers value, minus the headache of peak-event ticketing.

Hannah Towey co-leads the breakout session on outdoor travel.

Everyone is hiking, or so it seems. Helmed by Jamie Spain, travel bookings commerce editor, and Hannah Towey, news editor, this breakout explored nature as wellness and why it is we're increasingly longing for all things outdoorsy. However, our specialists offered a frank reality check on our dumbphone fantasies. “Guests all want to have access [to Wi-Fi] for emergency reasons at a minimum… I don’t have a single guest who wants to [fully] digital detox," Kate Doty, trip designer at Geographic Expeditions, said. It seems that many travelers want to be disconnected until the time comes for true disconnection, and Lou Lagrange, trip consultant at Luxury Travel Advisor, added, “Even planning for national park trips, [you have to] warn them there won’t be Wi-Fi.” However, the group observed that services such as having photographers on small ships, helps reduce a traveler's dependency on their phones.

There's still a real demand for glamping, as guests want access to nature but with a side of luxury. And when it comes to extreme weather events, instead of having travelers write off entire regions or countries, Doty has figured out collaborative ways to shelve them for potential future trips. In Travel Studio founder Kerri Lisa's case, it's a matter of reframing the perks of a destination and its seasons; the rainy season, for example, might be exceptionally lush and green. There's always something to be learned in welcoming a bit of playful unpredictability into our itineraries.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that if you’re a digital nomad or a location-independent business owner, you’re either overpaying for fragmented insurance coverage (travel, medical, etc.) or just badly underinsured.
  • Recent findings suggest that the travel insurance organization Safety Wing is looking to change that.
  • I use their travel insurance all the time and they have just debuted what they call Nomad Citizen that seeks to address the gaps in coverage.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that if you’re a digital nomad or a location-independent business owner, you’re either overpaying for fragmented insurance coverage (travel, medical, etc.) or just badly underinsured. You have a health plan, travel insurance, and maybe some medical evacuation coverage. But, when you work for yourself, you lack the kind of safety net protections you get with a corporate job. And you cannot use a country’s social safety net because, well, you’re not a citizen, right? You’re just roaming the world!

Recent findings suggest that the travel insurance organization Safety Wing is looking to change that. They have always wanted to create this all-in-one package for digital nomads that includes insurance, employee benefits, and a social safety net.

I use their travel insurance all the time and they have just debuted what they call Nomad Citizen that seeks to address the gaps in coverage.

Nomad Citizen is an annual membership that bundles health coverage, travel protection, income protection, and life insurance benefits into a single strategy. It’s for location-independent entrepreneurs and business owners who spend more than half the year outside their home country and whose lives and income cross borders as a default.

Nomad Citizen covers you globally with no residency restrictions (except for Puerto Rico).

It has been revealed that but who should sign-up? This is an interesting product. I definitely think there’s a niche for it. After all, let’s say you’re an entrepreneur in Bali and don’t have access to any social safety net. What happens if you get sick or really hurt and you’re out of work? A friend of mine in Mexico was hit by a car and severely hospitalized and ate into his travel insurance limits really swiftly. Afterwards, he couldn’t work for months while he was in rehab and started a GoFundMe for help. A product like Nomadic Citizen would have helped him. Or helped any of the other digital nomads who get injured on the road and have to raise funds.

I think this product is good for someone who is living in a country outside their own without access to social services and a robust social safety net. For example, if you live in Sweden and have access to all the benefits of the State, this product probably isn’t for you because they have tons of services but if you live in Thailand, Mexico, Indonesia, or France but don’t have access to benefits, or are just roaming the world, have a high income, work on your own, or have a family, then this product would be something to consider.

It has been revealed that for those signing up on or after July 1, 2026, the Nomad Citizen membership costs $443 per month for those 18 to 39. If you’re 40 – 49, it’s $665 per month, and $875 per month for 50-55. Children cost $143 per month (couples on the proposal can add their first child under 10 at no cost). You can pay monthly or annually.

A note about US coverage: Nomad Citizen is truly worldwide, including the US, although it should be noted that coverage limits were not designed for extensive use there…because well, the US health care system is just a mess.

In a recent development, income protection: The income protection benefit is probably the single most compelling reason Nomad Citizen exists. Traditional income protection or disability insurance requires a fixed employer, a permanent address, and residency in a specific country. Freelancers and sole traders working across borders are essentially uninsurable for income loss through conventional schemes, such as government assistance.

If you’re a freelancer or remote worker and you lose your income (you’re laid off, your contracts dry up, or you can’t work due to a medical condition), Nomad Citizen pays you up to $4,000 per month for up to 3 or 6 months while you get back on your feet. That benefit doesn’t exist anywhere else!

It has been revealed that health insurance: Up to $1.5 million in annual coverage for inpatient, outpatient, prescriptions, dental, vision, mental health, maternity, preventive care, wellness therapies, and more. This is just like health insurance where you live and covers everything you need. It is far more robust than regular travel insurance, which is only there for emergencies.

Travel coverage: Trip delays, cancellations, stolen electronics, lost luggage, evacuation, robbery, family visits during hospitalisation.

Sources indicate that parental leave: If you have a baby or become a legal guardian of a child, they pay US$4,000/month so you can take time off work without worrying about money. There is a waiting period of 3 years to access this benefit.

Long-term disability: If something really serious happens to you and you are permanently forced to stop working because, for instance,  you lose your eyesight, you’re diagnosed with cancer, you have a major stroke, or you can no longer do basic things like walk, dress yourself, or eat on your own, they pay you US$4,000/month up to age 75.

Visa assistance: Members can browse and apply for different governments’ versions of long-term visas designed for nomads (i.e. they can work on those visas) directly through our app interface without having to apply through the government websites. They handle all the direct communication with the government and quality check your application before submission to maximize the chances of approval.

Nomad Care Map: Find the best providers through their member-powered database of more than 4000 healthcare providers all over the world, with ratings for service and English level.

Recent findings suggest that payment cards: Use your SafetyWing card to pay for covered services up to $500. This auto-generates a claim that has already been paid so you do not have to wait for reimbursement. The SafetyWing card is a worldwide prepaid debit card that is sent to every Nomad Citizen member, which they can use to pay for doctor’s appointments or prescriptions without using their own money.

24/7 human support: You’ll have access to 24/7 live chat so you can get an answer from a real person within a few minutes.

Everything in one app: Claims, coverage details, customer care, provider search with Nomad Care Map, and visa assistance are all managed through a single app. There is no need to switch between a health insurer, a travel insurer, and a separate income protection provider (if one existed).

Sources indicate that for health coverage, you either pay out of pocket and file for reimbursement or contact the 24/7 team to arrange direct payment with the provider. For travel claims, you collect documentation (police reports, carrier delay notices, receipts) and submit a claim. For income protection, you work with SafetyWing to verify the loss and provide evidence that you’re actively seeking new income. Everything is managed through one app and they make it really simple and easy to do.

It has been revealed that I love SafetyWing’s mission and use their travel insurance on all my trips. This new Nomad Citizen product is perfect for people who are full-time digital nomads and want some sort of income protection as well as more robust health and travel coverage and the kind of social safety programs you would get if you lived in one place. After all, when you are a solopreneur, you do worry about what happens if you get injured, can’t work, or have a kid. It’s all on you, right? Nomad Citizen is the program that ensures that you won’t have to worry about this kind of stuff anymore.

How I Travel: Audra McDonald Needs a Humidifier in Her Hotel Room

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that theater legend Audra McDonald possesses one of the most powerful, lauded voices of her generation, a soprano so stunning that she’s been nominated for more Tony Awards than any other performer in history.
  • While her role in the period drama The Gilded Age doesn’t require singing—yet!—McDonald and the many Broadway legends in the cast released a holiday album this month, ‘Voices of the Gilded Age: The Christmas Album,’ and the fourth season is at the moment airing on HBO.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that theater legend Audra McDonald possesses one of the most powerful, lauded voices of her generation, a soprano so stunning that she’s been nominated for more Tony Awards than any other performer in history. So what elixirs, potions, and special teas does she keep with her to ensure the quality of her voice as she travels the world to sing? “I mask up on planes. I’m traveling all over the country to do concerts; I can’t land and be sick,” she says. “And I try to make sure there's a humidifier in the hotel room. Those are the two main things.”.

While her role in the period drama The Gilded Age doesn’t require singing—yet!—McDonald and the many Broadway legends in the cast released a holiday album this month, ‘Voices of the Gilded Age: The Christmas Album,’ and the fourth season is at the moment airing on HBO. She spoke with Condé Nast Traveler from Australia, where her husband Will Swenson is currently starring in the Oz production of A Beautiful Noise: The Neil Diamond Musical, about traveling with their 10-year-old daughter, the unspeakable glories of New Zealand, and why you simply can’t top New York City in the final months of the year.

The world’s best city for the holidays:.

According to recent reports, I don't think you can beat New York City. I've lived there for 36 years and it's always such a beautiful time. We have dear friends with a kid around my youngest child's age, and we've been going to the holiday spectacular at Radio City. My sister makes sure that she takes my daughters to The Nutcracker every year at City Ballet. We always try to go see the tree at Rockefeller Center. The one day I don't like in New York City during the holidays is Santa Con, but other than that, I'm down.

Her favorite venue on Earth in which to perform:.

There's something about Carnegie Hall [in Manhattan] that is magic. I last sang at Carnegie Hall about six, seven months ago—I'm on the board there now, as well—and the nerves I normally get [before a performance] are always tenfold when I'm getting ready there.

Then the minute I step out on that stage, the hall just gives you a hug that notes, You're here to do what you're supposed to do. You're supposed to make music, you're supposed to celebrate music, you're supposed to commune with your audience, and glorious sounds are supposed to be heard. Carnegie Hall is built for all the sound to be glorious. That [venue] takes care of me.

Her advice for traveling with kids:.

Don't worry about how they act up on a plane. Do what you can, but it's not the flight attendants’ first time at the rodeo. You're never going to see any of these other people again. When we flew out to Australia, my daughter got some weird stomach bug that started the minute they shut the door, and she vomited for the first eight hours of that 15-hour flight. The flight attendants just kept bringing bags and stuff and were like… [mimes a blasé hand gesture]. There was nothing we could do! We were over the ocean. I was giving myself grace. I was giving my poor daughter grace. I just wanted her to feel better, and I was doing the best I could. That’s what I would say to other parents. They’ve seen it all, so don’t worry about what other people are thinking. Everybody has headphones now! We’re fine!

How she spends her flight time:.

I am not preparing for work! That's the ADHD in me. I am also not sleeping because I cannot sleep on planes very well, unless I'm really knocked out with the help of sleeping pills or something, and I don't like to do that. I try to watch movies, but I'm not good at it, either. My dad was killed in a plane crash about 20 years ago, so normally what I'm doing on a plane—when I'm not taking care of my daughter vomiting—is watching the flight path and seeing where we are in the sky. Then, if there's Wi-Fi, I check to see the weather ahead. Like I'm helping! I don't know what I'm doing, but it calms me down to be like, “Okay, I see that there is weather up ahead, so I should expect that it's probably going to be bumpy.” I don't know if in my mind, I'm thinking [as if] I can warn the pilot. I’ve got to go to therapy, but that's what I do on a plane.

The best vacation she’s ever taken:.

New Zealand, holy wow. My husband and I were asked to sing on a Playbill cruise in Tahiti. We flew to Tahiti with our two daughters, and then I had three and a half weeks off before I started my Australian tour, so we went to New Zealand. I'm going to get emotional talking about it. Every place we visited—the North Island, the South Island, Queenstown, Rotorua, Hahei Beach, the Southern Alps, Christchurch, Wellington—all of it was just one wow after another. The people were lovely. We went to Hobbiton. We drove everywhere, and every second of it was mind-blowing. We even did the mailboat, where you go with this guy on a boat to deliver the mail in an area you can only access by water. I want to go back!

The destination she swears she loved before everyone else:.

When we first start going, I wasn’t hearing about a lot of people there, but now everybody goes to Portugal. We have friends who live there, so we started visiting a lot, and not just Lisbon or the Algarve or Porto, though we love Porto. It was also the beautiful countryside and hills and tiny little villages. The topography there is stunning. It’s getting more expensive now, but we used to get incredible bottles of wine for €3! In fact, we have a farm there now, we love it so much.

The hotel amenity she always checks for:.

Toothbrush and toothpaste. Not every hotel provides that, and I just love it when they do. If they've got a toothbrush and toothpaste in there, they've probably gotten a lot of the other amenities right too.

The farthest flung place she’s ever been recognized:.

Here in Australia. I was in the South Melbourne neighborhood we've been living in, and I went into a little bookstore near my daughter's school, and someone recognized me. They remarked, “Were you the one who recorded Emily Wilson's translation of The Iliad book on tape? I loved your work in that.” And I was like, “Whoa, what? Yes I did, wow, thank you.” Doing The Iliad on tape almost killed me. It was the hardest thing I've ever done, so the fact that she wanted to thank me for it? I don’t think my mom knows I did that!

I really want to take a trip to Africa. Obviously, I want to go to Ghana and see where our journey started. I want to go to Kenya and do a safari. I want to go on a trek to see the gorillas. I've been to Egypt, to Cairo, but that's the only time I've been to Africa. I want to wait a couple more years, until my daughter's about 13, and then I will take her. That's going to be our trip.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, this week, Virgin Atlantic celebrates 25 years of flying to India.
  • On the sidelines of the IATA Annual General Meeting, basically the UN General Assembly of airlines, the newly introduced strategic partnership for India was unveiled with very interesting nods to the future.
  • IndiGo carries more passengers in India than anyone else and will connect US and UK/European customers flying Virgin, Delta and Air France KLM onward in India, while also helping fill seats for these European and North American partners, as their own customers head West.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, this week, Virgin Atlantic celebrates 25 years of flying to India. In Virgin fashion, it’s doing so in style, with a joint announcement among partners Delta Airlines, Air France-KLM, and a new strategic partner IndiGo.

On the sidelines of the IATA Annual General Meeting, basically the UN General Assembly of airlines, the newly introduced strategic partnership for India was unveiled with very interesting nods to the future.

IndiGo carries more passengers in India than anyone else and will connect US and UK/European customers flying Virgin, Delta and Air France KLM onward in India, while also helping fill seats for these European and North American partners, as their own customers head West.

That’s probably a good thing, because with recent service additions, Virgin now flies a million seats a year to India and it sounds like others are piling on more flights too. It’s now one of the largest operators to India.

Recent findings suggest that I’ve been bullish on India as the next great center of the world for a while now. It’s not necessarily that I’m at all intelligent, it’s just based on the fact that India is the world’s largest population. But, when Ed Bastian, Delta’s formidable CEO says it, people tend to listen. Bastian mentioned India being the most notable aviation market globally now and signaled a return of direct services for the carrier as well.

Recent findings suggest that virgin has been a small step ahead, adding service regularly on their Delhi, Mumbai and Bangalore routes. IndiGo chose this alliance over formidable competition and this will certainly be a space to watch as more global airlines and alliances focus on India.

Geo-political activity points to India becoming a new manufacturing super power, in addition to its prolific work in tech, IT and customer service, not to mention blossoming tourism. These kind of globally connected businesses are big business, huge in fact, for corporate contracts and easy onward connectivity to regional sites is essential. The partnership makes sense.

In a somewhat rare and impressive signal of unity and seriousness towards India, Virgin Atlantic made their India crews part of the core Virgin family, rather than as contractors through a third party local company, known in aviation world as a GSA. This means Virgin’s India crews are a part of the full team, with benefits too.

When asked about loyalty implications of the new alliance, Virgin Atlantic CEO, Shai Weiss, noted a mutual passion for using loyalty to enhance guest experience far beyond just the earn and burn of points and miles. For future iterations, they’ve offered the following….

The MoU (memorandum of understanding) also creates a framework for deeper collaboration between the carriers on a bilateral and multilateral basis; contemplates commercial collaboration including network, loyalty, cargo and sales, subject to regulatory approvals; explores areas of non-commercial cooperation including aircraft maintenance, sustainability, training, ground handling; and acknowledges the need to develop advanced collaboration through use of technology to efficiently service joint customers.

IndiGo will provide onward connectivity for Virgin and the other strategic partners to 32 destinations, making it easier than ever to see Udaipur, Jaipur, Mumbai, Kashmir and delights further south in Bangalore and Goa.

I just returned from the lovely Leela Palace in Delhi, as I watched the news happen live.

According to recent reports, to me, India is a country of joy. Even people with truly nothing seem to find positivity and it’s generally a way of life here. Hospitality is as warm and steeped in tradition as it comes, too. It’s hot, it’s humid, but it’s an experience unlike any other and that’s something that’s harder to say these days than I’d like.

It has been revealed that the food, ugh. I adore. Sure, I’ll take a dosa from the South over a heavy curry from the North most days, but I love both and if you don’t love a good black daahl there’s something wrong with you.

In short, it’s already fairly easy to get to India but it’s about to get a whole lot easier and not just to hub cities too. More seats means more chances to use points, by the way!

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, former Maine Gov. Paul LePage, fifth from right, joins incoming members Thursday for their freshman class photo on the House steps outside the Capitol. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

Paul LePage, the former Maine governor who once stated he was “Donald Trump before Donald Trump,” is heading to Congress.

In a recent development, the Associated Press called the race for the open 2nd District on Thursday after the Maine Secretary of State’s office tabulated the votes under the state’s ranked choice voting system. LePage ended up ahead of Democratic state Auditor Matt Dunlap 50.8 percent to 49.2 percent.

In a recent development, dunlap had already conceded the race to LePage, who will succeed retiring Democratic Rep. Jared Golden in the sprawling district, which includes much of Maine outside the Portland and Augusta areas.

“Paul LePage is already hard at work for the people of Maine attending Congressional orientation, meeting with national leaders, and making it clear the political parties need to work together for the American people,” Brent Littlefield, a senior adviser to LePage, stated in a statement Thursday. “As Paul said, he will work with anyone, regardless of Party, to put Maine first.”.

Industry observers note that lePage’s win is a glimmer of good news for Republicans, who saw massive losses across the country in last week’s midterm elections. He is one of three Republicans, along with Texas’ Jace Yarbrough and Tennessee’s Brent Taylor, to have flipped a House seat, although Maine’s 2nd District is the only one of the three that wasn’t redrawn to favor the GOP.

According to recent reports, lePage’s win also means that at least one Republican will continue to represent New England in Congress, taking up the mantle from Maine Sen. Susan Collins, who lost her own reelection bid last week.

Industry observers note that golden, who was first elected in 2018, had been a top Republican target throughout his time in Congress. But the lawmaker, known for bucking his party, proved difficult to unseat in the past two election cycles.

“I also know a thing or two about winning in tough circumstances. So, I know you have to tip your hat to Paul LePage for winning in the midst of this Blue Tsunami,” Golden noted in a social media post last week.

In a recent development, dunlap initially launched his campaign as a primary challenge to Golden in the fall of 2025, only for the congressman to announce his retirement a month later. Dunlap went on to win a four-way contest for the Democratic nomination.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, lufthansa is finally adding proper business class recliners to a small portion of its Airbus A320 fleet.
  • Lufthansa has opened bookings for its newly introduced “Premium Business Seat,” which will initially be installed on six Airbus A320ceo aircraft.
  • Each aircraft will receive eight recliners in the first two rows, arranged 2-2.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, lufthansa is finally adding proper business class recliners to a small portion of its Airbus A320 fleet. The new seats will cost extra, even for passengers already booked in business class, but I welcome the option. After years of selling an economy seat with a blocked middle as business class, this is an upgrade worth getting excited about. It is a welcome change for an airline more accustomed to following competitors than setting the standard.

Lufthansa has opened bookings for its newly introduced “Premium Business Seat,” which will initially be installed on six Airbus A320ceo aircraft.

Each aircraft will receive eight recliners in the first two rows, arranged 2-2. Features include:.

The six aircraft will also receive Starlink Wi-Fi during the retrofit.

These are recliners rather than flat beds, but they will represent a substantial improvement over the standard European business class seat, particularly on longer flights, which for those unaware is simply a regular economy class seat with the adjacent seat blocked.

The first modified aircraft is scheduled to enter service on December 16, 2026, initially operating various routes.

Dedicated deployment begins in February 2027, with seat reservations now available for flights from March 1, 2027:.

Look for the Premium Business Seat designation when booking:.

Notice all three routes are leisure?

Lufthansa is retaining its standard business class offering behind the recliners. Business class passengers can select the larger seat during booking or subsequently through seat reservations, subject to the buy-up price: buying business class will not automatically get you a business class recliner on these routes.

I can already hear the objections: passengers are paying a premium for business class and then being asked to pay again for a better seat. But this is quite different than what intra-Europe business class has been for as long as I can remember on Lufthansa (except for the old A300s) and I would still rather have this option than continue with the blocked-middle arrangement as the only choice.

Lufthansa calls this a “commercial test.” Demand and the response to its booking options will determine whether the concept expands, but I think this concept is going to do great.

In a recent development, I wrote about the Eurowings Premium BIZ concept when it was announced last year. It was rather amusing that the budget carrier would introduce proper narrowbody business class seating before its “full service” Lufthansa Group siblings.

It has been revealed that that project was intended to test the concept for other airlines within the group. Now we are seeing a similar approach at Lufthansa itself. The conventional European model has an operational advantage: airlines can move the curtain to adjust the size of business class. Dedicated recliners make that space less flexible.

Industry observers note that installing a small permanent cabin while retaining conventional business class behind it strikes me as a reasonable compromise. Lufthansa can sell the larger seats to passengers willing to pay for them and still expand the rest of business class when demand warrants. I would particularly like to see this spread to longer routes across the group. An empty middle seat is welcome, but it becomes a rather thin comfort proposition when you are spending several hours onboard, especially with those uncomfortable Recaro slimline seats.

One Mile At A Time suggests that Air France should introduce proper business class seats throughout its Airbus A220 fleet. I love that idea…SWISS should do the same.

The A220 offers an especially compelling opportunity because its economy cabin is arranged 2-3. With adjacent seats blocked in business class, Air France sells only three seats per row.

A proper 2-2 business class cabin would allow it to sell four seats across while giving passengers a wider seat. Additional legroom would consume more cabin length, of course, so the calculation is not quite as simple as adding another paying passenger in every existing row, but I think the math would work.

It has been revealed that for illustration, replacing three conventional business class rows with two recliner rows would reduce capacity from nine passengers to eight. That is a modest reduction in exchange for a much better product, though the actual economics would depend on the seat dimensions and final layout.

It has been revealed that I have already experienced what this could look like on my Bulgaria Air A220-300 flight from Sofia to Amsterdam. The airline offered proper recliners in a 2-2 layout, with leg rests and power outlets. I found it an excellent way to spend three hours flying within Europe.

Air France and SWISS have invested heavily in its premium reputation. A small recliner cabin on the A220 would extend that investment to the European flights that often begin or end a longhaul business class journey.

We do not need a flat bed from Paris to Amsterdam or Zurich to London, but on longer European routes, a comfortable recliner would give me another reason to choose one carrier over another.

Lufthansa will install eight Premium Business Seats on each of six Airbus A320s, with bookings now open for select Frankfurt flights to Athens, Nice, and Cairo from March 2027.

The surcharge will bother some passengers, understandably, but I think it makes sense and am pleased to see Lufthansa offer a better seat and hope the test succeeds.

In a recent development, eurowings demonstrated a willingness to try something different. Lufthansa is following. Perhaps Air France, SWISS, and others will see an opportunity too. European business class has room to improve, and a seat that is actually different from economy is a very good place to start.

According to recent reports, president Donald Trump blames Pete Buttigieg for the nationwide FAA meltdown. Elon Musk, meanwhile, is pointing at the tTransportation Secretary Trump appointed, claiming Sean Duffy rejected an offer of free Starlink service. The finger-pointing continues, but neither accusation tells stranded passengers exactly why a router installation brought the system down.

Speaking to reporters on November 16, Trump singled out his predecessor’s transportation secretary for the failure that halted departures across the United States:.

According to recent reports, “Buttigieg ruined the system. He totally ruined it.”.

When asked what personal responsibility he accepted, Trump responded:.

“I don’t take any responsibility.”.

Sources indicate that he also praised Duffy and attributed the disruption to aging equipment. I have already addressed the problem with blaming the previous administration. America’s air traffic control infrastructure has suffered from decades of deferred investment. That includes the Biden administration, but also Trump’s first term and the administrations before it.

In a recent development, friday’s failure, however, occurred during work performed under the current administration. An explanation of what Buttigieg allegedly did wrong would be useful, but of course Buttigieg is just the whipping boy for an administration that demonstrates no personal responsibly for any of its deleterious actions.

It has been revealed that musk has offered a different accusation. In a post on X, he wrote:.

“Free Starlinks for FAA were offered to Sec Duffy, but he noted they were not needed. As it turns out, they were.”.

It has been revealed that free Starlinks for FAA were offered to Sec Duffy, but he noted they were not needed. As it turns out, they were. https://t.co/OZwDeiXOAr.

— Elon Musk (@elonmusk) November 16, 2026.

That is a pointed criticism of the same official Trump says handled the situation well, but Musk does not explain when the offer was made, what equipment or service was included, where it would have been deployed, or how it would have prevented this particular failure…what a surprise.

I would like Duffy to answer the allegation directly. Was there an offer? What did it cover? Why was it declined? If the proposal was unsuitable, explain why.

Sources indicate that musk should also substantiate his assertion that the service would have been needed here. Being able to offer satellite internet does not establish that his proposed “gift” would have kept this particular network operating.

In a recent development, I love Starlink as an airline passenger. It is easily the best inflight internet service available now, and it increasingly influences which flights I book. But that does not mean it is or would have been a solution to an air traffic control network failure.

According to the FAA’s explanation, excessive connection attempts flooded its telecommunications network, destabilizing aircraft communications and radar feeds. Investigators identified sites in El Dorado, Arkansas, and Amarillo, Texas. L3Harris had been working at El Dorado, including installing a new router. Blocking those locations apparently stabilized the network. The broadcasting function on the new routers was also disabled as a precaution.

Sources indicate that to support Musk’s claim, we would need to know whether his proposed Starlink connections would have bypassed the affected equipment and preserved the necessary communications. Perhaps Starlink could have provided useful redundancy…but maybe the proposed installation would have had no bearing on this failure.

Buttigieg has defended his record, pointing to improvements in controller staffing, runway safety, and flight cancellations during his tenure.

He also says he debuted the communications modernization project that the current administration is continuing. His response asks for an accounting of the money already authorized and an explanation of why the execution of that work triggered such a widespread failure.

As secretary, I made sure to leave air travel in better condition than when we arrived. We reversed a decade of decline in air traffic controller staffing, drove down runway safety incidents, and when I left office we were experiencing the lowest flight cancellation rates in… https://t.co/68KleIhFEc.

— Pete Buttigieg (@PeteButtigieg) November 16, 2026.

They do not mean Buttigieg’s tenure should escape scrutiny. The January 2023 nationwide ground stop occurred on his watch, and the system still required enormous investment when he left office while his boss prioritized student loan forgiveness and federal mask mandates instead of accelerating infrastructure programs like Air Traffic Control modernization.

Industry observers note that but acknowledging those shortcomings does not relieve the current administration of responsibility for its own decisions. Duffy has been Transportation Secretary for nearly two years. He oversees the department responsible for explaining this failure and should be held accountable for the actions under his watch.

According to recent reports, there is an obvious temptation to enjoy the spectacle: Trump blames Buttigieg while Musk suggests Trump’s own transportation secretary rejected help. I find the contradiction revealing, but passengers deserve something more useful than competing accusations.

The investigation must establish what changed in the network, why that change caused such a widespread disruption, and whether the safeguards surrounding the work were adequate. Congress should examine the Starlink allegation too, if Musk can provide a concrete proposal and evidence supporting his account.

It has been revealed that duffy may have had reasonable grounds to decline whatever Musk offered, but he should be able to articulate them. Likewise, Musk may have identified a missed opportunity, but he should be able to demonstrate his rather glaring accusation.

Recent findings suggest that and Trump should stop treating an investigation as unnecessary because he has already identified a political opponent to blame. The age of the equipment was known. The difficult task was upgrading it while maintaining reliable service. That is the work his administration undertook, and that is the work it must explain to a weary public.

Sources indicate that trump claims Buttigieg ruined the system and accepts no personal responsibility. Musk says Duffy rejected free Starlink service that was needed. Both claims deserve scrutiny and neither establishes the technical cause of Friday’s meltdown.

According to recent reports, I would be far more receptive to an administration that acknowledged a failure during a difficult modernization project and explained how it would improve the process. Instead, we keep receiving accusations, praise for the response, and demands for more money.

The passengers who lost days getting home deserve a candid explanation of what went wrong. So do the taxpayers being asked to fund the repair. Is this really a political matter that should divide us?
